Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 27, verses 1–14 (part 1 of 2):

Al-Qurtubi said: It is Meccan entirely, according to the consensus. Ibn al-Dari's, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Surat al-Naml was revealed at Mecca." Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn al-Zubayr something similar.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿Ta-Sin﴾. The discussion has already passed in detail in the openings of the surahs (fawatih al-suwar, the disjointed letters at the beginnings of surahs). If these letters are the name of the surah, then their place is in the nominative case as a subject (mubtada'), and what follows is its predicate (khabar). It is also permissible that it be the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "This is the name of this surah." If these letters are not the name of the surah, but are recited in the manner of enumeration, then they have no grammatical place (la mahall laha). The demonstrative in His saying "Tilka" (these) refers to the surah itself, since it has been mentioned in summary by its name. The demonstrative is a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is ﴿the verses of the Qur'an﴾, and the sentence is the predicate of the first subject, on the assumption that it is raised by the inception (ibtida'). ﴿And a clear Book﴾: the majority (al-Jumhur) read "Kitab" in the genitive, coordinated with "al-Qur'an," meaning: "These are the verses of the Qur'an and the verses of a clear Book." It may be that what is meant by His saying "wa-Kitab" is the Qur'an itself, in which case it is the coordination of some attributes with others while the referent is one. It may also be that what is meant by "al-Kitab" is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), or the surah itself. Ibn Abi 'Abla read "wa-Kitabun Mubin" with both in the nominative, coordinated with ("ayat"). 

It was said: On this reading, there is an omitted modified noun (mudaf mahdhuf), with the modifier (mudaf ilayhi) standing in its place, meaning: "wa-ayat Kitabin Mubin." Thus the verses are described with two attributes: Qur'anic, indicating that it is recited, along with an indication that it is an Arabic Qur'an that is miraculous; and Kitabi (of the Book), indicating that it is written, along with an indication that it possesses the quality of the revealed books. On this, it is not a case of coordinating one attribute with another while the referent is one. Then he added to the two attributes a third attribute, which is its clarity of meanings for the one who reads it, or it is from (abana) in the sense of (bana), that is, its meaning became manifest and its miraculousness became clear through the eloquence it contains.

The attribute "Qur'aniyya" is placed first here, in view of the priority of the state of being Qur'an over the state of being written. He placed it later in Surat al-Hijr, saying: ﴿Alif-Lam-Ra. These are the verses of the Book and a clear Qur'an﴾ [al-Hijr: 1], in view of its state in which it has come to be, for it is written, and writing is the cause of reading. And Allah knows best.

As for the definiteness of "al-Qur'an" here and the indefiniteness of "Kitab," and the definiteness of "al-Kitab" in Surat al-Hijr and the indefiniteness of "Qur'an," this is because each of the two is suitable for both definiteness and indefiniteness.

﴿A guidance and good tidings for the believers﴾: it is in a place of accusative case as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) from "al-ayat" or from "al-Kitab," meaning: "These are verses that guide and give good tidings." It is permissible that it be in a place of nominative case by inception, meaning: "It is guidance," or the two are two other predicates of "tilka," or the two are two verbal nouns (masdar) in the accusative governed by an implied verb, meaning: "It guides guidance and gives good tidings with good tidings."

Then He described the believers to whom belong the guidance and the good tidings.

He said: ﴿Those who establish the prayer and give the zakat﴾. The relative pronoun is in a place of genitive case, or it is a substitute (badal) or an explanation (bayan), or it is in the accusative for praise, or in the nominative by an implied subject.

What is meant by "the prayer" is the five daily prayers, and what is meant by "the zakat" is the obligatory zakat. The clause ﴿and they, in the Hereafter, they are certain﴾ is in a place of accusative case as a circumstantial qualifier. He repeated the pronoun to indicate exclusivity, meaning: none holds true certainty regarding the Hereafter except these who combine faith with righteous deeds. He made the predicate nominative to indicate renewal at every time and non-cessation.

Then, when He, glory be to Him, mentioned the people of happiness, He mentioned after them the people of misery, saying: ﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾, and they are the disbelievers, meaning: they do not affirm the Resurrection. ﴿We have made their deeds appear pleasing to them﴾. It was said: What is meant is that Allah made their evil deeds appear pleasing to them until they saw them as good.

It was also said: What is meant is that Allah made righteous deeds appear pleasing to them and mentioned to them what they contain of the good of this world and the Hereafter, but they did not accept that.

Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of the verse is: We made their recompense for their disbelief that We made appealing to them what they are engaged in. ﴿So they wander blindly﴾, meaning: they hesitate in it, bewildered, persistently, not guided to any path, nor reaching any reality.

It was said: the meaning of "ya'mahun" is "they persist in transgression."

Qatada said: "they play." As for the meaning of bewilderment, the poet said:

A desert whose edges are in a desert, blind to guidance, the bewildered, the confused.

The demonstrative in His saying "5 ulaika" refers to those mentioned before it, and it is the subject whose predicate is ﴿for them is the evil of the punishment﴾. It was said: in this world, such as killing and captivity. The reason for restricting it to the punishment of this world is His saying: ﴿and in the Hereafter they are the greatest losers﴾, meaning: they are the most severe of people in loss and the greatest in disappointment. Then He, glory be to Him, prepared a beneficial introduction for what He would mention after that of wondrous reports.

He said: ﴿And indeed, you are receiving the Qur'an from the Wise, the All-Knowing﴾, meaning: it is being cast upon you, and you receive it and take it from One of great wisdom and knowledge. It was said: "min ladun" here means "'inda" (with/from).

There are dialects of it, as has passed in Surat al-Kahf.

﴿When Musa said to his family﴾: the adverbial clause is in the accusative, governed by a hidden verb, which is "udhkur" (remember).

Al-Zajjaj said: The position of "idh" is accusative. The meaning: remember when Musa said, i.e., remember his story when he said to his family. What is meant by "his family" is his wife during his journey from Madyan to Egypt, and at that time he had with him only his wife, the daughter of Shu'ayb. So he referred to her with the word "ahl" (family), which indicates plurality, and similar to it is His saying: "Stay here" [Ta-Ha: 10; al-Qasas: 29]. The meaning of ﴿I have perceived a fire﴾ is: I saw it. ﴿I will bring you from it news﴾: the sin indicates the great distance of the fire. ﴿Or I will bring you a burning brand﴾. 'Asim, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read "shihab" with tanwin, while the rest read it as an annexed form (idafa) to "qabas." On the first reading, "qabas" is a substitute for "shihab" or its attribute, since it means "maqbus" (taken from a fire). On the second reading, the annexation is explanatory (li-l-bayan). The meaning on both readings: "I will bring you a flame of fire taken from its source," i.e., taken from its origin.

Al-Zajjaj said: Whoever puts tanwin makes "qabas" an attribute of "shihab." Al-Farra' said: this annexation is like the annexation in their saying "masjid al-jami'" and "salat al-ula," where a thing is annexed to itself because its names differ. 

Al-Nahhas said: It is the annexation of the species to the genus, as when you say "thawb khazz" (a silk garment) and "khatam hadid" (an iron ring).

He said: In other than the Qur'an, it is permissible to say "bi-shihabin qabasan" as an accusative masdar, or as an explanation, or as a circumstantial qualifier.

﴿So that you may warm yourselves﴾: meaning, hopefully you may warm yourselves by it, or in order that you may warm yourselves from the cold. It is said: "sala bi-l-nar" and "istala biha" when one warms oneself by it.

Al-Zajjaj said: Every white thing with light is a shihab.

Abu 'Ubayda said: The shihab is fire, and from it is the saying of Abu al-Najm:

As if it had been a blazing shihab, which shone with light, then became extinguished.

Tha'lab said: The origin of the shihab is a stick with a live coal at one end while the other end has no fire. The shihab is a shining ray. It was also said: a star is called a shihab, and from it is the poet's saying:

In his hand is a straight, well-formed spear, in which is a point like the flame of a brand.

﴿Then when he came to it﴾: i.e., when Musa came to the fire, ﴿he was called: Blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it﴾. ("An") is the explanatory particle for what is in the calling of meaning "saying," or it is the verbal ("an") meaning "that blessed is." It was said: it is the light ("an") of the heavy ("anna").

Al-Zajjaj said: "an" is in the place of accusative, meaning: "saying that..." and it is permissible that it be in the place of nominative as the substitute of what has not been named its agent (na'ib al-fa'il).

The more preferred view is that the deputy agent is a pronoun referring to Musa.

Ubayy, Ibn 'Abbas, and Mujahid read "an buruikati al-nar wa-man hawlaha" [that the fire was blessed and whoever is around it], as narrated by Abu Hatim.

Al-Kisa'i related from the Arabs: "barakaka Allah," "barak Allah fika," "barak 'alayki," and "barak laka," and al-Farra' related the same.

Ibn Jarir said: He said "buruka man fi al-nar" and did not say "buruka 'ala al-nar," according to the dialect of those who say "barakaka Allah," meaning: blessed upon whoever is in the fire, and that is Musa, or upon whoever is near the fire, not that he was in its midst.

Al-Suddi said: There were angels in the fire, and the fire here was merely light, but Musa thought it was fire, and when he reached it he found it to be light.

It is related from al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr that what is meant by "whoever is in the fire" is Allah, glory be to Him, meaning His light.

It was said: blessed is what is in the fire of the command of Allah, glory be to Him, which made it in that state.

Al-Wahidi said: The way of the exegetes is that what is meant by "the fire" is the light. Then He, glory be to Him, declared His own transcendence, saying: ﴿And glory be to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾, and in it is an expression of wonder for Musa at that.

﴿O Musa, indeed I am Allah, the Mighty, the Wise﴾. The pronoun is for the matter (damir al-sha'n), meaning: "It is I, Allah, the Mighty, the Overpowering, the Dominant, the Wise in His command and His action."

It was said: Musa said: "My Lord, who is it who called me?" Then Allah, glory be to Him, answered him with His saying: "Indeed it is I, Allah." Then He, glory be to Him, commanded him to throw down his staff, so that he would know what miracle Allah, glory be to Him, would bring about through his hand.

The clause ﴿And throw down your staff﴾ is coordinated with "buriku" (blessed), and there is an omission in the speech; the estimate is: "So he threw it from his hand, and it became a serpent."

﴿But when he saw it moving as if it were a jann﴾: al-Zajjaj said: The staff began to move as the jann moves, and it is the white serpent. He compared it to the jann in the lightness of its movement, and in another place he compared it to a thu'ban (large serpent) for its size. The plural of "jann" is "jinan," and it is the small, light-bodied serpent. Al-Kalbi said: it was neither small nor large.

﴿He turned back fleeing﴾ from fear, ﴿and did not return﴾: meaning he did not come back. It is said: "'aqqaba fulan" when he returned, and every one who returns is "mu'aqqib." It was also said: he did not stop and did not look back.

The first is preferable, because "ta'qib" is the return after the flight, and when that occurred from him, Allah, glory be to Him, said: ﴿O Musa, do not fear﴾, meaning: of the serpent and its harm. ﴿Indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence﴾, meaning: whoever I have sent with My message does not fear in My presence, so you too do not fear.

It was said: The negation of fear from the messengers is not at all times, but at the time of addressing them, for at that time they are wholly absorbed.

Then He made an exception, a disjunctive exception, saying: ﴿Except for one who has wronged, then substitutes good after evil—indeed, I am Forgiving and Merciful﴾, meaning: but whoever sins in wronging himself through disobedience, ﴿then substitutes good﴾, meaning: repentance and remorse, ﴿after evil﴾, meaning: after an evil deed, ﴿indeed, I am Forgiving and Merciful﴾. It was said: the exception is from an implied omitted element, meaning: "The messengers do not fear in My presence, but others fear, those who have wronged, except one who has wronged, then substituted good after evil, etc." Thus said al-Farra'.

Al-Nahhas said: An exception from an omitted element is impossible, because it is an exception from something that has not been mentioned.

It is related from al-Farra' that he said: "illa" here means "wa" (and).

It was said: The exception is connected to what was mentioned, not to what was omitted.

The meaning: "Except one of the messengers who wronged by committing minor sins from which none is free." Al-Nahhas chose this and said: He knew who among them disobeyed, so He excepted him, saying: "except one who has wronged," even though I have forgiven him, like Adam, David, the brothers of Joseph, and Musa for killing the Copt.

There is no barrier to fear after forgiveness, for our Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, to whom Allah forgave what preceded of his sin and what followed, used to say: "I wish I were a tree that is cut down."

﴿And put your hand into your pocket﴾: the "jayb" here is the well-known (pocket/collar opening). In al-Qasas [28:32] it says: "Insert your hand into your bosom," and in "adkhil" there is an emphasis not found in "usluk." ﴿It will come out white, without harm﴾: meaning, without leprosy or the like of afflictions, so it is a precaution.

His saying "takhruj" is the answer to "adkhil yadaka."

It was said: There is an omission in the speech, its estimate being: "Insert your hand, it will enter, and bring it out, it will come out." There is no need for this omission, nor any compulsion for it.

The exegetes said: Musa wore a woolen cloak with no sleeve and no lower garment, so he inserted his hand into his pocket and brought it out, and behold, it shone like lightning. His saying ﴿among nine signs﴾: Abu al-Baqa' said: it is in a place of accusative as a circumstantial qualifier from the subject of "takhruj," and this is far-fetched. It was said: it is connected to an omitted element, meaning: "Go among nine signs."

It was said that it is connected to His words, "Throw down your staff" and "Put your hand into your bosom," as part of the nine signs, or "together with nine signs."

It was also said that the meaning is: "They are two of nine," namely the staff and the hand. The signs would then be eleven: these two, the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, the obliteration, the drought in their deserts, and the shortfall in their crops.

Al-Nahhas said: "The best that has been said about this is that this verse, meaning the hand, is included among the nine signs." Al-Mahdawi and al-Qushayri said the same.

Al-Qushayri said: "You say, 'I went out with ten men, and you were one of them,' meaning, 'I went out as the tenth of ten.' So *fi* here has the sense of *min* (from), because of its closeness to it, just as you say, 'Take for me ten camels, in which there are two stallions,' meaning, 'from them.'"

Al-Asma'i, concerning the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

*"Will one ever enjoy life again, whose last covenant was thirty months, in three states?"*

Here *fi* means *min* (from). It was also said that *fi* means *ma'a* (with).

﴿To Pharaoh and his people.﴾ Al-Farra' said: "There is an implied element in the speech, meaning: 'You are sent, or dispatched, to Pharaoh and his people.'" Al-Zajjaj said the same.

﴿Indeed, they were a people who were defiantly disobedient.﴾ This clause gives the reason for what precedes it.

﴿So when Our signs came to them, clearly visible.﴾ That is, Our signs that were at the hand of Musa came to them, while being *mubsira*, meaning clear and evident, as if, because of their great clarity, they were making themselves visible. Compare His words: ﴿And We gave Thamud the she-camel as a visible sign﴾ [al-Isra 17:59]. Al-Akhfash said: "It is also possible that *mubsira* means 'making things visible' in the sense that the active participle has the sense of the passive participle (*ism al-mafʿul*). The detailed discussion of this has already been presented."

Ali ibn al-Husayn and Qatada read *mabsara*, with a fatha on the *mim* and the *sad*, meaning a place where much seeing occurs, as one says, "A child is a cause of cowardice (*majbana*) and of stinginess (*mabkhala*)."

﴿They said, "This is obvious magic."﴾ That is, when the signs came to them, they said this statement: that it is clear magic.

﴿And they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them.﴾ That is, they denied them while their souls were certain of them. The *waw* here is for the circumstantial clause (*hal*), and ﴿wrongfully and arrogantly﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state: "as wrongdoers and haughty." It is also possible that both are in the accusative as a cause (*ʿilla*), meaning: "What drove them to that wrongdoing and arrogance." It is also possible that they are an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (*maṣdar*), meaning: "They denied them with a denial that was wrongful and arrogant."

Abu ʿUbayda said: "The *ba'* in ﴿and they denied them﴾ is superfluous, meaning: 'and they denied it.'"

Al-Zajjaj said: "The implied meaning is: 'They denied them wrongfully and arrogantly,' that is, out of polytheism and pride, refusing to believe in what Musa brought, while knowing that it was from Allah."

So observe, O Muhammad, ﴿how was the end of the corrupters?﴾ That is: reflect on this, for in it there is a lesson for those who take heed. Their final fate was that they were drowned in the sea, in that terrifying manner.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His words: ﴿So when he came to it, he was called: "Blessed is whoever is in the fire,"﴾ that is, Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, Himself, was the light of the Lord of the worlds in the tree, ﴿and whoever is around it﴾ meaning the angels.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him concerning the verse: "Allah was in the light; He was called from the light." ﴿And whoever is around it﴾: the angels.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from him also: "Allah called to him while he was in the light."

Al-Firyabi, Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him also, concerning ﴿that blessed is whoever is in the fire﴾: "The fire was blessed."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatada: "In the codex of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb: 'The fire was blessed, and whoever is around it.' As for the fire, they claim that it is the light of the Lord of the worlds."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas: "*Anna buurika*" means: "It was sanctified."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Majah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh in *al-ʿAzama*, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa al-Sifat*, through the chain of Abu ʿUbayda, from Abu Musa al-Ashʿari, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) stood among us and said: "Indeed Allah does not sleep, and it is not fitting for Him to sleep. He lowers the scale and raises it. The deeds of the night are raised to Him before the deeds of the day, and the deeds of the day before the night. His veil is light; if it were removed, the splendors of His face would burn away everything that His sight reaches."

Then Abu ʿUbayda recited: ﴿that blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it, and glory be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾

The hadith is originally recorded in Sahih Muslim from the narration of Amr ibn Murra.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas: "Musa had a woolen cloak that did not reach beyond his elbows. He was told, 'Put your hand into your bosom,' and he did so."

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him concerning His words: ﴿and their souls were convinced of them, wrongfully and arrogantly﴾: "*Takabburan* (arrogance); their souls were convinced of them." This is an instance of *taqdim wa ta'khir* (inversion of word order).

What is meant by "his family" is his wife during his journey from Madyan to Egypt, and at that time he had with him only his wife, the daughter of Shu'ayb. So he referred to her with the word "ahl" (family), which indicates plurality, and similar to it is His saying: "Stay here" [Ta-Ha: 10; al-Qasas: 29]. The meaning of ﴿I have perceived a fire﴾ is: I saw it. ﴿I will bring you from it news﴾: the sin indicates the great distance of the fire. ﴿Or I will bring you a burning brand﴾. 'Asim, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read "shihab" with tanwin, while the rest read it as an annexed form (idafa) to "qabas." On the first reading, "qabas" is a substitute for "shihab" or its attribute, since it means "maqbus" (taken from a fire). On the second reading, the annexation is explanatory (li-l-bayan). The meaning on both readings: "I will bring you a flame of fire taken from its source," i.e., taken from its origin.

Al-Zajjaj said: Whoever puts tanwin makes "qabas" an attribute of "shihab." Al-Farra' said: this annexation is like the annexation in their saying "masjid al-jami'" and "salat al-ula," where a thing is annexed to itself because its names differ. 

Al-Nahhas said: It is the annexation of the species to the genus, as when you say "thawb khazz" (a silk garment) and "khatam hadid" (an iron ring).

He said: In other than the Qur'an, it is permissible to say "bi-shihabin qabasan" as an accusative masdar, or as an explanation, or as a circumstantial qualifier.

﴿So that you may warm yourselves﴾: meaning, hopefully you may warm yourselves by it, or in order that you may warm yourselves from the cold. It is said: "sala bi-l-nar" and "istala biha" when one warms oneself by it.

Al-Zajjaj said: Every white thing with light is a shihab.

Abu 'Ubayda said: The shihab is fire, and from it is the saying of Abu al-Najm:

As if it had been a blazing shihab, which shone with light, then became extinguished.

Tha'lab said: The origin of the shihab is a stick with a live coal at one end while the other end has no fire. The shihab is a shining ray. It was also said: a star is called a shihab, and from it is the poet's saying:

In his hand is a straight, well-formed spear, in which is a point like the flame of a brand.

﴿Then when he came to it﴾: i.e., when Musa came to the fire, ﴿he was called: Blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it﴾. ("An") is the explanatory particle for what is in the calling of meaning "saying," or it is the verbal ("an") meaning "that blessed is." It was said: it is the light ("an") of the heavy ("anna").

Al-Zajjaj said: "an" is in the place of accusative, meaning: "saying that..." and it is permissible that it be in the place of nominative as the substitute of what has not been named its agent (na'ib al-fa'il).

The more preferred view is that the deputy agent is a pronoun referring to Musa.

Ubayy, Ibn 'Abbas, and Mujahid read "an buruikati al-nar wa-man hawlaha" [that the fire was blessed and whoever is around it], as narrated by Abu Hatim.

Al-Kisa'i related from the Arabs: "barakaka Allah," "barak Allah fika," "barak 'alayki," and "barak laka," and al-Farra' related the same.

Ibn Jarir said: He said "buruka man fi al-nar" and did not say "buruka 'ala al-nar," according to the dialect of those who say "barakaka Allah," meaning: blessed upon whoever is in the fire, and that is Musa, or upon whoever is near the fire, not that he was in its midst.

Al-Suddi said: There were angels in the fire, and the fire here was merely light, but Musa thought it was fire, and when he reached it he found it to be light.

It is related from al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr that what is meant by "whoever is in the fire" is Allah, glory be to Him, meaning His light.

It was said: blessed is what is in the fire of the command of Allah, glory be to Him, which made it in that state.

Al-Wahidi said: The way of the exegetes is that what is meant by "the fire" is the light. Then He, glory be to Him, declared His own transcendence, saying: ﴿And glory be to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾, and in it is an expression of wonder for Musa at that.

﴿O Musa, indeed I am Allah, the Mighty, the Wise﴾. The pronoun is for the matter (damir al-sha'n), meaning: "It is I, Allah, the Mighty, the Overpowering, the Dominant, the Wise in His command and His action."

It was said: Musa said: "My Lord, who is it who called me?" Then Allah, glory be to Him, answered him with His saying: "Indeed it is I, Allah." Then He, glory be to Him, commanded him to throw down his staff, so that he would know what miracle Allah, glory be to Him, would bring about through his hand.

The clause ﴿And throw down your staff﴾ is coordinated with "buriku" (blessed), and there is an omission in the speech; the estimate is: "So he threw it from his hand, and it became a serpent."

﴿But when he saw it moving as if it were a jann﴾: al-Zajjaj said: The staff began to move as the jann moves, and it is the white serpent. He compared it to the jann in the lightness of its movement, and in another place he compared it to a thu'ban (large serpent) for its size. The plural of "jann" is "jinan," and it is the small, light-bodied serpent. Al-Kalbi said: it was neither small nor large.

﴿He turned back fleeing﴾ from fear, ﴿and did not return﴾: meaning he did not come back. It is said: "'aqqaba fulan" when he returned, and every one who returns is "mu'aqqib." It was also said: he did not stop and did not look back.

The first is preferable, because "ta'qib" is the return after the flight, and when that occurred from him, Allah, glory be to Him, said: ﴿O Musa, do not fear﴾, meaning: of the serpent and its harm. ﴿Indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence﴾, meaning: whoever I have sent with My message does not fear in My presence, so you too do not fear.

It was said: The negation of fear from the messengers is not at all times, but at the time of addressing them, for at that time they are wholly absorbed.

Then He made an exception, a disjunctive exception, saying: ﴿Except for one who has wronged, then substitutes good after evil—indeed, I am Forgiving and Merciful﴾, meaning: but whoever sins in wronging himself through disobedience, ﴿then substitutes good﴾, meaning: repentance and remorse, ﴿after evil﴾, meaning: after an evil deed, ﴿indeed, I am Forgiving and Merciful﴾. It was said: the exception is from an implied omitted element, meaning: "The messengers do not fear in My presence, but others fear, those who have wronged, except one who has wronged, then substituted good after evil, etc." Thus said al-Farra'.

Al-Nahhas said: An exception from an omitted element is impossible, because it is an exception from something that has not been mentioned.

It is related from al-Farra' that he said: "illa" here means "wa" (and).

It was said: The exception is connected to what was mentioned, not to what was omitted.

The meaning: "Except one of the messengers who wronged by committing minor sins from which none is free." Al-Nahhas chose this and said: He knew who among them disobeyed, so He excepted him, saying: "except one who has wronged," even though I have forgiven him, like Adam, David, the brothers of Joseph, and Musa for killing the Copt.

There is no barrier to fear after forgiveness, for our Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, to whom Allah forgave what preceded of his sin and what followed, used to say: "I wish I were a tree that is cut down."

﴿And put your hand into your pocket﴾: the "jayb" here is the well-known (pocket/collar opening). In al-Qasas [28:32] it says: "Insert your hand into your bosom," and in "adkhil" there is an emphasis not found in "usluk." ﴿It will come out white, without harm﴾: meaning, without leprosy or the like of afflictions, so it is a precaution.

His saying "takhruj" is the answer to "adkhil yadaka."

It was said: There is an omission in the speech, its estimate being: "Insert your hand, it will enter, and bring it out, it will come out." There is no need for this omission, nor any compulsion for it.

The exegetes said: Musa wore a woolen cloak with no sleeve and no lower garment, so he inserted his hand into his pocket and brought it out, and behold, it shone like lightning. His saying ﴿among nine signs﴾: Abu al-Baqa' said: it is in a place of accusative as a circumstantial qualifier from the subject of "takhruj," and this is far-fetched. It was said: it is connected to an omitted element, meaning: "Go among nine signs."

It was said that it is connected to His words, "Throw down your staff" and "Put your hand into your bosom," as part of the nine signs, or "together with nine signs."

It was also said that the meaning is: "They are two of nine," namely the staff and the hand. The signs would then be eleven: these two, the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, the obliteration, the drought in their deserts, and the shortfall in their crops.

Al-Nahhas said: "The best that has been said about this is that this verse, meaning the hand, is included among the nine signs." Al-Mahdawi and al-Qushayri said the same.

Al-Qushayri said: "You say, 'I went out with ten men, and you were one of them,' meaning, 'I went out as the tenth of ten.' So *fi* here has the sense of *min* (from), because of its closeness to it, just as you say, 'Take for me ten camels, in which there are two stallions,' meaning, 'from them.'"

Al-Asma'i, concerning the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

*"Will one ever enjoy life again, whose last covenant was thirty months, in three states?"*

Here *fi* means *min* (from). It was also said that *fi* means *ma'a* (with).

﴿To Pharaoh and his people.﴾ Al-Farra' said: "There is an implied element in the speech, meaning: 'You are sent, or dispatched, to Pharaoh and his people.'" Al-Zajjaj said the same.

﴿Indeed, they were a people who were defiantly disobedient.﴾ This clause gives the reason for what precedes it.

﴿So when Our signs came to them, clearly visible.﴾ That is, Our signs that were at the hand of Musa came to them, while being *mubsira*, meaning clear and evident, as if, because of their great clarity, they were making themselves visible. Compare His words: ﴿And We gave Thamud the she-camel as a visible sign﴾ [al-Isra 17:59]. Al-Akhfash said: "It is also possible that *mubsira* means 'making things visible' in the sense that the active participle has the sense of the passive participle (*ism al-mafʿul*). The detailed discussion of this has already been presented."

Ali ibn al-Husayn and Qatada read *mabsara*, with a fatha on the *mim* and the *sad*, meaning a place where much seeing occurs, as one says, "A child is a cause of cowardice (*majbana*) and of stinginess (*mabkhala*)."

﴿They said, "This is obvious magic."﴾ That is, when the signs came to them, they said this statement: that it is clear magic.

﴿And they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them.﴾ That is, they denied them while their souls were certain of them. The *waw* here is for the circumstantial clause (*hal*), and ﴿wrongfully and arrogantly﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state: "as wrongdoers and haughty." It is also possible that both are in the accusative as a cause (*ʿilla*), meaning: "What drove them to that wrongdoing and arrogance." It is also possible that they are an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (*maṣdar*), meaning: "They denied them with a denial that was wrongful and arrogant."

Abu ʿUbayda said: "The *ba'* in ﴿and they denied them﴾ is superfluous, meaning: 'and they denied it.'"

Al-Zajjaj said: "The implied meaning is: 'They denied them wrongfully and arrogantly,' that is, out of polytheism and pride, refusing to believe in what Musa brought, while knowing that it was from Allah."

So observe, O Muhammad, ﴿how was the end of the corrupters?﴾ That is: reflect on this, for in it there is a lesson for those who take heed. Their final fate was that they were drowned in the sea, in that terrifying manner.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His words: ﴿So when he came to it, he was called: "Blessed is whoever is in the fire,"﴾ that is, Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, Himself, was the light of the Lord of the worlds in the tree, ﴿and whoever is around it﴾ meaning the angels.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him concerning the verse: "Allah was in the light; He was called from the light." ﴿And whoever is around it﴾: the angels.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from him also: "Allah called to him while he was in the light."

Al-Firyabi, Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him also, concerning ﴿that blessed is whoever is in the fire﴾: "The fire was blessed."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatada: "In the codex of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb: 'The fire was blessed, and whoever is around it.' As for the fire, they claim that it is the light of the Lord of the worlds."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas: "*Anna buurika*" means: "It was sanctified."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Majah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh in *al-ʿAzama*, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa al-Sifat*, through the chain of Abu ʿUbayda, from Abu Musa al-Ashʿari, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) stood among us and said: "Indeed Allah does not sleep, and it is not fitting for Him to sleep. He lowers the scale and raises it. The deeds of the night are raised to Him before the deeds of the day, and the deeds of the day before the night. His veil is light; if it were removed, the splendors of His face would burn away everything that His sight reaches."

Then Abu ʿUbayda recited: ﴿that blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it, and glory be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾

The hadith is originally recorded in Sahih Muslim from the narration of Amr ibn Murra.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas: "Musa had a woolen cloak that did not reach beyond his elbows. He was told, 'Put your hand into your bosom,' and he did so."

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him concerning His words: ﴿and their souls were convinced of them, wrongfully and arrogantly﴾: "*Takabburan* (arrogance); their souls were convinced of them." This is an instance of *taqdim wa ta'khir* (inversion of word order).

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 27, verses 1–14 (part 1 of 2):

Al-Qurtubi said: It is Meccan entirely, according to the consensus. Ibn al-Dari's, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Surat al-Naml was revealed at Mecca." Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn al-Zubayr something similar.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿Ta-Sin﴾. The discussion has already passed in detail in the openings of the surahs (fawatih al-suwar, the disjointed letters at the beginnings of surahs). If these letters are the name of the surah, then their place is in the nominative case as a subject (mubtada'), and what follows is its predicate (khabar). It is also permissible that it be the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "This is the name of this surah." If these letters are not the name of the surah, but are recited in the manner of enumeration, then they have no grammatical place (la mahall laha). The demonstrative in His saying "Tilka" (these) refers to the surah itself, since it has been mentioned in summary by its name. The demonstrative is a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is ﴿the verses of the Qur'an﴾, and the sentence is the predicate of the first subject, on the assumption that it is raised by the inception (ibtida'). ﴿And a clear Book﴾: the majority (al-Jumhur) read "Kitab" in the genitive, coordinated with "al-Qur'an," meaning: "These are the verses of the Qur'an and the verses of a clear Book." It may be that what is meant by His saying "wa-Kitab" is the Qur'an itself, in which case it is the coordination of some attributes with others while the referent is one. It may also be that what is meant by "al-Kitab" is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), or the surah itself. Ibn Abi 'Abla read "wa-Kitabun Mubin" with both in the nominative, coordinated with ("ayat"). 

It was said: On this reading, there is an omitted modified noun (mudaf mahdhuf), with the modifier (mudaf ilayhi) standing in its place, meaning: "wa-ayat Kitabin Mubin." Thus the verses are described with two attributes: Qur'anic, indicating that it is recited, along with an indication that it is an Arabic Qur'an that is miraculous; and Kitabi (of the Book), indicating that it is written, along with an indication that it possesses the quality of the revealed books. On this, it is not a case of coordinating one attribute with another while the referent is one. Then he added to the two attributes a third attribute, which is its clarity of meanings for the one who reads it, or it is from (abana) in the sense of (bana), that is, its meaning became manifest and its miraculousness became clear through the eloquence it contains.

The attribute "Qur'aniyya" is placed first here, in view of the priority of the state of being Qur'an over the state of being written. He placed it later in Surat al-Hijr, saying: ﴿Alif-Lam-Ra. These are the verses of the Book and a clear Qur'an﴾ [al-Hijr: 1], in view of its state in which it has come to be, for it is written, and writing is the cause of reading. And Allah knows best.

As for the definiteness of "al-Qur'an" here and the indefiniteness of "Kitab," and the definiteness of "al-Kitab" in Surat al-Hijr and the indefiniteness of "Qur'an," this is because each of the two is suitable for both definiteness and indefiniteness.

﴿A guidance and good tidings for the believers﴾: it is in a place of accusative case as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) from "al-ayat" or from "al-Kitab," meaning: "These are verses that guide and give good tidings." It is permissible that it be in a place of nominative case by inception, meaning: "It is guidance," or the two are two other predicates of "tilka," or the two are two verbal nouns (masdar) in the accusative governed by an implied verb, meaning: "It guides guidance and gives good tidings with good tidings."

Then He described the believers to whom belong the guidance and the good tidings.

He said: ﴿Those who establish the prayer and give the zakat﴾. The relative pronoun is in a place of genitive case, or it is a substitute (badal) or an explanation (bayan), or it is in the accusative for praise, or in the nominative by an implied subject.

What is meant by "the prayer" is the five daily prayers, and what is meant by "the zakat" is the obligatory zakat. The clause ﴿and they, in the Hereafter, they are certain﴾ is in a place of accusative case as a circumstantial qualifier. He repeated the pronoun to indicate exclusivity, meaning: none holds true certainty regarding the Hereafter except these who combine faith with righteous deeds. He made the predicate nominative to indicate renewal at every time and non-cessation.

Then, when He, glory be to Him, mentioned the people of happiness, He mentioned after them the people of misery, saying: ﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾, and they are the disbelievers, meaning: they do not affirm the Resurrection. ﴿We have made their deeds appear pleasing to them﴾. It was said: What is meant is that Allah made their evil deeds appear pleasing to them until they saw them as good.

It was also said: What is meant is that Allah made righteous deeds appear pleasing to them and mentioned to them what they contain of the good of this world and the Hereafter, but they did not accept that.

Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of the verse is: We made their recompense for their disbelief that We made appealing to them what they are engaged in. ﴿So they wander blindly﴾, meaning: they hesitate in it, bewildered, persistently, not guided to any path, nor reaching any reality.

It was said: the meaning of "ya'mahun" is "they persist in transgression."

Qatada said: "they play." As for the meaning of bewilderment, the poet said:

A desert whose edges are in a desert, blind to guidance, the bewildered, the confused.

The demonstrative in His saying "5 ulaika" refers to those mentioned before it, and it is the subject whose predicate is ﴿for them is the evil of the punishment﴾. It was said: in this world, such as killing and captivity. The reason for restricting it to the punishment of this world is His saying: ﴿and in the Hereafter they are the greatest losers﴾, meaning: they are the most severe of people in loss and the greatest in disappointment. Then He, glory be to Him, prepared a beneficial introduction for what He would mention after that of wondrous reports.

He said: ﴿And indeed, you are receiving the Qur'an from the Wise, the All-Knowing﴾, meaning: it is being cast upon you, and you receive it and take it from One of great wisdom and knowledge. It was said: "min ladun" here means "'inda" (with/from).

There are dialects of it, as has passed in Surat al-Kahf.

﴿When Musa said to his family﴾: the adverbial clause is in the accusative, governed by a hidden verb, which is "udhkur" (remember).

Al-Zajjaj said: The position of "idh" is accusative. The meaning: remember when Musa said, i.e., remember his story when he said to his family. What is meant by "his family" is his wife during his journey from Madyan to Egypt, and at that time he had with him only his wife, the daughter of Shu'ayb. So he referred to her with the word "ahl" (family), which indicates plurality, and similar to it is His saying: "Stay here" [Ta-Ha: 10; al-Qasas: 29]. The meaning of ﴿I have perceived a fire﴾ is: I saw it. ﴿I will bring you from it news﴾: the sin indicates the great distance of the fire. ﴿Or I will bring you a burning brand﴾. 'Asim, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read "shihab" with tanwin, while the rest read it as an annexed form (idafa) to "qabas." On the first reading, "qabas" is a substitute for "shihab" or its attribute, since it means "maqbus" (taken from a fire). On the second reading, the annexation is explanatory (li-l-bayan). The meaning on both readings: "I will bring you a flame of fire taken from its source," i.e., taken from its origin.

Al-Zajjaj said: Whoever puts tanwin makes "qabas" an attribute of "shihab." Al-Farra' said: this annexation is like the annexation in their saying "masjid al-jami'" and "salat al-ula," where a thing is annexed to itself because its names differ. 

Al-Nahhas said: It is the annexation of the species to the genus, as when you say "thawb khazz" (a silk garment) and "khatam hadid" (an iron ring).

He said: In other than the Qur'an, it is permissible to say "bi-shihabin qabasan" as an accusative masdar, or as an explanation, or as a circumstantial qualifier.

﴿So that you may warm yourselves﴾: meaning, hopefully you may warm yourselves by it, or in order that you may warm yourselves from the cold. It is said: "sala bi-l-nar" and "istala biha" when one warms oneself by it.

Al-Zajjaj said: Every white thing with light is a shihab.

Abu 'Ubayda said: The shihab is fire, and from it is the saying of Abu al-Najm:

As if it had been a blazing shihab, which shone with light, then became extinguished.

Tha'lab said: The origin of the shihab is a stick with a live coal at one end while the other end has no fire. The shihab is a shining ray. It was also said: a star is called a shihab, and from it is the poet's saying:

In his hand is a straight, well-formed spear, in which is a point like the flame of a brand.

﴿Then when he came to it﴾: i.e., when Musa came to the fire, ﴿he was called: Blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it﴾. ("An") is the explanatory particle for what is in the calling of meaning "saying," or it is the verbal ("an") meaning "that blessed is." It was said: it is the light ("an") of the heavy ("anna").

Al-Zajjaj said: "an" is in the place of accusative, meaning: "saying that..." and it is permissible that it be in the place of nominative as the substitute of what has not been named its agent (na'ib al-fa'il).

The more preferred view is that the deputy agent is a pronoun referring to Musa.

Ubayy, Ibn 'Abbas, and Mujahid read "an buruikati al-nar wa-man hawlaha" [that the fire was blessed and whoever is around it], as narrated by Abu Hatim.

Al-Kisa'i related from the Arabs: "barakaka Allah," "barak Allah fika," "barak 'alayki," and "barak laka," and al-Farra' related the same.

Ibn Jarir said: He said "buruka man fi al-nar" and did not say "buruka 'ala al-nar," according to the dialect of those who say "barakaka Allah," meaning: blessed upon whoever is in the fire, and that is Musa, or upon whoever is near the fire, not that he was in its midst.

Al-Suddi said: There were angels in the fire, and the fire here was merely light, but Musa thought it was fire, and when he reached it he found it to be light.

It is related from al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr that what is meant by "whoever is in the fire" is Allah, glory be to Him, meaning His light.

It was said: blessed is what is in the fire of the command of Allah, glory be to Him, which made it in that state.

Al-Wahidi said: The way of the exegetes is that what is meant by "the fire" is the light. Then He, glory be to Him, declared His own transcendence, saying: ﴿And glory be to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾, and in it is an expression of wonder for Musa at that.

﴿O Musa, indeed I am Allah, the Mighty, the Wise﴾. The pronoun is for the matter (damir al-sha'n), meaning: "It is I, Allah, the Mighty, the Overpowering, the Dominant, the Wise in His command and His action."

It was said: Musa said: "My Lord, who is it who called me?" Then Allah, glory be to Him, answered him with His saying: "Indeed it is I, Allah." Then He, glory be to Him, commanded him to throw down his staff, so that he would know what miracle Allah, glory be to Him, would bring about through his hand.

The clause ﴿And throw down your staff﴾ is coordinated with "buriku" (blessed), and there is an omission in the speech; the estimate is: "So he threw it from his hand, and it became a serpent."

﴿But when he saw it moving as if it were a jann﴾: al-Zajjaj said: The staff began to move as the jann moves, and it is the white serpent. He compared it to the jann in the lightness of its movement, and in another place he compared it to a thu'ban (large serpent) for its size. The plural of "jann" is "jinan," and it is the small, light-bodied serpent. Al-Kalbi said: it was neither small nor large.

﴿He turned back fleeing﴾ from fear, ﴿and did not return﴾: meaning he did not come back. It is said: "'aqqaba fulan" when he returned, and every one who returns is "mu'aqqib." It was also said: he did not stop and did not look back.

The first is preferable, because "ta'qib" is the return after the flight, and when that occurred from him, Allah, glory be to Him, said: ﴿O Musa, do not fear﴾, meaning: of the serpent and its harm. ﴿Indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence﴾, meaning: whoever I have sent with My message does not fear in My presence, so you too do not fear.

It was said: The negation of fear from the messengers is not at all times, but at the time of addressing them, for at that time they are wholly absorbed.

Then He made an exception, a disjunctive exception, saying: ﴿Except for one who has wronged, then substitutes good after evil—indeed, I am Forgiving and Merciful﴾, meaning: but whoever sins in wronging himself through disobedience, ﴿then substitutes good﴾, meaning: repentance and remorse, ﴿after evil﴾, meaning: after an evil deed, ﴿indeed, I am Forgiving and Merciful﴾. It was said: the exception is from an implied omitted element, meaning: "The messengers do not fear in My presence, but others fear, those who have wronged, except one who has wronged, then substituted good after evil, etc." Thus said al-Farra'.

Al-Nahhas said: An exception from an omitted element is impossible, because it is an exception from something that has not been mentioned.

It is related from al-Farra' that he said: "illa" here means "wa" (and).

It was said: The exception is connected to what was mentioned, not to what was omitted.

The meaning: "Except one of the messengers who wronged by committing minor sins from which none is free." Al-Nahhas chose this and said: He knew who among them disobeyed, so He excepted him, saying: "except one who has wronged," even though I have forgiven him, like Adam, David, the brothers of Joseph, and Musa for killing the Copt.

There is no barrier to fear after forgiveness, for our Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, to whom Allah forgave what preceded of his sin and what followed, used to say: "I wish I were a tree that is cut down."

﴿And put your hand into your pocket﴾: the "jayb" here is the well-known (pocket/collar opening). In al-Qasas [28:32] it says: "Insert your hand into your bosom," and in "adkhil" there is an emphasis not found in "usluk." ﴿It will come out white, without harm﴾: meaning, without leprosy or the like of afflictions, so it is a precaution.

His saying "takhruj" is the answer to "adkhil yadaka."

It was said: There is an omission in the speech, its estimate being: "Insert your hand, it will enter, and bring it out, it will come out." There is no need for this omission, nor any compulsion for it.

The exegetes said: Musa wore a woolen cloak with no sleeve and no lower garment, so he inserted his hand into his pocket and brought it out, and behold, it shone like lightning. His saying ﴿among nine signs﴾: Abu al-Baqa' said: it is in a place of accusative as a circumstantial qualifier from the subject of "takhruj," and this is far-fetched. It was said: it is connected to an omitted element, meaning: "Go among nine signs."

It was said that it is connected to His words, "Throw down your staff" and "Put your hand into your bosom," as part of the nine signs, or "together with nine signs."

It was also said that the meaning is: "They are two of nine," namely the staff and the hand. The signs would then be eleven: these two, the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, the obliteration, the drought in their deserts, and the shortfall in their crops.

Al-Nahhas said: "The best that has been said about this is that this verse, meaning the hand, is included among the nine signs." Al-Mahdawi and al-Qushayri said the same.

Al-Qushayri said: "You say, 'I went out with ten men, and you were one of them,' meaning, 'I went out as the tenth of ten.' So *fi* here has the sense of *min* (from), because of its closeness to it, just as you say, 'Take for me ten camels, in which there are two stallions,' meaning, 'from them.'"

Al-Asma'i, concerning the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

*"Will one ever enjoy life again, whose last covenant was thirty months, in three states?"*

Here *fi* means *min* (from). It was also said that *fi* means *ma'a* (with).

﴿To Pharaoh and his people.﴾ Al-Farra' said: "There is an implied element in the speech, meaning: 'You are sent, or dispatched, to Pharaoh and his people.'" Al-Zajjaj said the same.

﴿Indeed, they were a people who were defiantly disobedient.﴾ This clause gives the reason for what precedes it.

﴿So when Our signs came to them, clearly visible.﴾ That is, Our signs that were at the hand of Musa came to them, while being *mubsira*, meaning clear and evident, as if, because of their great clarity, they were making themselves visible. Compare His words: ﴿And We gave Thamud the she-camel as a visible sign﴾ [al-Isra 17:59]. Al-Akhfash said: "It is also possible that *mubsira* means 'making things visible' in the sense that the active participle has the sense of the passive participle (*ism al-mafʿul*). The detailed discussion of this has already been presented."

Ali ibn al-Husayn and Qatada read *mabsara*, with a fatha on the *mim* and the *sad*, meaning a place where much seeing occurs, as one says, "A child is a cause of cowardice (*majbana*) and of stinginess (*mabkhala*)."

﴿They said, "This is obvious magic."﴾ That is, when the signs came to them, they said this statement: that it is clear magic.

﴿And they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them.﴾ That is, they denied them while their souls were certain of them. The *waw* here is for the circumstantial clause (*hal*), and ﴿wrongfully and arrogantly﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state: "as wrongdoers and haughty." It is also possible that both are in the accusative as a cause (*ʿilla*), meaning: "What drove them to that wrongdoing and arrogance." It is also possible that they are an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (*maṣdar*), meaning: "They denied them with a denial that was wrongful and arrogant."

Abu ʿUbayda said: "The *ba'* in ﴿and they denied them﴾ is superfluous, meaning: 'and they denied it.'"

Al-Zajjaj said: "The implied meaning is: 'They denied them wrongfully and arrogantly,' that is, out of polytheism and pride, refusing to believe in what Musa brought, while knowing that it was from Allah."

So observe, O Muhammad, ﴿how was the end of the corrupters?﴾ That is: reflect on this, for in it there is a lesson for those who take heed. Their final fate was that they were drowned in the sea, in that terrifying manner.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His words: ﴿So when he came to it, he was called: "Blessed is whoever is in the fire,"﴾ that is, Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, Himself, was the light of the Lord of the worlds in the tree, ﴿and whoever is around it﴾ meaning the angels.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him concerning the verse: "Allah was in the light; He was called from the light." ﴿And whoever is around it﴾: the angels.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from him also: "Allah called to him while he was in the light."

Al-Firyabi, Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him also, concerning ﴿that blessed is whoever is in the fire﴾: "The fire was blessed."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatada: "In the codex of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb: 'The fire was blessed, and whoever is around it.' As for the fire, they claim that it is the light of the Lord of the worlds."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas: "*Anna buurika*" means: "It was sanctified."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Majah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh in *al-ʿAzama*, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa al-Sifat*, through the chain of Abu ʿUbayda, from Abu Musa al-Ashʿari, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) stood among us and said: "Indeed Allah does not sleep, and it is not fitting for Him to sleep. He lowers the scale and raises it. The deeds of the night are raised to Him before the deeds of the day, and the deeds of the day before the night. His veil is light; if it were removed, the splendors of His face would burn away everything that His sight reaches."

Then Abu ʿUbayda recited: ﴿that blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it, and glory be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾

The hadith is originally recorded in Sahih Muslim from the narration of Amr ibn Murra.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas: "Musa had a woolen cloak that did not reach beyond his elbows. He was told, 'Put your hand into your bosom,' and he did so."

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him concerning His words: ﴿and their souls were convinced of them, wrongfully and arrogantly﴾: "*Takabburan* (arrogance); their souls were convinced of them." This is an instance of *taqdim wa ta'khir* (inversion of word order).

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 27, verses 1–14 (part 1 of 2):

Al-Qurtubi said: It is Meccan entirely, according to the consensus. Ibn al-Dari's, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Surat al-Naml was revealed at Mecca." Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn al-Zubayr something similar.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿Ta-Sin﴾. The discussion has already passed in detail in the openings of the surahs (fawatih al-suwar, the disjointed letters at the beginnings of surahs). If these letters are the name of the surah, then their place is in the nominative case as a subject (mubtada'), and what follows is its predicate (khabar). It is also permissible that it be the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "This is the name of this surah." If these letters are not the name of the surah, but are recited in the manner of enumeration, then they have no grammatical place (la mahall laha). The demonstrative in His saying "Tilka" (these) refers to the surah itself, since it has been mentioned in summary by its name. The demonstrative is a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is ﴿the verses of the Qur'an﴾, and the sentence is the predicate of the first subject, on the assumption that it is raised by the inception (ibtida'). ﴿And a clear Book﴾: the majority (al-Jumhur) read "Kitab" in the genitive, coordinated with "al-Qur'an," meaning: "These are the verses of the Qur'an and the verses of a clear Book." It may be that what is meant by His saying "wa-Kitab" is the Qur'an itself, in which case it is the coordination of some attributes with others while the referent is one. It may also be that what is meant by "al-Kitab" is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), or the surah itself. Ibn Abi 'Abla read "wa-Kitabun Mubin" with both in the nominative, coordinated with ("ayat"). 

It was said: On this reading, there is an omitted modified noun (mudaf mahdhuf), with the modifier (mudaf ilayhi) standing in its place, meaning: "wa-ayat Kitabin Mubin." Thus the verses are described with two attributes: Qur'anic, indicating that it is recited, along with an indication that it is an Arabic Qur'an that is miraculous; and Kitabi (of the Book), indicating that it is written, along with an indication that it possesses the quality of the revealed books. On this, it is not a case of coordinating one attribute with another while the referent is one. Then he added to the two attributes a third attribute, which is its clarity of meanings for the one who reads it, or it is from (abana) in the sense of (bana), that is, its meaning became manifest and its miraculousness became clear through the eloquence it contains.

The attribute "Qur'aniyya" is placed first here, in view of the priority of the state of being Qur'an over the state of being written. He placed it later in Surat al-Hijr, saying: ﴿Alif-Lam-Ra. These are the verses of the Book and a clear Qur'an﴾ [al-Hijr: 1], in view of its state in which it has come to be, for it is written, and writing is the cause of reading. And Allah knows best.

As for the definiteness of "al-Qur'an" here and the indefiniteness of "Kitab," and the definiteness of "al-Kitab" in Surat al-Hijr and the indefiniteness of "Qur'an," this is because each of the two is suitable for both definiteness and indefiniteness.

﴿A guidance and good tidings for the believers﴾: it is in a place of accusative case as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) from "al-ayat" or from "al-Kitab," meaning: "These are verses that guide and give good tidings." It is permissible that it be in a place of nominative case by inception, meaning: "It is guidance," or the two are two other predicates of "tilka," or the two are two verbal nouns (masdar) in the accusative governed by an implied verb, meaning: "It guides guidance and gives good tidings with good tidings."

Then He described the believers to whom belong the guidance and the good tidings.

He said: ﴿Those who establish the prayer and give the zakat﴾. The relative pronoun is in a place of genitive case, or it is a substitute (badal) or an explanation (bayan), or it is in the accusative for praise, or in the nominative by an implied subject.

What is meant by "the prayer" is the five daily prayers, and what is meant by "the zakat" is the obligatory zakat. The clause ﴿and they, in the Hereafter, they are certain﴾ is in a place of accusative case as a circumstantial qualifier. He repeated the pronoun to indicate exclusivity, meaning: none holds true certainty regarding the Hereafter except these who combine faith with righteous deeds. He made the predicate nominative to indicate renewal at every time and non-cessation.

Then, when He, glory be to Him, mentioned the people of happiness, He mentioned after them the people of misery, saying: ﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾, and they are the disbelievers, meaning: they do not affirm the Resurrection. ﴿We have made their deeds appear pleasing to them﴾. It was said: What is meant is that Allah made their evil deeds appear pleasing to them until they saw them as good.

It was also said: What is meant is that Allah made righteous deeds appear pleasing to them and mentioned to them what they contain of the good of this world and the Hereafter, but they did not accept that.

Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of the verse is: We made their recompense for their disbelief that We made appealing to them what they are engaged in. ﴿So they wander blindly﴾, meaning: they hesitate in it, bewildered, persistently, not guided to any path, nor reaching any reality.

It was said: the meaning of "ya'mahun" is "they persist in transgression."

Qatada said: "they play." As for the meaning of bewilderment, the poet said:

A desert whose edges are in a desert, blind to guidance, the bewildered, the confused.

The demonstrative in His saying "5 ulaika" refers to those mentioned before it, and it is the subject whose predicate is ﴿for them is the evil of the punishment﴾. It was said: in this world, such as killing and captivity. The reason for restricting it to the punishment of this world is His saying: ﴿and in the Hereafter they are the greatest losers﴾, meaning: they are the most severe of people in loss and the greatest in disappointment. Then He, glory be to Him, prepared a beneficial introduction for what He would mention after that of wondrous reports.

He said: ﴿And indeed, you are receiving the Qur'an from the Wise, the All-Knowing﴾, meaning: it is being cast upon you, and you receive it and take it from One of great wisdom and knowledge. It was said: "min ladun" here means "'inda" (with/from).

There are dialects of it, as has passed in Surat al-Kahf.

﴿When Musa said to his family﴾: the adverbial clause is in the accusative, governed by a hidden verb, which is "udhkur" (remember).

Al-Zajjaj said: The position of "idh" is accusative. The meaning: remember when Musa said, i.e., remember his story when he said to his family. What is meant by "his family" is his wife during his journey from Madyan to Egypt, and at that time he had with him only his wife, the daughter of Shu'ayb. So he referred to her with the word "ahl" (family), which indicates plurality, and similar to it is His saying: "Stay here" [Ta-Ha: 10; al-Qasas: 29]. The meaning of ﴿I have perceived a fire﴾ is: I saw it. ﴿I will bring you from it news﴾: the sin indicates the great distance of the fire. ﴿Or I will bring you a burning brand﴾. 'Asim, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read "shihab" with tanwin, while the rest read it as an annexed form (idafa) to "qabas." On the first reading, "qabas" is a substitute for "shihab" or its attribute, since it means "maqbus" (taken from a fire). On the second reading, the annexation is explanatory (li-l-bayan). The meaning on both readings: "I will bring you a flame of fire taken from its source," i.e., taken from its origin.

Al-Zajjaj said: Whoever puts tanwin makes "qabas" an attribute of "shihab." Al-Farra' said: this annexation is like the annexation in their saying "masjid al-jami'" and "salat al-ula," where a thing is annexed to itself because its names differ. 

Al-Nahhas said: It is the annexation of the species to the genus, as when you say "thawb khazz" (a silk garment) and "khatam hadid" (an iron ring).

He said: In other than the Qur'an, it is permissible to say "bi-shihabin qabasan" as an accusative masdar, or as an explanation, or as a circumstantial qualifier.

﴿So that you may warm yourselves﴾: meaning, hopefully you may warm yourselves by it, or in order that you may warm yourselves from the cold. It is said: "sala bi-l-nar" and "istala biha" when one warms oneself by it.

Al-Zajjaj said: Every white thing with light is a shihab.

Abu 'Ubayda said: The shihab is fire, and from it is the saying of Abu al-Najm:

As if it had been a blazing shihab, which shone with light, then became extinguished.

Tha'lab said: The origin of the shihab is a stick with a live coal at one end while the other end has no fire. The shihab is a shining ray. It was also said: a star is called a shihab, and from it is the poet's saying:

In his hand is a straight, well-formed spear, in which is a point like the flame of a brand.

﴿Then when he came to it﴾: i.e., when Musa came to the fire, ﴿he was called: Blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it﴾. ("An") is the explanatory particle for what is in the calling of meaning "saying," or it is the verbal ("an") meaning "that blessed is." It was said: it is the light ("an") of the heavy ("anna").

Al-Zajjaj said: "an" is in the place of accusative, meaning: "saying that..." and it is permissible that it be in the place of nominative as the substitute of what has not been named its agent (na'ib al-fa'il).

The more preferred view is that the deputy agent is a pronoun referring to Musa.

Ubayy, Ibn 'Abbas, and Mujahid read "an buruikati al-nar wa-man hawlaha" [that the fire was blessed and whoever is around it], as narrated by Abu Hatim.

Al-Kisa'i related from the Arabs: "barakaka Allah," "barak Allah fika," "barak 'alayki," and "barak laka," and al-Farra' related the same.

Ibn Jarir said: He said "buruka man fi al-nar" and did not say "buruka 'ala al-nar," according to the dialect of those who say "barakaka Allah," meaning: blessed upon whoever is in the fire, and that is Musa, or upon whoever is near the fire, not that he was in its midst.

Al-Suddi said: There were angels in the fire, and the fire here was merely light, but Musa thought it was fire, and when he reached it he found it to be light.

It is related from al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr that what is meant by "whoever is in the fire" is Allah, glory be to Him, meaning His light.

It was said: blessed is what is in the fire of the command of Allah, glory be to Him, which made it in that state.

Al-Wahidi said: The way of the exegetes is that what is meant by "the fire" is the light. Then He, glory be to Him, declared His own transcendence, saying: ﴿And glory be to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾, and in it is an expression of wonder for Musa at that.

﴿O Musa, indeed I am Allah, the Mighty, the Wise﴾. The pronoun is for the matter (damir al-sha'n), meaning: "It is I, Allah, the Mighty, the Overpowering, the Dominant, the Wise in His command and His action."

It was said: Musa said: "My Lord, who is it who called me?" Then Allah, glory be to Him, answered him with His saying: "Indeed it is I, Allah." Then He, glory be to Him, commanded him to throw down his staff, so that he would know what miracle Allah, glory be to Him, would bring about through his hand.

The clause ﴿And throw down your staff﴾ is coordinated with "buriku" (blessed), and there is an omission in the speech; the estimate is: "So he threw it from his hand, and it became a serpent."

﴿But when he saw it moving as if it were a jann﴾: al-Zajjaj said: The staff began to move as the jann moves, and it is the white serpent. He compared it to the jann in the lightness of its movement, and in another place he compared it to a thu'ban (large serpent) for its size. The plural of "jann" is "jinan," and it is the small, light-bodied serpent. Al-Kalbi said: it was neither small nor large.

﴿He turned back fleeing﴾ from fear, ﴿and did not return﴾: meaning he did not come back. It is said: "'aqqaba fulan" when he returned, and every one who returns is "mu'aqqib." It was also said: he did not stop and did not look back.

The first is preferable, because "ta'qib" is the return after the flight, and when that occurred from him, Allah, glory be to Him, said: ﴿O Musa, do not fear﴾, meaning: of the serpent and its harm. ﴿Indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence﴾, meaning: whoever I have sent with My message does not fear in My presence, so you too do not fear.

It was said: The negation of fear from the messengers is not at all times, but at the time of addressing them, for at that time they are wholly absorbed.

Then He made an exception, a disjunctive exception, saying: ﴿Except for one who has wronged, then substitutes good after evil—indeed, I am Forgiving and Merciful﴾, meaning: but whoever sins in wronging himself through disobedience, ﴿then substitutes good﴾, meaning: repentance and remorse, ﴿after evil﴾, meaning: after an evil deed, ﴿indeed, I am Forgiving and Merciful﴾. It was said: the exception is from an implied omitted element, meaning: "The messengers do not fear in My presence, but others fear, those who have wronged, except one who has wronged, then substituted good after evil, etc." Thus said al-Farra'.

Al-Nahhas said: An exception from an omitted element is impossible, because it is an exception from something that has not been mentioned.

It is related from al-Farra' that he said: "illa" here means "wa" (and).

It was said: The exception is connected to what was mentioned, not to what was omitted.

The meaning: "Except one of the messengers who wronged by committing minor sins from which none is free." Al-Nahhas chose this and said: He knew who among them disobeyed, so He excepted him, saying: "except one who has wronged," even though I have forgiven him, like Adam, David, the brothers of Joseph, and Musa for killing the Copt.

There is no barrier to fear after forgiveness, for our Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, to whom Allah forgave what preceded of his sin and what followed, used to say: "I wish I were a tree that is cut down."

﴿And put your hand into your pocket﴾: the "jayb" here is the well-known (pocket/collar opening). In al-Qasas [28:32] it says: "Insert your hand into your bosom," and in "adkhil" there is an emphasis not found in "usluk." ﴿It will come out white, without harm﴾: meaning, without leprosy or the like of afflictions, so it is a precaution.

His saying "takhruj" is the answer to "adkhil yadaka."

It was said: There is an omission in the speech, its estimate being: "Insert your hand, it will enter, and bring it out, it will come out." There is no need for this omission, nor any compulsion for it.

The exegetes said: Musa wore a woolen cloak with no sleeve and no lower garment, so he inserted his hand into his pocket and brought it out, and behold, it shone like lightning. His saying ﴿among nine signs﴾: Abu al-Baqa' said: it is in a place of accusative as a circumstantial qualifier from the subject of "takhruj," and this is far-fetched. It was said: it is connected to an omitted element, meaning: "Go among nine signs."

It was said that it is connected to His words, "Throw down your staff" and "Put your hand into your bosom," as part of the nine signs, or "together with nine signs."

It was also said that the meaning is: "They are two of nine," namely the staff and the hand. The signs would then be eleven: these two, the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, the obliteration, the drought in their deserts, and the shortfall in their crops.

Al-Nahhas said: "The best that has been said about this is that this verse, meaning the hand, is included among the nine signs." Al-Mahdawi and al-Qushayri said the same.

Al-Qushayri said: "You say, 'I went out with ten men, and you were one of them,' meaning, 'I went out as the tenth of ten.' So *fi* here has the sense of *min* (from), because of its closeness to it, just as you say, 'Take for me ten camels, in which there are two stallions,' meaning, 'from them.'"

Al-Asma'i, concerning the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

*"Will one ever enjoy life again, whose last covenant was thirty months, in three states?"*

Here *fi* means *min* (from). It was also said that *fi* means *ma'a* (with).

﴿To Pharaoh and his people.﴾ Al-Farra' said: "There is an implied element in the speech, meaning: 'You are sent, or dispatched, to Pharaoh and his people.'" Al-Zajjaj said the same.

﴿Indeed, they were a people who were defiantly disobedient.﴾ This clause gives the reason for what precedes it.

﴿So when Our signs came to them, clearly visible.﴾ That is, Our signs that were at the hand of Musa came to them, while being *mubsira*, meaning clear and evident, as if, because of their great clarity, they were making themselves visible. Compare His words: ﴿And We gave Thamud the she-camel as a visible sign﴾ [al-Isra 17:59]. Al-Akhfash said: "It is also possible that *mubsira* means 'making things visible' in the sense that the active participle has the sense of the passive participle (*ism al-mafʿul*). The detailed discussion of this has already been presented."
