This is supported by the fact that thanking with the tongue is only fitting when it is preceded by an act of the heart, namely the resolve to perform obedience and abandon disobedience. ﴿Who has favored us over many of His believing servants﴾, meaning: He favored us with knowledge, prophethood, and the subjugation of the birds, the jinn, and mankind. They did not regard themselves as superior to everyone, out of humility.

The verse indicates the nobility of knowledge and the elevation of its status, that the blessing of knowledge is among the greatest blessings with which Allah favors His servants, and that whoever is given it has been given a virtue over many of the servants and granted a magnificent honor.

﴿And Sulayman inherited from Dawud﴾, meaning he inherited knowledge and prophethood.

Qatadah and al-Kalbi said: Dawud had nineteen male sons, and Sulayman inherited his prophethood from among them. Had the intended meaning been the inheritance of wealth, He would not have singled out Sulayman, since all of his sons were equal in that regard. Most of the exegetes also said this. Therefore this inheritance is a metaphorical inheritance, as in the words of the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "The scholars are the heirs of the prophets."

﴿And he said, "O people, we have been taught the speech of the birds"﴾. Sulayman spoke these words addressing the people, by way of relating the blessing Allah had bestowed upon him and giving thanks for the favor He singled him out with. He mentioned the speech of the birds first because it is a special blessing granted to him, which no one else shares with him.

Al-Farra' said: "The speech of the birds" is their language, which was treated like the speech of a man. He recited the verse of Humayd ibn Thawr:

"It is strange to her that her song should be eloquent, while it did not fail to be [clear] in her speech"

The meaning of the verse is: we understood what the birds say.

Some exegetes said: he was taught the speech of all animals, and he mentioned the birds specifically because they were among his troops, travelling with him to shade him from the sun.

Qatadah and al-Sha'bi said: he was taught only the speech of the birds, and this is not refuted by the ant, since it is one of the birds: ants often grow wings and fly. Thus this ant whose speech he heard and understood was of that kind.

﴿And we have been given of everything﴾ means: everything that need calls for, such as knowledge, prophethood, wisdom, wealth, the subjugation of the jinn, mankind, birds, winds, wild beasts, and animals, and everything that is between the heaven and the earth.

Sulayman used the plural of majesty (nun al-ʿazamah), and he meant himself, to show his condition of being obeyed and not opposed. This was not out of arrogance or self-magnification. The reference in His words ﴿Indeed, this﴾ is to what was previously mentioned of teaching and giving. ﴿Surely this is the manifest bounty﴾, meaning the evident and clear [favor], which is hidden from no one, or that which displays Our excellence.

(p-1075) ﴿And Sulayman's forces were gathered together for him, of the jinn and mankind and birds﴾. Ḥashr means gathering, so his troops were assembled for him from these categories.

The exegetes have gone to great lengths in describing the size of his army, and many of them exaggerated to a degree that minds find improbable and that is not sound according to transmission. Even if it were sound, there would be in Divine power something greater and more extensive than that. ﴿And they were held in ranks﴾, meaning each group had a warden who kept the first of them back from the last, so that they would stand in their ranks. It is said: wazaʿahu yazaʿuhu wazʿan, meaning he restrained him. The wazi' in war is the one assigned to the rows, who restrains those who go forward; from this comes the verse of al-Nabighah:

"When I rebuked white hair for youth, and said: 'Alas! Be still, for the white hair is a restrainer.'"

And the words of another:

"Whoever is not restrained by his intellect and his modesty, there is no restrainer for him from the grey of his temples."

And the words of another:

"Only a person of full intellect and perfection restrains the stubborn soul from desire, among people."

It is also said that it derives from tawzi', meaning dispersal; it is said: "The people are awzaʿ," meaning groups.

﴿Until, when they came upon the valley of the ants﴾. Ḥattā (until) is the particle after which speech begins, and it marks the end point of what precedes it. The meaning is: "they were held in ranks until the attainment of this end, which is their arriving at the valley of the ants." That is, they were proceeding with some of them prevented from separating from others, until, when they came to the valley, etc. ʿAlā wadi al-namli is connected to atau (came), and it was used with ʿalā because they were carried by the wind, so they were above it.

The meaning: they crossed the valley and reached its far end. All the readers stopped on wād without a yā', following the orthography, since it was not deleted due to the meeting of two sukūns, as in His words ﴿Who hewed out the rocks in the valley﴾ [al-Fajr: 9]. Only al-Kisa'i stopped with the yā', saying: "What necessitates deletion is only the meeting of two sukūns in continuous speech."

Ka'b said: the valley of the ants is in al-Ta'if. Qatadah and Muqatil said: it is in al-Sham (Syria).

﴿An ant said﴾. This is the response to idha (when). It is as if, when it saw them heading toward the valley, it fled and alerted the rest of the ants, calling out to them, saying: ﴿O ants, enter your dwellings﴾. It addressed the ants as one would address rational beings, since they understand that address. The masakin (dwellings) are the places in which ants live.

It is said: this ant whom Sulayman heard was female, as evidenced by the feminine form of the verb attributed to it.

Abu Hayyan rejected this, saying: the attachment of the taʾ in qalat does not indicate that the ant is feminine. It is valid to say of a male: qalat, because it is "namlah" (a female-form noun). Even if it has the taʾ, it is one of those in which the masculine cannot be distinguished from the feminine by the gender of the verb, but rather is distinguished by reporting whether it is male or female. Nothing of great benefit depends on this, nor on examining the name of the ant, nor on the fabricated stories and false narrations that have been related.

Al-Hasan, Talhah, and Ma'mar ibn Sulayman read "namlatun" and "al-namul" with a ḍammah on the mīm and a fatḥah on the nūn, in the pattern of rajul and samurah. Sulayman al-Taymi read with two ḍammahs on both.

﴿Let not Sulayman and his troops crush you﴾. Al-ḥaṭm means breaking; it is said: ḥaṭamtuhu ḥaṭman, meaning I broke it, breaking. Taḥaṭṭama means to be shattered. This prohibition is outwardly addressed to the ants, but in reality it is addressed to Sulayman. It is thus of the type: "Let me not see you here." It may be a substitute for the imperative, and it may be an answer to the imperative.

Abu Hayyan said: as for its analysis as an answer to the imperative, that is only possible on the reading of al-A'mash, who read "la yaḥṭimkum" with jazm and without the nun of emphasis. But with the nun of emphasis, that is not permitted except in poetry.

Sibawayh said: it is rare in poetry; they treated it like the prohibition, since it is jussive.

Ubayy read "udkhulu masakinakunna" (enter your dwellings, feminine plural). Shahr ibn Hawshab read "maskanakum." Al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Qatadah, and ʿIsa al-Hamdani read "la yuḥaṭṭimannakum" with a ḍammah on the yā', a fatḥah on the ḥā', and a shaddah on the ṭā'. Ibn Ishaq, Ya'qub, and Abu ʿAmr in one narration read with the sukūn of the nun of emphasis.

The clause ﴿while they do not perceive﴾ is in the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) relating to the subject of yaḥṭimannakum, meaning: they will not perceive your being crushed, nor will they know your location. It has also been said that the meaning is: "and the ants do not perceive that Sulayman understands their speech," but this is far-fetched.

﴿So he smiled, laughing at her speech﴾. Ibn al-Sumayfa' read "ḍaḥikan" (laughter, as a masdar). According to the reading of the majority, ḍāḥikan is an emphatic circumstantial (ḥāl mu'akkidah), because laughter has already been understood from smiling. It has also been said that it is a projected circumstantial (ḥāl muqaddarah), since smiling is the beginning of laughter. It is also said that since smiling may be due to anger, laughter clarifies it. It is also said that the laughter of the prophets is only smiling and nothing more. On the reading of Ibn al-Sumayfa', ḍaḥikan is a masdar in the accusative governed by a deleted verb, or in the position of a circumstantial. Sulayman's laughter was out of wonder at her speech, her understanding, and her guidance to warning the ants.

﴿And he said, "My Lord, enable me to be grateful for Your blessing with which You have favored me and my parents"﴾. The explanation of awziʿni (enable me) has already been given shortly before, in His words ﴿So they were held in ranks﴾ [al-Naml: 17; Fussilat: 19]. In al-Kashshaf it is said: The literal meaning of awziʿni is: "make me restrain the thanks for Your blessings within me, and restrain it, and bind it, so that it does not escape from me, until I never cease to be thankful to You." End of quote.

Al-Wahidi said: "awziʿni" means: "inspire me to be grateful for Your blessing with which You favored me." It is said: "So-and-so is muwazzaʿ with such-and-such," meaning he is devoted to it. End of quote.

Al-Qurtubi said: it derives from wazi'a, as if he said: "Restrain me from what displeases You." End of quote.

The second object of awziʿni is: "that I be grateful for Your blessing with which You favored me."

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of awziʿni is: "prevent me from being ungrateful for Your blessing." This is an explanation by a necessary implication. The meaning of ﴿and upon my parents﴾ is his supplication that Allah enable him to be thankful for His blessing upon his parents, just as He enabled him to be thankful for His blessing upon himself, since bestowing favor upon them is a bestowal of favor upon him, and that requires gratitude from him to Allah, Glorified is He. Then he asked that Allah add to him the consequences of His blessings to their precedents, especially the religious blessings, so he said: ﴿And that I do righteous deeds which You are pleased with﴾, meaning: a righteous deed which You are pleased with from me. Then he prayed that Allah, Glorified is He, would place him in the Hereafter among the righteous, for that is the ultimate goal to which the request relates. So he said: ﴿And admit me by Your mercy among Your righteous servants﴾. The meaning is: admit me into their company, record my name among their names, and gather me in their group to the abode of the righteous, which is Paradise. O Allah, I call upon You with what this noble Prophet called upon You, so accept that from me and bestow Your favor upon me with it, for although I am deficient in deeds, Your bounty is the cause of attaining good.

This verse thus proclaims, with the loudest voice and the clearest explanation, that entry into Paradise, which is the abode of the believers (p-1076), is by Your favor and not by their deeds, just as Your truthful Messenger (ﷺ) said in what is established in the Sahih: "Be steadfast, strive to be close [to the right path], and know that none of you will enter Paradise by his deeds." They said: "Not even you, O Messenger of God?" He said: "Not even I, unless Allah covers me with His mercy." So when there is nothing but Your vast favor, abandoning the request for it from You is incapacity, and neglecting the means of reaching You so that it reaches him is a waste.

Then Glorified is He began to mention the story of Bilqis and what happened between her and Sulayman, and that was by means of the hoopoe. So He said: ﴿And he inspected the birds﴾. Tafaqqud means searching for what has been lost to you and inquiring about its condition. Al-ṭayr is a collective noun for everything that flies. The meaning is that he searched for the birds that were missing and inquired about the condition of those that were absent, and the birds used to accompany him on his journey and shade him with their wings.

﴿And he said, "What is wrong with me, that I do not see the hoopoe? Or is he among the absent?"﴾. That is: "What is the matter with the hoopoe that I do not see him?" This speech is among the inverted speech that the Arabs use frequently. It has also been said: there is no need to claim inversion; rather it is a question about what prevents him from seeing the hoopoe, as if he said: "What is with me that I do not see him? Is it because of some screen that conceals him from me, or for some other reason?" Then it became clear to him that he was absent, so he said: ﴿Or is he among the absent?﴾. The am here is the disconnected one that carries the sense of a change of subject (idrab). Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muhaysin, Hisham, and Ayyub read "ma liya" with a fatḥah on the yā'. They also read so in Ya Sin: ﴿And why should I not worship Him who created me﴾ [Ya Sin: 22] with a fatḥah on the yā'. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Ya'qub read with a sukūn on it in both places. The rest read with a fatḥah on the one in Ya Sin and a sukūn on the one here.

Abu ʿAmr said: because the one here is interrogative, while the one in Ya Sin is negative. Abu Hatim and Abu ʿUbayd preferred the sukūn.

﴿I will surely punish him with a severe punishment, or I will surely slaughter him﴾.

﴿Concerning this severe punishment, the scholars differed as to what it was. Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj said: it is that he (the hoopoe) be plucked of all his feathers. Yazid ibn Ruman said: it is that the feathers of his two wings be plucked. It was also said: it is that he be confined with his like (i.e., with others of his kind). It was also said: it is that he be prevented from serving him. In this there is evidence that the punishment is proportioned to the offence, not to the size of the body.

His saying ﴿عَذَابًا﴾ (ʿadhāban, "a punishment") is either an ism al-maṣdar (verbal noun, a noun of action that is not a true infinitive) or a maṣdar (infinitive) with its extra elements omitted, like His saying: ﴿وَاللَّهُ أَنْبَتَكُمْ مِنَ الْأَرْضِ نَبَاتًا﴾ [Nuh: 17] ("And God made you grow from the earth as a growth"), and ﴿أَوْ لَيَأْتِيَنِّي بِسُلْطَانٍ مُبِينٍ﴾ ("or he must bring me a clear authority"). Ibn Kathir alone read it with the emphatic nun (nūn al-tawkīd) doubled, followed by the nun of protection (nūn al-wiqāya). The rest read with a doubled nun only, which is the nun of emphasis. ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar read it with a doubled nun, vowelled with a fatḥa, not joined to a yā'. The clear authority (al-sulṭān al-mubīn) is the evident proof in his absence.

﴿فَمَكَثَ غَيْرَ بَعِيدٍ﴾ means: the hoopoe remained for a period not far off (i.e., not long).

The majority read ﴿مَكُثَ﴾ with a ḍamma on the kāf. ʿĀṣim alone read it with a fatḥa. The meaning in both readings is: he stayed for a period not far off.

Sibawayh said: makatha yamkuthu mukūthan is like qaʿada yaqʿudu quʿūdan.

It was also said that the pronoun in ﴿مَكَثَ﴾ refers to Solomon. The meaning would then be: Solomon remained, after the inspection and the threat, for a period not long. The first view is preferable.

﴿فَقَالَ أَحَطْتُ بِمَا لَمْ تُحِطْ بِهِ﴾ means: I have come to know what you have not come to know of the matter. Iḥāṭa (encompassing) is knowledge of a thing from all its aspects. There is probably an omission in the speech, and the sense is: the hoopoe remained for a period not far off, then came and was rebuked for his absence, and he said by way of excuse, ﴿أَحَطْتُ بِمَا لَمْ تُحِطْ بِهِ﴾.

Al-Farraʾ said: it is permissible to assimilate the tāʾ into the ṭāʾ (idgham, assimilation of one consonant into another), so one says aḥuṭṭu, and to assimilate the ṭāʾ into the tāʾ, so one says aḥattu.

﴿وَجِئْتُكَ مِنْ سَبَإٍ بِنَبَإٍ يَقِينٍ﴾. The majority read ﴿مِنْ سَبَإٍ﴾ with tanwīn (nunation, i.e., declined), taking it as the name of a man from whom a people were named. The poet's verse testifies to this:

"The arrivers, and Taym on the heights of Saba',
the hides of buffalo have chafed their necks."

Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read it with a fatḥa on the hamza and without tanwīn, taking it as the name of a city. Al-Zajjaj denied that it is the name of a man and said: Saba' is the name of a city known as Maʾrib of Yemen, between it and Sanaʾ three days' distance.

It was also said that it is the name of a woman after whom the city was named.

Al-Qurtubi said: the correct view is that it is the name of a man, as in the book of al-Tirmidhi from the ḥadīth of Farwa ibn Musayk al-Muradi. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: this was hidden from al-Zajjaj, so he blundered like a blind-night stumbler (khabṭa ʿashwāʾ). Al-Farraʾ claimed that al-Ruʾāsī asked Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ about Saba', and he said: "I do not know what it is." Al-Naḥḥās said: Abu ʿAmr is too exalted to say this. He said: the matter concerning Saba' is what the transmitted report has established, that originally it is the name of a man. If you apply tanwīn to it, it is because it has become the name of a tribe; if you do not apply tanwīn, you make it the name of a tribe, like Thamud. However, the preferred form according to Sibawayh is with tanwīn. End of quotation.

I say: there is no doubt that Saba' is the name of a city in Yemen where Bilqis was, and it is also the name of a man of Qaḥṭān, namely Saba' ibn Yashjub ibn Yaʿrub ibn Qaḥṭān ibn Hud. But what is meant here is that the hoopoe came to Solomon with news of what he had seen in the city of Saba', described as such, and there will come at the end of this discussion, from transmitted reports, what clarifies and supports this. The meaning of the verse is that the hoopoe came to Solomon from this city with a certain news. A nabaʾ is a weighty news. When the hoopoe said to Solomon what he said, Solomon said to him: "And what is that?" He said:

﴿إِنِّي وَجَدْتُ امْرَأَةً تَمْلِكُهُمْ﴾ ("I found a woman ruling over them"). She was Bilqis, daughter of Sharahil. The hoopoe found her ruling the people of Saba'. This sentence serves as an explanation and elaboration of the sentence before it. That is: this certain news is that this woman rules over them.

﴿وَأُوتِيَتْ مِنْ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ﴾ ("and she has been given of everything") contains hyperbole. The meaning is that she was given of every one of the things she needs. It was also said: the meaning is: she was given of everything in her time, some thing, and "some thing" is omitted because the speech indicates it.

﴿وَلَهَا عَرْشٌ عَظِيمٌ﴾ ("and she has a mighty throne"): that is, a great throne. It was described as great because, as it is said, it was of gold, eighty cubits long, forty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high into the sky, set with pearls, red rubies and green emeralds. It was also said: the throne here means kingship. The first view is preferable, because of His saying: ﴿أَيُّكُمْ يَأْتِينِي بِعَرْشِهَا﴾ ("Which of you will bring me her throne?").

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: what necessarily follows from the verse is that she was a queen over the cities of Yemen, possessing a great kingdom and a great throne, and she was an unbeliever from a disbelieving people.

﴿وَجَدْتُهَا وَقَوْمَهَا يَسْجُدُونَ لِلشَّمْسِ مِنْ دُونِ اللَّهِ﴾ ("I found her and her people prostrating to the sun instead of God"): that is, they worship it, exceeding the worship of God, may He be glorified. It was said: they were Magians. It was said: they were zindīqs (heretics). ﴿وَزَيَّنَ لَهُمُ الشَّيْطَانُ أَعْمَالَهُمْ﴾ ("and Satan made their deeds appealing to them"), namely the worship of the sun and the rest of their works of disbelief. ﴿فَصَدَّهُمْ عَنِ السَّبِيلِ﴾ ("and so he barred them from the way"): that is, Satan barred them, through that adornment, from the clear path, which is faith in God and affirming His oneness. ﴿فَهُمْ لَا يَهْتَدُونَ﴾ ("so they are not guided") to that.

﴿أَلَّا يَسْجُدُوا﴾ (allā yasjudū). The majority read the lām with shadda (tashdīd) in ﴿أَلَّا﴾.

Ibn al-Anbari said: stopping at ﴿فَهُمْ لَا يَهْتَدُونَ﴾ is not a complete stop according to the one who doubles the lām in ﴿أَلَّا﴾, because the meaning is: "Satan made their deeds appealing to them so that they do not prostrate."

Al-Naḥḥās said: it is ﴿أَنْ﴾ (an) with ﴿لَا﴾ (lā) entering upon it, and it is in the accusative position.

Al-Akhfash said: that is, he made it appealing to them that they should not prostrate to God, meaning "lest they prostrate to God."

Al-Kisāʾī said: it is in the accusative position governed by ﴿صَدَّهُمْ﴾ ("barred them"), that is: "so he barred them from prostrating," in the sense of "lest they prostrate." On both views it is an object of purpose (mafʿūl lahu).

Al-Yazidi said: it is a substitute (badal) for ﴿أَعْمَالَهُمْ﴾ ("their deeds") in the accusative position.

Abu ʿAmr said: it is in the genitive position as a substitute for ﴿السَّبِيلِ﴾ ("the way").

It was also said: the governing word for it is ﴿لَا يَهْتَدُونَ﴾ ("they are not guided"), that is: "they are not guided to prostrate to God," and in this view ﴿لَا﴾ is extra, like His saying: ﴿مَا مَنَعَكَ أَلَّا تَسْجُدَ﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 12] ("What prevented you from prostrating?").

According to the reading of the majority, this verse is not a place of prostration, because it is a report about them, that they abandoned prostration, either through the adornment, or through barring, or through preventing guidance. Al-Zajjaj preferred its being a reason for the barring, and al-Farraʾ preferred its being a reason for ﴿زَيَّنَ﴾ ("made appealing"). He said: he made their deeds appealing to them lest they prostrate, then the lām was omitted.

Al-Zuhri and al-Kisāʾī read ﴿أَلَّا﴾ with lightening (takhfīf). Al-Kisāʾī said: I did not hear the elders reading it except with lightening, on the intention of a command, so ﴿أَلَا﴾ in this reading is a particle of alerting and opening (ḥarf tanbīh wa-istiftāḥ), and what follows it is a vocative particle (ḥarf nidāʾ), and ﴿اسْجُدُوا﴾ is an imperative verb. In this reading the script should have been ﴿أَلَا يَا اسْجُدُوا﴾, but the Companions, may God be pleased with them, dropped the alif of ﴿يَا﴾ and the hamzat al-waṣl of ﴿اسْجُدُوا﴾ in error, and joined the yā' to the sīn of ﴿اسْجُدُوا﴾, so the written form became ﴿أَلَا يَسْجُدُوا﴾. The called-upon noun is omitted, and its estimate is: "Ah, O people, prostrate!" The Arabs often omit the vocative noun in their speech, and from this is the saying of the poet:

"Ah, O abode of Mayy, be safe in decay,
and may the rain never cease to pour upon your gravel plains."

And the saying of another:

"Ah, be safe, there be safe, there be safe,
three greetings, even if you do not speak."

And the saying of another also:

"Ah, be safe, O Hind, Hind of the Banu Bakr."

And this is common in their poetry.

Al-Zajjaj said: the reading with lightening requires the obligation of prostration, unlike the reading with doubling. Abu Ḥatim and Abu ʿUbayd preferred the reading with doubling. Al-Zajjaj said: the reading with lightening has a good aspect, except that in it the report is cut off from the matter of Saba', then there is a return after that to mentioning them.

The reading with doubling is a report that follows one part after another without a break in its middle. Al-Naḥḥās said likewise. On this reading the clause ﴿أَلَّا يَسْجُدُوا﴾ is an interjected statement, either from the speech of the hoopoe, or from the speech of Solomon, or from the speech of God, may He be glorified.

In this reading there is also the reading of ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud, "هَلْ لَا تَسْجُدُوا" (hal lā tasjudū), with the second person (tāʾ of address), and in the reading of Ubayy, "أَلَّا تَسْجُدُوا" (allā tasjudū), also with the second person.

﴿الَّذِي يُخْرِجُ الْخَبْءَ فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ﴾ ("who brings forth what is hidden in the heavens and the earth"): that is, He makes manifest what is concealed and hidden in them. It is said: I hid the thing, akhbaʾuhu khabʾan, and al-khabʾ is what you have hidden.

Al-Zajjaj said: it has come in the exegesis that al-khabʾ here means the rain from the sky and the plants from the earth. It was also said: the hidden things of the earth are its treasures and its plants. Qatada said: al-khabʾ is the secret. Al-Naḥḥās said: that is, what is absent in the heavens and the earth. Ubayy and ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar read "الخَبَ" (al-khabā, without hamza) with a fatḥa on the bāʾ, by lightening. ʿAbd Allah, ʿIkrima and Malik ibn Dinar read "الخَبَا" (al-khabā) with an alif. Abu Ḥatim said: this is not permissible in Arabic. It was answered that Sibawayh reported from the Arabs that the alif replaces the hamza when a sukūn precedes it. In the reading of ʿAbd Allah it is "يُخْرِجُ الخَبَ مِنَ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ" ("He brings forth the hidden from the heavens and the earth").

Al-Farraʾ said: "min" (from) and "fī" (in) alternate with each other. The relative clause may be in the genitive position as a qualifier (naʿt) of God, may He be glorified, or as a substitute (badal) of Him, or as an explanation (bayān) of Him. It may be in the accusative position by way of praise, and it may be in the nominative position as the predicate of an omitted subject.

The clause ﴿وَيَعْلَمُ مَا تُخْفُونَ وَمَا تُعْلِنُونَ﴾ ("and He knows what you conceal and what you disclose") is conjoined to ﴿يُخْرِجُ﴾ ("brings forth"). The majority read both verbs with the yā' (third person). Al-Juḥdari, ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar, Ḥafs and al-Kisāʾī read them with the tāʾ (second person, address). As for the first reading, it is because the pronouns preceding it are third-person pronouns. As for the second reading, it is because in the reading of al-Zuhri and al-Kisāʾī the command to prostrate is included, and the address to them with it, so this, in their view, is part of that address.

The meaning is: God, may He be glorified, brings forth from this human world what is hidden in it by His knowledge of it, just as He brings forth what is hidden in the heavens and the earth. Then, after describing the Lord, may He be glorified, with what has preceded, which indicates the greatness of His power, the sublimity of His authority, the obligation of affirming His oneness and singling Him out for worship, He said:

﴿اللَّهُ لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا هُوَ رَبُّ الْعَرْشِ الْعَظِيمِ﴾ ("God; there is no god but Him, the Lord of the Mighty Throne"). The majority read ﴿الْعَظِيمِ﴾ with the genitive, as a qualifier of ﴿الْعَرْشِ﴾ ("the Throne"). Ibn Muḥaysin read it with the nominative, as a qualifier of ﴿الرَّبِّ﴾ ("the Lord"). The Throne was singled out for mention because it is the greatest of created things, as is established in the report traced back to the Messenger of God, may God's blessings and peace be upon him and his family.

Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported from ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz that he wrote: "God has not bestowed a blessing upon a servant and then the servant praised God for it, except that his praise was better than his blessing. Were you not to know this except from the revealed Book of God, He, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿وَلَقَدْ آتَيْنَا دَاوُدَ وَسُلَيْمَانَ عِلْمًا وَقَالَا الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ الَّذِي فَضَّلَنَا عَلَى كَثِيرٍ مِنْ عِبَادِهِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ ("And We gave David and Solomon knowledge, and they said: 'Praise belongs to God, who has favoured us over many of His believing servants'") [al-Naml: 15]. And what blessing is better than what David and Solomon were given?"

I say: there is nothing in the verse that indicates what he (may God have mercy on him) understood from it. What it indicates is that they both praised God, may He be glorified, for the blessings with which He had favoured them; so from where does it indicate that His praise is better than His blessing?

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported from Qatada concerning His saying: ﴿وَوَرِثَ سُلَيْمَانُ دَاوُدَ﴾ ("And Solomon inherited David") [al-Naml: 16]: he said: the inheritance is his prophethood, his kingship and his knowledge.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ahmad in al-Zuhd, and Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported from Abu al-Ṣiddīq al-Nājī, who said: Solomon ibn Dawud went out seeking rain for the people. He passed by an ant lying on its back, raising its legs towards the sky, and it was saying: "O God, we are a creation of Your creation, we have no independence from Your provision. So either You give us water, or You destroy us." Then Solomon said to the people: "Return, for you have been watered by the supplication of another."

Al-Hakim narrated in al-Mustadrak, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, who said: Sulayman was given the dominion of the east and the west of the earth. Sulayman ruled for seven hundred years and six months. He ruled all the people of the world, of the jinn, mankind, the beasts, the birds and the predators. He was given everything and the speech of everything. In his time marvelous crafts were made. When Allah wished to take him to Himself, it was revealed to him that he should entrust the knowledge of Allah and His wisdom to his brother. The sons of Dawud were four hundred and eighty men, prophets without messages.

Al-Dhahabi said: This is false. Stories have been related about the greatness of Sulayman's kingdom, and the soul is not at ease in mentioning any of them, so refraining from mentioning them is better.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿So they are held back﴾, that he said: they are pushed back.

Ibn Jarir narrated from him, regarding His saying ﴿So they are held back﴾, that he said: for each class a group of guards was appointed, whose first ranks were turned back upon the last, so that none of them would get ahead of him in the march, as kings do.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿grant me the inspiration﴾, that he said: inspire me.

'Abd ibn Humayd narrated a similar statement from al-Hasan.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated through several chains from Ibn 'Abbas that he was asked how Sulayman checked on the hoopoe among the birds. He said: Sulayman alighted at a station and did not know where the water was, and the hoopoe used to guide Sulayman to the water. So he wanted to ask about it, but found it missing. It was said: How could that be, when a trap is set for it, earth is thrown over it, and a boy sets a snare for it, hides it and catches it? He said: When the decree comes, sight departs.

'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿I will surely punish him with a severe punishment﴾, that he said: I will pluck out all his feathers. A similar statement is narrated from a group of the Successors. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Hasan that he said: the name of Sulayman's hoopoe was Ghabar.

I say: From where did al-Hasan, may Allah have mercy on him, obtain knowledge of this? Likewise, what Ibn 'Asakir narrated from him: that the name of the ant was Haras, that she was from a tribe called the Sons of the Devil, that she was lame, and that she was the size of a wolf. He, may Allah have mercy on him, was the most scrupulous of people about transmitting falsehood. We know that nothing has been authentically related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on this matter, and we know that al-Hasan has no connected chain of narration to Sulayman or to any of his companions. Therefore this knowledge is taken from the Ahl al-Kitab (People of the Book), and we have been commanded: "Neither believe them nor disbelieve them." If someone allows himself leniency in narrating from them on the basis of what was reported: "Narrate from the Children of Israel, and there is no harm," then that does not apply, without doubt, to what concerns the interpretation of the Book of Allah, the Exalted, but rather to the stories that happened to them.

We have repeatedly drawn attention to this kind of thing whenever strange interpretations come up.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿or he must bring me a clear authority﴾, that he said: the report of the truth, true and clear.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from 'Ikrimah, who said: Ibn 'Abbas said: every "authority" (sultan) in the Qur'an is a proof. He mentioned this verse, then said: And what authority did the hoopoe have? He meant that "authority" here means proof, not the authority which is kingship.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, regarding His saying ﴿I have encompassed what you have not encompassed﴾, that he said: I have come to know what you have not come to know.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him ﴿and I have come to you from Saba'﴾, that he said: Saba' is in the land of Yemen, which is called Ma'rib, between it and San'a is a three-night journey. ﴿with certain news﴾: with true information.

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir also narrated from him ﴿I found a woman ruling over them﴾, that he said: her name was Bilqis, daughter of Dhi Sharah, and she was strong and poetic.

It is narrated from al-Hasan, Qatadah and Zuhayr ibn Muhammad that she was Bilqis, daughter of Sharahil. From Ibn Jurayj: she was the daughter of Dhi Sharh.

Ibn Jarir, Abu al-Shaykh in al-'Azamah, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "One of the two parents of Bilqis was a jinn."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿and she has a magnificent throne﴾, that he said: a noble throne of gold, its legs of jewels and pearls, of fine craftsmanship and great price.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, regarding His saying ﴿who brings forth what is hidden﴾, that he said: He knows every hidden thing in the heavens and the earth.

When He had finished with the story of Moses, Glorified is He, He moved to the story of Dawud (David) and his son Sulayman (Solomon). These stories, and what comes before and after them, serve as an elaboration and confirmation of His words: ﴿And indeed, you are receiving the Qur'an from One who is Wise and Knowing﴾ [al-Naml: 6]. The tanwin in ʿilman (knowledge) is either for the category (naw', meaning "a portion of knowledge") or for magnification (ta'zim, meaning "much knowledge"). The waw in His words ﴿And they said, "All praise is for Allah"﴾ is a conjunction (ʿatf) on a deleted element, because this context calls for a fa' (then). The sense is: "And We gave them both knowledge, so they acted upon it, and they said, 'All praise is for Allah.'" This is supported by the fact that thanking with the tongue is only fitting when it is preceded by an act of the heart, namely the resolve to perform obedience and abandon disobedience. ﴿Who has favored us over many of His believing servants﴾, meaning: He favored us with knowledge, prophethood, and the subjugation of the birds, the jinn, and mankind. They did not regard themselves as superior to everyone, out of humility.

The verse indicates the nobility of knowledge and the elevation of its status, that the blessing of knowledge is among the greatest blessings with which Allah favors His servants, and that whoever is given it has been given a virtue over many of the servants and granted a magnificent honor.

﴿And Sulayman inherited from Dawud﴾, meaning he inherited knowledge and prophethood.

Qatadah and al-Kalbi said: Dawud had nineteen male sons, and Sulayman inherited his prophethood from among them. Had the intended meaning been the inheritance of wealth, He would not have singled out Sulayman, since all of his sons were equal in that regard. Most of the exegetes also said this. Therefore this inheritance is a metaphorical inheritance, as in the words of the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "The scholars are the heirs of the prophets."

﴿And he said, "O people, we have been taught the speech of the birds"﴾. Sulayman spoke these words addressing the people, by way of relating the blessing Allah had bestowed upon him and giving thanks for the favor He singled him out with. He mentioned the speech of the birds first because it is a special blessing granted to him, which no one else shares with him.

Al-Farra' said: "The speech of the birds" is their language, which was treated like the speech of a man. He recited the verse of Humayd ibn Thawr:

"It is strange to her that her song should be eloquent, while it did not fail to be [clear] in her speech"

The meaning of the verse is: we understood what the birds say.

Some exegetes said: he was taught the speech of all animals, and he mentioned the birds specifically because they were among his troops, travelling with him to shade him from the sun.

Qatadah and al-Sha'bi said: he was taught only the speech of the birds, and this is not refuted by the ant, since it is one of the birds: ants often grow wings and fly. Thus this ant whose speech he heard and understood was of that kind.

﴿And we have been given of everything﴾ means: everything that need calls for, such as knowledge, prophethood, wisdom, wealth, the subjugation of the jinn, mankind, birds, winds, wild beasts, and animals, and everything that is between the heaven and the earth.

Sulayman used the plural of majesty (nun al-ʿazamah), and he meant himself, to show his condition of being obeyed and not opposed. This was not out of arrogance or self-magnification. The reference in His words ﴿Indeed, this﴾ is to what was previously mentioned of teaching and giving. ﴿Surely this is the manifest bounty﴾, meaning the evident and clear [favor], which is hidden from no one, or that which displays Our excellence.

(p-1075) ﴿And Sulayman's forces were gathered together for him, of the jinn and mankind and birds﴾. Ḥashr means gathering, so his troops were assembled for him from these categories.

The exegetes have gone to great lengths in describing the size of his army, and many of them exaggerated to a degree that minds find improbable and that is not sound according to transmission. Even if it were sound, there would be in Divine power something greater and more extensive than that. ﴿And they were held in ranks﴾, meaning each group had a warden who kept the first of them back from the last, so that they would stand in their ranks. It is said: wazaʿahu yazaʿuhu wazʿan, meaning he restrained him. The wazi' in war is the one assigned to the rows, who restrains those who go forward; from this comes the verse of al-Nabighah:

"When I rebuked white hair for youth, and said: 'Alas! Be still, for the white hair is a restrainer.'"

And the words of another:

"Whoever is not restrained by his intellect and his modesty, there is no restrainer for him from the grey of his temples."

And the words of another:

"Only a person of full intellect and perfection restrains the stubborn soul from desire, among people."

It is also said that it derives from tawzi', meaning dispersal; it is said: "The people are awzaʿ," meaning groups.

﴿Until, when they came upon the valley of the ants﴾. Ḥattā (until) is the particle after which speech begins, and it marks the end point of what precedes it. The meaning is: "they were held in ranks until the attainment of this end, which is their arriving at the valley of the ants." That is, they were proceeding with some of them prevented from separating from others, until, when they came to the valley, etc. ʿAlā wadi al-namli is connected to atau (came), and it was used with ʿalā because they were carried by the wind, so they were above it.

The meaning: they crossed the valley and reached its far end. All the readers stopped on wād without a yā', following the orthography, since it was not deleted due to the meeting of two sukūns, as in His words ﴿Who hewed out the rocks in the valley﴾ [al-Fajr: 9]. Only al-Kisa'i stopped with the yā', saying: "What necessitates deletion is only the meeting of two sukūns in continuous speech."

Ka'b said: the valley of the ants is in al-Ta'if. Qatadah and Muqatil said: it is in al-Sham (Syria).

﴿An ant said﴾. This is the response to idha (when). It is as if, when it saw them heading toward the valley, it fled and alerted the rest of the ants, calling out to them, saying: ﴿O ants, enter your dwellings﴾. It addressed the ants as one would address rational beings, since they understand that address. The masakin (dwellings) are the places in which ants live.

It is said: this ant whom Sulayman heard was female, as evidenced by the feminine form of the verb attributed to it.

Abu Hayyan rejected this, saying: the attachment of the taʾ in qalat does not indicate that the ant is feminine. It is valid to say of a male: qalat, because it is "namlah" (a female-form noun). Even if it has the taʾ, it is one of those in which the masculine cannot be distinguished from the feminine by the gender of the verb, but rather is distinguished by reporting whether it is male or female. Nothing of great benefit depends on this, nor on examining the name of the ant, nor on the fabricated stories and false narrations that have been related.

Al-Hasan, Talhah, and Ma'mar ibn Sulayman read "namlatun" and "al-namul" with a ḍammah on the mīm and a fatḥah on the nūn, in the pattern of rajul and samurah. Sulayman al-Taymi read with two ḍammahs on both.

﴿Let not Sulayman and his troops crush you﴾. Al-ḥaṭm means breaking; it is said: ḥaṭamtuhu ḥaṭman, meaning I broke it, breaking. Taḥaṭṭama means to be shattered. This prohibition is outwardly addressed to the ants, but in reality it is addressed to Sulayman. It is thus of the type: "Let me not see you here." It may be a substitute for the imperative, and it may be an answer to the imperative.

Abu Hayyan said: as for its analysis as an answer to the imperative, that is only possible on the reading of al-A'mash, who read "la yaḥṭimkum" with jazm and without the nun of emphasis. But with the nun of emphasis, that is not permitted except in poetry.

Sibawayh said: it is rare in poetry; they treated it like the prohibition, since it is jussive.

Ubayy read "udkhulu masakinakunna" (enter your dwellings, feminine plural). Shahr ibn Hawshab read "maskanakum." Al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Qatadah, and ʿIsa al-Hamdani read "la yuḥaṭṭimannakum" with a ḍammah on the yā', a fatḥah on the ḥā', and a shaddah on the ṭā'. Ibn Ishaq, Ya'qub, and Abu ʿAmr in one narration read with the sukūn of the nun of emphasis.

The clause ﴿while they do not perceive﴾ is in the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) relating to the subject of yaḥṭimannakum, meaning: they will not perceive your being crushed, nor will they know your location. It has also been said that the meaning is: "and the ants do not perceive that Sulayman understands their speech," but this is far-fetched.

﴿So he smiled, laughing at her speech﴾. Ibn al-Sumayfa' read "ḍaḥikan" (laughter, as a masdar). According to the reading of the majority, ḍāḥikan is an emphatic circumstantial (ḥāl mu'akkidah), because laughter has already been understood from smiling. It has also been said that it is a projected circumstantial (ḥāl muqaddarah), since smiling is the beginning of laughter. It is also said that since smiling may be due to anger, laughter clarifies it. It is also said that the laughter of the prophets is only smiling and nothing more. On the reading of Ibn al-Sumayfa', ḍaḥikan is a masdar in the accusative governed by a deleted verb, or in the position of a circumstantial. Sulayman's laughter was out of wonder at her speech, her understanding, and her guidance to warning the ants.

﴿And he said, "My Lord, enable me to be grateful for Your blessing with which You have favored me and my parents"﴾. The explanation of awziʿni (enable me) has already been given shortly before, in His words ﴿So they were held in ranks﴾ [al-Naml: 17; Fussilat: 19]. In al-Kashshaf it is said: The literal meaning of awziʿni is: "make me restrain the thanks for Your blessings within me, and restrain it, and bind it, so that it does not escape from me, until I never cease to be thankful to You." End of quote.

Al-Wahidi said: "awziʿni" means: "inspire me to be grateful for Your blessing with which You favored me." It is said: "So-and-so is muwazzaʿ with such-and-such," meaning he is devoted to it. End of quote.

Al-Qurtubi said: it derives from wazi'a, as if he said: "Restrain me from what displeases You." End of quote.

The second object of awziʿni is: "that I be grateful for Your blessing with which You favored me."

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of awziʿni is: "prevent me from being ungrateful for Your blessing." This is an explanation by a necessary implication. The meaning of ﴿and upon my parents﴾ is his supplication that Allah enable him to be thankful for His blessing upon his parents, just as He enabled him to be thankful for His blessing upon himself, since bestowing favor upon them is a bestowal of favor upon him, and that requires gratitude from him to Allah, Glorified is He. Then he asked that Allah add to him the consequences of His blessings to their precedents, especially the religious blessings, so he said: ﴿And that I do righteous deeds which You are pleased with﴾, meaning: a righteous deed which You are pleased with from me. Then he prayed that Allah, Glorified is He, would place him in the Hereafter among the righteous, for that is the ultimate goal to which the request relates. So he said: ﴿And admit me by Your mercy among Your righteous servants﴾. The meaning is: admit me into their company, record my name among their names, and gather me in their group to the abode of the righteous, which is Paradise. O Allah, I call upon You with what this noble Prophet called upon You, so accept that from me and bestow Your favor upon me with it, for although I am deficient in deeds, Your bounty is the cause of attaining good.

This verse thus proclaims, with the loudest voice and the clearest explanation, that entry into Paradise, which is the abode of the believers (p-1076), is by Your favor and not by their deeds, just as Your truthful Messenger (ﷺ) said in what is established in the Sahih: "Be steadfast, strive to be close [to the right path], and know that none of you will enter Paradise by his deeds." They said: "Not even you, O Messenger of God?" He said: "Not even I, unless Allah covers me with His mercy." So when there is nothing but Your vast favor, abandoning the request for it from You is incapacity, and neglecting the means of reaching You so that it reaches him is a waste.

Then Glorified is He began to mention the story of Bilqis and what happened between her and Sulayman, and that was by means of the hoopoe. So He said: ﴿And he inspected the birds﴾. Tafaqqud means searching for what has been lost to you and inquiring about its condition. Al-ṭayr is a collective noun for everything that flies. The meaning is that he searched for the birds that were missing and inquired about the condition of those that were absent, and the birds used to accompany him on his journey and shade him with their wings.

﴿And he said, "What is wrong with me, that I do not see the hoopoe? Or is he among the absent?"﴾. That is: "What is the matter with the hoopoe that I do not see him?" This speech is among the inverted speech that the Arabs use frequently. It has also been said: there is no need to claim inversion; rather it is a question about what prevents him from seeing the hoopoe, as if he said: "What is with me that I do not see him? Is it because of some screen that conceals him from me, or for some other reason?" Then it became clear to him that he was absent, so he said: ﴿Or is he among the absent?﴾. The am here is the disconnected one that carries the sense of a change of subject (idrab). Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muhaysin, Hisham, and Ayyub read "ma liya" with a fatḥah on the yā'. They also read so in Ya Sin: ﴿And why should I not worship Him who created me﴾ [Ya Sin: 22] with a fatḥah on the yā'. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Ya'qub read with a sukūn on it in both places. The rest read with a fatḥah on the one in Ya Sin and a sukūn on the one here.

Abu ʿAmr said: because the one here is interrogative, while the one in Ya Sin is negative. Abu Hatim and Abu ʿUbayd preferred the sukūn.

﴿I will surely punish him with a severe punishment, or I will surely slaughter him﴾.

﴿Concerning this severe punishment, the scholars differed as to what it was. Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj said: it is that he (the hoopoe) be plucked of all his feathers. Yazid ibn Ruman said: it is that the feathers of his two wings be plucked. It was also said: it is that he be confined with his like (i.e., with others of his kind). It was also said: it is that he be prevented from serving him. In this there is evidence that the punishment is proportioned to the offence, not to the size of the body.

His saying ﴿عَذَابًا﴾ (ʿadhāban, "a punishment") is either an ism al-maṣdar (verbal noun, a noun of action that is not a true infinitive) or a maṣdar (infinitive) with its extra elements omitted, like His saying: ﴿وَاللَّهُ أَنْبَتَكُمْ مِنَ الْأَرْضِ نَبَاتًا﴾ [Nuh: 17] ("And God made you grow from the earth as a growth"), and ﴿أَوْ لَيَأْتِيَنِّي بِسُلْطَانٍ مُبِينٍ﴾ ("or he must bring me a clear authority"). Ibn Kathir alone read it with the emphatic nun (nūn al-tawkīd) doubled, followed by the nun of protection (nūn al-wiqāya). The rest read with a doubled nun only, which is the nun of emphasis. ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar read it with a doubled nun, vowelled with a fatḥa, not joined to a yā'. The clear authority (al-sulṭān al-mubīn) is the evident proof in his absence.

﴿فَمَكَثَ غَيْرَ بَعِيدٍ﴾ means: the hoopoe remained for a period not far off (i.e., not long).

The majority read ﴿مَكُثَ﴾ with a ḍamma on the kāf. ʿĀṣim alone read it with a fatḥa. The meaning in both readings is: he stayed for a period not far off.

Sibawayh said: makatha yamkuthu mukūthan is like qaʿada yaqʿudu quʿūdan.

It was also said that the pronoun in ﴿مَكَثَ﴾ refers to Solomon. The meaning would then be: Solomon remained, after the inspection and the threat, for a period not long. The first view is preferable.

﴿فَقَالَ أَحَطْتُ بِمَا لَمْ تُحِطْ بِهِ﴾ means: I have come to know what you have not come to know of the matter. Iḥāṭa (encompassing) is knowledge of a thing from all its aspects. There is probably an omission in the speech, and the sense is: the hoopoe remained for a period not far off, then came and was rebuked for his absence, and he said by way of excuse, ﴿أَحَطْتُ بِمَا لَمْ تُحِطْ بِهِ﴾.

Al-Farraʾ said: it is permissible to assimilate the tāʾ into the ṭāʾ (idgham, assimilation of one consonant into another), so one says aḥuṭṭu, and to assimilate the ṭāʾ into the tāʾ, so one says aḥattu.

﴿وَجِئْتُكَ مِنْ سَبَإٍ بِنَبَإٍ يَقِينٍ﴾. The majority read ﴿مِنْ سَبَإٍ﴾ with tanwīn (nunation, i.e., declined), taking it as the name of a man from whom a people were named. The poet's verse testifies to this:

"The arrivers, and Taym on the heights of Saba',
the hides of buffalo have chafed their necks."

Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read it with a fatḥa on the hamza and without tanwīn, taking it as the name of a city. Al-Zajjaj denied that it is the name of a man and said: Saba' is the name of a city known as Maʾrib of Yemen, between it and Sanaʾ three days' distance.

It was also said that it is the name of a woman after whom the city was named.

Al-Qurtubi said: the correct view is that it is the name of a man, as in the book of al-Tirmidhi from the ḥadīth of Farwa ibn Musayk al-Muradi. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: this was hidden from al-Zajjaj, so he blundered like a blind-night stumbler (khabṭa ʿashwāʾ). Al-Farraʾ claimed that al-Ruʾāsī asked Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ about Saba', and he said: "I do not know what it is." Al-Naḥḥās said: Abu ʿAmr is too exalted to say this. He said: the matter concerning Saba' is what the transmitted report has established, that originally it is the name of a man. If you apply tanwīn to it, it is because it has become the name of a tribe; if you do not apply tanwīn, you make it the name of a tribe, like Thamud. However, the preferred form according to Sibawayh is with tanwīn. End of quotation.

I say: there is no doubt that Saba' is the name of a city in Yemen where Bilqis was, and it is also the name of a man of Qaḥṭān, namely Saba' ibn Yashjub ibn Yaʿrub ibn Qaḥṭān ibn Hud. But what is meant here is that the hoopoe came to Solomon with news of what he had seen in the city of Saba', described as such, and there will come at the end of this discussion, from transmitted reports, what clarifies and supports this. The meaning of the verse is that the hoopoe came to Solomon from this city with a certain news. A nabaʾ is a weighty news. When the hoopoe said to Solomon what he said, Solomon said to him: "And what is that?" He said:

﴿إِنِّي وَجَدْتُ امْرَأَةً تَمْلِكُهُمْ﴾ ("I found a woman ruling over them"). She was Bilqis, daughter of Sharahil. The hoopoe found her ruling the people of Saba'. This sentence serves as an explanation and elaboration of the sentence before it. That is: this certain news is that this woman rules over them.

﴿وَأُوتِيَتْ مِنْ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ﴾ ("and she has been given of everything") contains hyperbole. The meaning is that she was given of every one of the things she needs. It was also said: the meaning is: she was given of everything in her time, some thing, and "some thing" is omitted because the speech indicates it.

﴿وَلَهَا عَرْشٌ عَظِيمٌ﴾ ("and she has a mighty throne"): that is, a great throne. It was described as great because, as it is said, it was of gold, eighty cubits long, forty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high into the sky, set with pearls, red rubies and green emeralds. It was also said: the throne here means kingship. The first view is preferable, because of His saying: ﴿أَيُّكُمْ يَأْتِينِي بِعَرْشِهَا﴾ ("Which of you will bring me her throne?").

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: what necessarily follows from the verse is that she was a queen over the cities of Yemen, possessing a great kingdom and a great throne, and she was an unbeliever from a disbelieving people.

﴿وَجَدْتُهَا وَقَوْمَهَا يَسْجُدُونَ لِلشَّمْسِ مِنْ دُونِ اللَّهِ﴾ ("I found her and her people prostrating to the sun instead of God"): that is, they worship it, exceeding the worship of God, may He be glorified. It was said: they were Magians. It was said: they were zindīqs (heretics). ﴿وَزَيَّنَ لَهُمُ الشَّيْطَانُ أَعْمَالَهُمْ﴾ ("and Satan made their deeds appealing to them"), namely the worship of the sun and the rest of their works of disbelief. ﴿فَصَدَّهُمْ عَنِ السَّبِيلِ﴾ ("and so he barred them from the way"): that is, Satan barred them, through that adornment, from the clear path, which is faith in God and affirming His oneness. ﴿فَهُمْ لَا يَهْتَدُونَ﴾ ("so they are not guided") to that.

﴿أَلَّا يَسْجُدُوا﴾ (allā yasjudū). The majority read the lām with shadda (tashdīd) in ﴿أَلَّا﴾.

Ibn al-Anbari said: stopping at ﴿فَهُمْ لَا يَهْتَدُونَ﴾ is not a complete stop according to the one who doubles the lām in ﴿أَلَّا﴾, because the meaning is: "Satan made their deeds appealing to them so that they do not prostrate."

Al-Naḥḥās said: it is ﴿أَنْ﴾ (an) with ﴿لَا﴾ (lā) entering upon it, and it is in the accusative position.

Al-Akhfash said: that is, he made it appealing to them that they should not prostrate to God, meaning "lest they prostrate to God."

Al-Kisāʾī said: it is in the accusative position governed by ﴿صَدَّهُمْ﴾ ("barred them"), that is: "so he barred them from prostrating," in the sense of "lest they prostrate." On both views it is an object of purpose (mafʿūl lahu).

Al-Yazidi said: it is a substitute (badal) for ﴿أَعْمَالَهُمْ﴾ ("their deeds") in the accusative position.

Abu ʿAmr said: it is in the genitive position as a substitute for ﴿السَّبِيلِ﴾ ("the way").

It was also said: the governing word for it is ﴿لَا يَهْتَدُونَ﴾ ("they are not guided"), that is: "they are not guided to prostrate to God," and in this view ﴿لَا﴾ is extra, like His saying: ﴿مَا مَنَعَكَ أَلَّا تَسْجُدَ﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 12] ("What prevented you from prostrating?").

According to the reading of the majority, this verse is not a place of prostration, because it is a report about them, that they abandoned prostration, either through the adornment, or through barring, or through preventing guidance. Al-Zajjaj preferred its being a reason for the barring, and al-Farraʾ preferred its being a reason for ﴿زَيَّنَ﴾ ("made appealing"). He said: he made their deeds appealing to them lest they prostrate, then the lām was omitted.

Al-Zuhri and al-Kisāʾī read ﴿أَلَّا﴾ with lightening (takhfīf). Al-Kisāʾī said: I did not hear the elders reading it except with lightening, on the intention of a command, so ﴿أَلَا﴾ in this reading is a particle of alerting and opening (ḥarf tanbīh wa-istiftāḥ), and what follows it is a vocative particle (ḥarf nidāʾ), and ﴿اسْجُدُوا﴾ is an imperative verb. In this reading the script should have been ﴿أَلَا يَا اسْجُدُوا﴾, but the Companions, may God be pleased with them, dropped the alif of ﴿يَا﴾ and the hamzat al-waṣl of ﴿اسْجُدُوا﴾ in error, and joined the yā' to the sīn of ﴿اسْجُدُوا﴾, so the written form became ﴿أَلَا يَسْجُدُوا﴾. The called-upon noun is omitted, and its estimate is: "Ah, O people, prostrate!" The Arabs often omit the vocative noun in their speech, and from this is the saying of the poet:

"Ah, O abode of Mayy, be safe in decay,
and may the rain never cease to pour upon your gravel plains."

And the saying of another:

"Ah, be safe, there be safe, there be safe,
three greetings, even if you do not speak."

And the saying of another also:

"Ah, be safe, O Hind, Hind of the Banu Bakr."

And this is common in their poetry.

Al-Zajjaj said: the reading with lightening requires the obligation of prostration, unlike the reading with doubling. Abu Ḥatim and Abu ʿUbayd preferred the reading with doubling. Al-Zajjaj said: the reading with lightening has a good aspect, except that in it the report is cut off from the matter of Saba', then there is a return after that to mentioning them.

The reading with doubling is a report that follows one part after another without a break in its middle. Al-Naḥḥās said likewise. On this reading the clause ﴿أَلَّا يَسْجُدُوا﴾ is an interjected statement, either from the speech of the hoopoe, or from the speech of Solomon, or from the speech of God, may He be glorified.

In this reading there is also the reading of ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud, "هَلْ لَا تَسْجُدُوا" (hal lā tasjudū), with the second person (tāʾ of address), and in the reading of Ubayy, "أَلَّا تَسْجُدُوا" (allā tasjudū), also with the second person.

﴿الَّذِي يُخْرِجُ الْخَبْءَ فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ﴾ ("who brings forth what is hidden in the heavens and the earth"): that is, He makes manifest what is concealed and hidden in them. It is said: I hid the thing, akhbaʾuhu khabʾan, and al-khabʾ is what you have hidden.

Al-Zajjaj said: it has come in the exegesis that al-khabʾ here means the rain from the sky and the plants from the earth. It was also said: the hidden things of the earth are its treasures and its plants. Qatada said: al-khabʾ is the secret. Al-Naḥḥās said: that is, what is absent in the heavens and the earth. Ubayy and ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar read "الخَبَ" (al-khabā, without hamza) with a fatḥa on the bāʾ, by lightening. ʿAbd Allah, ʿIkrima and Malik ibn Dinar read "الخَبَا" (al-khabā) with an alif. Abu Ḥatim said: this is not permissible in Arabic. It was answered that Sibawayh reported from the Arabs that the alif replaces the hamza when a sukūn precedes it. In the reading of ʿAbd Allah it is "يُخْرِجُ الخَبَ مِنَ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ" ("He brings forth the hidden from the heavens and the earth").

Al-Farraʾ said: "min" (from) and "fī" (in) alternate with each other. The relative clause may be in the genitive position as a qualifier (naʿt) of God, may He be glorified, or as a substitute (badal) of Him, or as an explanation (bayān) of Him. It may be in the accusative position by way of praise, and it may be in the nominative position as the predicate of an omitted subject.

The clause ﴿وَيَعْلَمُ مَا تُخْفُونَ وَمَا تُعْلِنُونَ﴾ ("and He knows what you conceal and what you disclose") is conjoined to ﴿يُخْرِجُ﴾ ("brings forth"). The majority read both verbs with the yā' (third person). Al-Juḥdari, ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar, Ḥafs and al-Kisāʾī read them with the tāʾ (second person, address). As for the first reading, it is because the pronouns preceding it are third-person pronouns. As for the second reading, it is because in the reading of al-Zuhri and al-Kisāʾī the command to prostrate is included, and the address to them with it, so this, in their view, is part of that address.

The meaning is: God, may He be glorified, brings forth from this human world what is hidden in it by His knowledge of it, just as He brings forth what is hidden in the heavens and the earth. Then, after describing the Lord, may He be glorified, with what has preceded, which indicates the greatness of His power, the sublimity of His authority, the obligation of affirming His oneness and singling Him out for worship, He said:

﴿اللَّهُ لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا هُوَ رَبُّ الْعَرْشِ الْعَظِيمِ﴾ ("God; there is no god but Him, the Lord of the Mighty Throne"). The majority read ﴿الْعَظِيمِ﴾ with the genitive, as a qualifier of ﴿الْعَرْشِ﴾ ("the Throne"). Ibn Muḥaysin read it with the nominative, as a qualifier of ﴿الرَّبِّ﴾ ("the Lord"). The Throne was singled out for mention because it is the greatest of created things, as is established in the report traced back to the Messenger of God, may God's blessings and peace be upon him and his family.

Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported from ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz that he wrote: "God has not bestowed a blessing upon a servant and then the servant praised God for it, except that his praise was better than his blessing. Were you not to know this except from the revealed Book of God, He, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿وَلَقَدْ آتَيْنَا دَاوُدَ وَسُلَيْمَانَ عِلْمًا وَقَالَا الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ الَّذِي فَضَّلَنَا عَلَى كَثِيرٍ مِنْ عِبَادِهِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ ("And We gave David and Solomon knowledge, and they said: 'Praise belongs to God, who has favoured us over many of His believing servants'") [al-Naml: 15]. And what blessing is better than what David and Solomon were given?"

I say: there is nothing in the verse that indicates what he (may God have mercy on him) understood from it. What it indicates is that they both praised God, may He be glorified, for the blessings with which He had favoured them; so from where does it indicate that His praise is better than His blessing?

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported from Qatada concerning His saying: ﴿وَوَرِثَ سُلَيْمَانُ دَاوُدَ﴾ ("And Solomon inherited David") [al-Naml: 16]: he said: the inheritance is his prophethood, his kingship and his knowledge.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ahmad in al-Zuhd, and Ibn Abi Ḥatim reported from Abu al-Ṣiddīq al-Nājī, who said: Solomon ibn Dawud went out seeking rain for the people. He passed by an ant lying on its back, raising its legs towards the sky, and it was saying: "O God, we are a creation of Your creation, we have no independence from Your provision. So either You give us water, or You destroy us." Then Solomon said to the people: "Return, for you have been watered by the supplication of another."

Al-Hakim narrated in al-Mustadrak, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, who said: Sulayman was given the dominion of the east and the west of the earth. Sulayman ruled for seven hundred years and six months. He ruled all the people of the world, of the jinn, mankind, the beasts, the birds and the predators. He was given everything and the speech of everything. In his time marvelous crafts were made. When Allah wished to take him to Himself, it was revealed to him that he should entrust the knowledge of Allah and His wisdom to his brother. The sons of Dawud were four hundred and eighty men, prophets without messages.

Al-Dhahabi said: This is false. Stories have been related about the greatness of Sulayman's kingdom, and the soul is not at ease in mentioning any of them, so refraining from mentioning them is better.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿So they are held back﴾, that he said: they are pushed back.

Ibn Jarir narrated from him, regarding His saying ﴿So they are held back﴾, that he said: for each class a group of guards was appointed, whose first ranks were turned back upon the last, so that none of them would get ahead of him in the march, as kings do.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿grant me the inspiration﴾, that he said: inspire me.

'Abd ibn Humayd narrated a similar statement from al-Hasan.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated through several chains from Ibn 'Abbas that he was asked how Sulayman checked on the hoopoe among the birds. He said: Sulayman alighted at a station and did not know where the water was, and the hoopoe used to guide Sulayman to the water. So he wanted to ask about it, but found it missing. It was said: How could that be, when a trap is set for it, earth is thrown over it, and a boy sets a snare for it, hides it and catches it? He said: When the decree comes, sight departs.

'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿I will surely punish him with a severe punishment﴾, that he said: I will pluck out all his feathers. A similar statement is narrated from a group of the Successors. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Hasan that he said: the name of Sulayman's hoopoe was Ghabar.

I say: From where did al-Hasan, may Allah have mercy on him, obtain knowledge of this? Likewise, what Ibn 'Asakir narrated from him: that the name of the ant was Haras, that she was from a tribe called the Sons of the Devil, that she was lame, and that she was the size of a wolf. He, may Allah have mercy on him, was the most scrupulous of people about transmitting falsehood. We know that nothing has been authentically related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on this matter, and we know that al-Hasan has no connected chain of narration to Sulayman or to any of his companions. Therefore this knowledge is taken from the Ahl al-Kitab (People of the Book), and we have been commanded: "Neither believe them nor disbelieve them." If someone allows himself leniency in narrating from them on the basis of what was reported: "Narrate from the Children of Israel, and there is no harm," then that does not apply, without doubt, to what concerns the interpretation of the Book of Allah, the Exalted, but rather to the stories that happened to them.

We have repeatedly drawn attention to this kind of thing whenever strange interpretations come up.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿or he must bring me a clear authority﴾, that he said: the report of the truth, true and clear.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from 'Ikrimah, who said: Ibn 'Abbas said: every "authority" (sultan) in the Qur'an is a proof. He mentioned this verse, then said: And what authority did the hoopoe have? He meant that "authority" here means proof, not the authority which is kingship.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, regarding His saying ﴿I have encompassed what you have not encompassed﴾, that he said: I have come to know what you have not come to know.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him ﴿and I have come to you from Saba'﴾, that he said: Saba' is in the land of Yemen, which is called Ma'rib, between it and San'a is a three-night journey. ﴿with certain news﴾: with true information.

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir also narrated from him ﴿I found a woman ruling over them﴾, that he said: her name was Bilqis, daughter of Dhi Sharah, and she was strong and poetic.

It is narrated from al-Hasan, Qatadah and Zuhayr ibn Muhammad that she was Bilqis, daughter of Sharahil. From Ibn Jurayj: she was the daughter of Dhi Sharh.

Ibn Jarir, Abu al-Shaykh in al-'Azamah, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "One of the two parents of Bilqis was a jinn."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿and she has a magnificent throne﴾, that he said: a noble throne of gold, its legs of jewels and pearls, of fine craftsmanship and great price.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, regarding His saying ﴿who brings forth what is hidden﴾, that he said: He knows every hidden thing in the heavens and the earth.

When He had finished with the story of Moses, Glorified is He, He moved to the story of Dawud (David) and his son Sulayman (Solomon). These stories, and what comes before and after them, serve as an elaboration and confirmation of His words: ﴿And indeed, you are receiving the Qur'an from One who is Wise and Knowing﴾ [al-Naml: 6]. The tanwin in ʿilman (knowledge) is either for the category (naw', meaning "a portion of knowledge") or for magnification (ta'zim, meaning "much knowledge"). The waw in His words ﴿And they said, "All praise is for Allah"﴾ is a conjunction (ʿatf) on a deleted element, because this context calls for a fa' (then). The sense is: "And We gave them both knowledge, so they acted upon it, and they said, 'All praise is for Allah.'" This is supported by the fact that thanking with the tongue is only fitting when it is preceded by an act of the heart, namely the resolve to perform obedience and abandon disobedience. ﴿Who has favored us over many of His believing servants﴾, meaning: He favored us with knowledge, prophethood, and the subjugation of the birds, the jinn, and mankind. They did not regard themselves as superior to everyone, out of humility.

The verse indicates the nobility of knowledge and the elevation of its status, that the blessing of knowledge is among the greatest blessings with which Allah favors His servants, and that whoever is given it has been given a virtue over many of the servants and granted a magnificent honor.

﴿And Sulayman inherited from Dawud﴾, meaning he inherited knowledge and prophethood.

Qatadah and al-Kalbi said: Dawud had nineteen male sons, and Sulayman inherited his prophethood from among them. Had the intended meaning been the inheritance of wealth, He would not have singled out Sulayman, since all of his sons were equal in that regard. Most of the exegetes also said this. Therefore this inheritance is a metaphorical inheritance, as in the words of the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "The scholars are the heirs of the prophets."

﴿And he said, "O people, we have been taught the speech of the birds"﴾. Sulayman spoke these words addressing the people, by way of relating the blessing Allah had bestowed upon him and giving thanks for the favor He singled him out with. He mentioned the speech of the birds first because it is a special blessing granted to him, which no one else shares with him.

Al-Farra' said: "The speech of the birds" is their language, which was treated like the speech of a man. He recited the verse of Humayd ibn Thawr:

"It is strange to her that her song should be eloquent, while it did not fail to be [clear] in her speech"

The meaning of the verse is: we understood what the birds say.

Some exegetes said: he was taught the speech of all animals, and he mentioned the birds specifically because they were among his troops, travelling with him to shade him from the sun.

Qatadah and al-Sha'bi said: he was taught only the speech of the birds, and this is not refuted by the ant, since it is one of the birds: ants often grow wings and fly. Thus this ant whose speech he heard and understood was of that kind.

﴿And we have been given of everything﴾ means: everything that need calls for, such as knowledge, prophethood, wisdom, wealth, the subjugation of the jinn, mankind, birds, winds, wild beasts, and animals, and everything that is between the heaven and the earth.

Sulayman used the plural of majesty (nun al-ʿazamah), and he meant himself, to show his condition of being obeyed and not opposed. This was not out of arrogance or self-magnification. The reference in His words ﴿Indeed, this﴾ is to what was previously mentioned of teaching and giving. ﴿Surely this is the manifest bounty﴾, meaning the evident and clear [favor], which is hidden from no one, or that which displays Our excellence.

(p-1075) ﴿And Sulayman's forces were gathered together for him, of the jinn and mankind and birds﴾. Ḥashr means gathering, so his troops were assembled for him from these categories.

The exegetes have gone to great lengths in describing the size of his army, and many of them exaggerated to a degree that minds find improbable and that is not sound according to transmission. Even if it were sound, there would be in Divine power something greater and more extensive than that. ﴿And they were held in ranks﴾, meaning each group had a warden who kept the first of them back from the last, so that they would stand in their ranks. It is said: wazaʿahu yazaʿuhu wazʿan, meaning he restrained him. The wazi' in war is the one assigned to the rows, who restrains those who go forward; from this comes the verse of al-Nabighah:

"When I rebuked white hair for youth, and said: 'Alas! Be still, for the white hair is a restrainer.'"

And the words of another:

"Whoever is not restrained by his intellect and his modesty, there is no restrainer for him from the grey of his temples."

And the words of another:

"Only a person of full intellect and perfection restrains the stubborn soul from desire, among people."

It is also said that it derives from tawzi', meaning dispersal; it is said: "The people are awzaʿ," meaning groups.

﴿Until, when they came upon the valley of the ants﴾. Ḥattā (until) is the particle after which speech begins, and it marks the end point of what precedes it. The meaning is: "they were held in ranks until the attainment of this end, which is their arriving at the valley of the ants." That is, they were proceeding with some of them prevented from separating from others, until, when they came to the valley, etc. ʿAlā wadi al-namli is connected to atau (came), and it was used with ʿalā because they were carried by the wind, so they were above it.

The meaning: they crossed the valley and reached its far end. All the readers stopped on wād without a yā', following the orthography, since it was not deleted due to the meeting of two sukūns, as in His words ﴿Who hewed out the rocks in the valley﴾ [al-Fajr: 9]. Only al-Kisa'i stopped with the yā', saying: "What necessitates deletion is only the meeting of two sukūns in continuous speech."

Ka'b said: the valley of the ants is in al-Ta'if. Qatadah and Muqatil said: it is in al-Sham (Syria).

﴿An ant said﴾. This is the response to idha (when). It is as if, when it saw them heading toward the valley, it fled and alerted the rest of the ants, calling out to them, saying: ﴿O ants, enter your dwellings﴾. It addressed the ants as one would address rational beings, since they understand that address. The masakin (dwellings) are the places in which ants live.

It is said: this ant whom Sulayman heard was female, as evidenced by the feminine form of the verb attributed to it.

Abu Hayyan rejected this, saying: the attachment of the taʾ in qalat does not indicate that the ant is feminine. It is valid to say of a male: qalat, because it is "namlah" (a female-form noun). Even if it has the taʾ, it is one of those in which the masculine cannot be distinguished from the feminine by the gender of the verb, but rather is distinguished by reporting whether it is male or female. Nothing of great benefit depends on this, nor on examining the name of the ant, nor on the fabricated stories and false narrations that have been related.

Al-Hasan, Talhah, and Ma'mar ibn Sulayman read "namlatun" and "al-namul" with a ḍammah on the mīm and a fatḥah on the nūn, in the pattern of rajul and samurah. Sulayman al-Taymi read with two ḍammahs on both.

﴿Let not Sulayman and his troops crush you﴾. Al-ḥaṭm means breaking; it is said: ḥaṭamtuhu ḥaṭman, meaning I broke it, breaking. Taḥaṭṭama means to be shattered. This prohibition is outwardly addressed to the ants, but in reality it is addressed to Sulayman. It is thus of the type: "Let me not see you here." It may be a substitute for the imperative, and it may be an answer to the imperative.

Abu Hayyan said: as for its analysis as an answer to the imperative, that is only possible on the reading of al-A'mash, who read "la yaḥṭimkum" with jazm and without the nun of emphasis. But with the nun of emphasis, that is not permitted except in poetry.

Sibawayh said: it is rare in poetry; they treated it like the prohibition, since it is jussive.

Ubayy read "udkhulu masakinakunna" (enter your dwellings, feminine plural). Shahr ibn Hawshab read "maskanakum." Al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Qatadah, and ʿIsa al-Hamdani read "la yuḥaṭṭimannakum" with a ḍammah on the yā', a fatḥah on the ḥā', and a shaddah on the ṭā'. Ibn Ishaq, Ya'qub, and Abu ʿAmr in one narration read with the sukūn of the nun of emphasis.

The clause ﴿while they do not perceive﴾ is in the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) relating to the subject of yaḥṭimannakum, meaning: they will not perceive your being crushed, nor will they know your location. It has also been said that the meaning is: "and the ants do not perceive that Sulayman understands their speech," but this is far-fetched.

﴿So he smiled, laughing at her speech﴾. Ibn al-Sumayfa' read "ḍaḥikan" (laughter, as a masdar). According to the reading of the majority, ḍāḥikan is an emphatic circumstantial (ḥāl mu'akkidah), because laughter has already been understood from smiling. It has also been said that it is a projected circumstantial (ḥāl muqaddarah), since smiling is the beginning of laughter. It is also said that since smiling may be due to anger, laughter clarifies it. It is also said that the laughter of the prophets is only smiling and nothing more. On the reading of Ibn al-Sumayfa', ḍaḥikan is a masdar in the accusative governed by a deleted verb, or in the position of a circumstantial. Sulayman's laughter was out of wonder at her speech, her understanding, and her guidance to warning the ants.

﴿And he said, "My Lord, enable me to be grateful for Your blessing with which You have favored me and my parents"﴾. The explanation of awziʿni (enable me) has already been given shortly before, in His words ﴿So they were held in ranks﴾ [al-Naml: 17; Fussilat: 19]. In al-Kashshaf it is said: The literal meaning of awziʿni is: "make me restrain the thanks for Your blessings within me, and restrain it, and bind it, so that it does not escape from me, until I never cease to be thankful to You." End of quote.

Al-Wahidi said: "awziʿni" means: "inspire me to be grateful for Your blessing with which You favored me." It is said: "So-and-so is muwazzaʿ with such-and-such," meaning he is devoted to it. End of quote.

Al-Qurtubi said: it derives from wazi'a, as if he said: "Restrain me from what displeases You." End of quote.

The second object of awziʿni is: "that I be grateful for Your blessing with which You favored me."
