By al-ṭarf (glance) is meant the moving and opening of the eyelids for looking, and its returning (irtidād) is their closing.

It was said: it refers to the meaning of al-maṭrūf, that is, the thing that one looks at. It was also said: it is the eyelid itself, and it is expressed by it to indicate speed of action, as you say to your companion: do that in a glance (lahẓah).

This was said by Mujahid. Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: he said to Sulayman: Look at the sky, and he did not blink until he brought it and placed it before him.

The meaning: until your glance returns to you after you extend it toward the sky. The first of these views is the most likely.

Then the third: ﴿So when he saw it set firmly before him﴾. It was said: there is an ellipsis in the verse, and the implied meaning is: Sulayman permitted him, so he called upon Allah and brought it. Then, when Sulayman saw it set firmly before him (p-1081), that is, he saw the throne present with him. ﴿He said: This is of the favor of my Lord, to test me whether I will be grateful or ungrateful﴾. The reference in his saying "this" is to the presence of the throne. "To test me" means: to examine me, whether I will thank Him for it and acknowledge that it is from His favor, without any power or strength from me; or whether I will be ungrateful by abandoning thanks and not fulfilling it.

Al-Akhfash said: the meaning is: that He may look whether I will be grateful or ungrateful. Others said: the meaning of "to test me" is "to make me worship Him," and this is a metaphor, since the original meaning of ibtilāʾ (testing) is examination. ﴿And whoever is grateful, he is grateful only for his own self﴾, because by gratitude he merits the perfection and continuation of the blessing. The meaning: the benefit of that does not return except to the one who is grateful. ﴿And whoever is ungrateful﴾ by abandoning thanks, ﴿then indeed my Lord is Free of need﴾ from his gratitude, ﴿Generous﴾ in not hastening punishment by removing His blessings from him and taking back what He had given him of them. The ʾam in ﴿am akfur﴾ (or am I ungrateful) is the connecting ʾam (al-ʾam al-muttaṣilah), which is used to link two alternatives.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying ﴿Take this letter of mine and deliver it to them, then withdraw from them﴾: he said: be near them ﴿and see what they will return﴾. So he set off with the letter until, when he reached the middle of her throne, he threw the letter to her, and it was read to her, and in it was: ﴿Indeed it is from Sulayman, and indeed it says: In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾.

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from him regarding ﴿a noble letter﴾ that he said: it was sealed. Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Maymun ibn Mihran that the Prophet (ﷺ) "used to write: In your name, O Allah, until the revelation came: ﴿Indeed it is from Sulayman, and indeed it says: In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾."

Abu Dawud transmitted in his Marasil from Abu Malik, marfūʿan (traced to the Prophet), the like of it.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying ﴿Advise me in my matter﴾, that he said: she gathered the chiefs of her kingdom and consulted them about her opinion. Their opinion and hers agreed to invade him. So she set out, until when she was near, she said: I will send to him a gift. If he accepts it, then he is a king, and I will fight him; and if he rejects it, I will follow him, for he is a prophet. When her envoys approached Sulayman, he knew their news, so he ordered the devils, and they overlaid a thousand palaces of gold and silver. When her envoys saw the palaces of gold, they said: What will he do with our gift when his palaces are of gold and silver? When they entered upon him with their gift, ﴿he said: Would you aid me with wealth?﴾ Then Sulayman said: ﴿Which of you will bring me her throne before they come to me in submission?﴾ Sulayman's scribe said: Raise your gaze. So he raised his gaze, and when his glance returned to him, behold, there was the throne. ﴿He said: Disguise her throne for her﴾. So they removed its gems, its supports, and whatever was on it of anything. Then it was said to her: ﴿Is your throne like this?﴾ She said: ﴿It is as though it were it﴾ [al-Naml: 42]. He ordered the devils, and they made for her a smooth palace of glass, and in it were made images of fish. So ﴿it was said to her: Enter the palace﴾ [al-Naml: 44]. She uncovered her shins, and behold, there was hair on them. At that point he ordered the preparation of depilatory (nūrah), and it was prepared. Then it was said to her: ﴿Indeed, it is a palace smoothed with glass.﴾ She said: ﴿My Lord, indeed I have wronged myself, and I have submitted with Sulayman to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾. [al-Naml: 44]

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him regarding His saying ﴿Indeed, kings, when they enter a town, they ruin it﴾, that he said: when they take it by force, they lay it waste.

Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him, and said: The Lord, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿And thus they do﴾.

Ibn Abi Shaybah in al-Musannaf, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him regarding His saying ﴿And indeed I am sending to them a gift﴾, that he said: she sent a brick of gold. When they came, behold, the walls of the city were of gold. That is His saying ﴿Would you aid me with wealth?﴾, and so on.

Thabit al-Bunani said: she sent to him sheets of gold in cases of brocade.

Mujahid said: female slaves whose clothing was the clothing of boys, and boys whose clothing was the clothing of girls.

Ikrimah said: she sent two hundred horses, on each horse a boy and a girl, and on each horse a color that was not on the other.

Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: the gift was jewels. It was also said other than this, which there is no benefit in lengthening by mentioning.

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted through the chain of ʿAli ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying ﴿before they come to me in submission﴾, that he said: obedient.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him, that he said: the name of the ʿifrīt was Ṣakhr.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also regarding ﴿before you rise from your place﴾, that he said: from your seat.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also regarding ﴿He who had knowledge of the Scripture said﴾, that he said: he is Āṣif ibn Barkhiyā, and he was a righteous man who knew the Greatest Name.

Abu ʿUbayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid, who said regarding the reading of Ibn Masʿud: "He who had knowledge of the Scripture said: I will look into the Book of my Lord, then I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you." He said: then that scholar spoke a word that entered the throne into a tunnel beneath the earth until it emerged before them.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying ﴿before your glance returns to you﴾, that he said: he said to Sulayman: Look at the sky. He said: so he did not blink until he brought it to him, and placed it before him.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn ʿAsakir transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: The throne of the woman of Sheba did not travel between the earth and the sky, but the earth was split open with it, so it moved beneath the earth until it appeared before Sulayman.

The commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 27, verses 27–40 (part 1 of 2):

The clause ﴿He said, "We shall see"﴾ is a resumptive clause (*mustaʾnafa*), answering an implied question. Its meaning is: Sulayman said to the hoopoe, "We shall see regarding what you have told us of this story: ﴿whether you have spoken the truth or you have been among the liars﴾." This interrogative clause is in the accusative position as the object of *sanandhuru* ("we shall see"), and *am* (أم) here is the *muttasila* (connecting) *am*. His saying ﴿or you have been among the liars﴾ is more emphatic than saying "or have you lied," because the meaning is: "among those who have the attribute of lying, for whom it has become a disposition (*khuluq*)" (p-1079).

*Al-naẓar* is contemplation and close examination. It contains guidance to seeking out information, uncovering realities, and not accepting the report of informants out of blind imitation (*taqlid*) or reliance on them, when one is able to verify it by some means.

Then Sulayman explained this "looking" that he had promised. He said: ﴿Take this letter of mine and throw it to them﴾, that is, to the people of Sheba.

Al-Zajjaj said: regarding *alqihi* ("throw it") there are five forms: the *yāʾ* is pronounced and omitted; the *kasra* is pronounced to indicate the *yāʾ*; the *hāʾ* is given a *ḍamma* with a *wāw* pronounced; the *wāw* is omitted with the *ḍamma* retained to indicate it; and the *hāʾ* is given a *sukūn*.

Abu ʿAmr, Hamza and Abu Bakr recited with this fifth form. Qalun recited with the *kasra* on the *hāʾ* only, without a *yāʾ*. Two variants are transmitted from Hisham: pronouncing the *yāʾ* and omitting it with the *kasra* on the *hāʾ*. The rest recited with the *yāʾ* pronounced.

The phrase ﴿this letter of mine﴾ may be understood with *hādhā* as an adjective of *kitāb* ("letter"), or as an apposition (*badal*) to it, or as an explanatory clarification (*bayān*) of it. He specifically assigned the hoopoe to deliver the letter because it was the one who reported the story, and because it had shown signs of understanding and knowledge that made it fit for the role of a messenger.

﴿Then withdraw from them﴾, that is, step aside from them. He commanded this because stepping aside after delivering the letter is among the finest etiquettes that the envoys of kings observe. What is meant is to withdraw to a place from which it can hear their conversation, so that it may inform Sulayman of what it heard. It was said that *tawallī* means returning to him, but the first view is preferable because of His saying: ﴿then see what they return with﴾, that is, reflect and consider what they say to one another and what they discuss among themselves.

She (i.e., Bilqis) said: ﴿O assembly, a noble letter has been delivered to me﴾. There is an ellipsis in the speech, and the implied sense is: the hoopoe went and threw it to them, and she heard them say: "O assembly," and so on. She described the letter as *karīm* ("noble") because it came from a great person in her estimation, so she magnified it out of honour for Sulayman. It was also said she described it so because it contained noble speech, and it was said she described it so because it reached her sealed with the seal of Sulayman; and the dignity of a letter is its sealing, as is reported in a hadith traced to the Prophet (ﷺ). Then she explained what this letter contained.

She said: ﴿It is from Sulayman, and it begins: "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate"﴾, that is, what it contained of speech and what it included of words opens with the invocation of the Name, and after the invocation: ﴿Do not exalt yourselves over me﴾, that is, do not act arrogantly as tyrannical kings do. The *an* here is the explanatory *an* (*al-mufassira*). It was said it is the verbal *an* (*maṣdariyya*), and the *lā* is prohibitive; it was also said it is negative. The clause's position is nominative, as an apposition to *kitāb* ("letter"), or as the predicate of an omitted subject, that is: "it is: do not exalt yourselves."

The majority recited ﴿It is from Sulayman, and it begins﴾ with the *kasra* on both, as a resumption (*istiʾnaf*). ʿIkrima and Ibn Abi ʿAblah recited with a *fatḥa* on both, according to the omission of the preposition. Ubayy recited "inna min Sulayman wa-inna bismillah" by omitting the two pronouns and giving the two *nūns* a *sukūn*, as being explanatory. ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿud recited "wa-innahu min Sulayman" with an added *wāw*, and this is also reported from Ubayy. Ashhab al-ʿUqayli and Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ recited ﴿do not exalt yourselves﴾ with the *ghayn* (*an lā taghlū*), from *ghuluww*, which is going beyond the limit in greatness. ﴿And come to me in submission﴾, that is, submitting to the religion, believing in what you have been brought.

She (Bilqis) said: ﴿O assembly, advise me in my affair﴾. *Al-malaʾ* means the notables of the people, and the meaning is: "O notables, counsel me and make clear to me the right course in this matter, and answer me with what sound judgment requires." She expressed the request for counsel with *iftāʾ* ("giving a legal opinion") because in it lies a resolution to what has become unclear to her in the matter. There is an ellipsis in the speech, and the implied sense is: when Bilqis read the letter she gathered the notables of her people and said to them: "O assembly, a letter has been delivered to me," "O assembly, advise me." She repeated *qālat* ("she said") for greater emphasis on what she was saying to them. Then she increased her courtesy and her winning over of their hearts, so that they would sincerely advise her and counsel her with what is right. She said: ﴿I have never decided on a matter until you witness it﴾, that is, I have never settled on any affair until you are present before me and counsel me.

They (the notables) answered her: ﴿We are possessed of strength﴾ in numbers and equipment, ﴿and possessed of great might﴾ in war and battle, having such courage and valour that we defend ourselves, our land and our kingdom. Then they entrusted the matter to her, knowing the soundness of her opinion and the strength of her intellect, and they said: ﴿The command is yours﴾, that is, it is left to your opinion and judgment. ﴿So see what you will command﴾, that is, reflect on what you will command us, for we are listeners to your command and obedient to it.

When she heard their entrusting the matter to her, ﴿she said: "Indeed, when kings enter a town, they corrupt it"﴾, that is, when they enter any of the towns, they ruin its buildings, change its meanings, destroy its wealth and scatter the shared bond of its people. ﴿And they make the most honourable of its people abased﴾, that is, they humiliate its nobles and lower their ranks, so that they become abased. They do this only so that their rule may be complete, their dominion firmly established, and awe may take root in their hearts.

Al-Zajjaj said: that is, if they enter it by force, through fighting and conquest. The purpose of her saying this was to warn her people against Sulayman's march toward them and his entry into their lands. Allah, glorified is He, confirmed what she said, and He said: ﴿And thus they do﴾, that is, they do the same deed.

Ibn al-Anbari said: the pause at His saying ﴿and make the most honourable of its people abased﴾ is a complete pause (*waqf tāmm*), then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said, confirming her words: ﴿And thus they do﴾. It was also said this clause is part of her own speech, so it is part of what she said. According to the first view, this clause is resumptive and has no place in the grammatical structure (*lā maḥalla lahā min al-iʿrāb*).

Then, when she had presented them with this preface and explained to them the harm in kings entering their land, she made clear to them the view she held and stated its rightness to them. She said: ﴿And I am sending them a gift﴾, that is, I will test this man by sending my envoys to him with a gift containing precious wealth. If he is a king, we will please him with it and be spared his affair; and if he is a prophet, it will not satisfy him, because the ultimate aim of his purpose and the final goal of his desire is calling to the religion, so nothing will save us from him except answering him, following him, adopting his religion and walking his path. For this reason she said: ﴿So I will see what the envoys will return with﴾. The *fā'* here is for coordination with *mursila* ("sending"), and *bima* is connected to *yarjiʿu* ("return"). The meaning is: "I shall observe what my envoys return with from the messengers bearing the gift, whether acceptance or rejection, and act according to what that requires." The commentators have been lengthy in mentioning this gift, and later in this discussion the closest of what has been said to correctness and soundness will be explained.

﴿When [the envoy] came to Sulayman﴾, that is, when her envoy bearing the gift came to Sulayman. The pronoun here refers to the category (*jins*), so it does not contradict their being a group, as her saying "what the envoys will return with" indicates. ʿAbdullah recited "when they came to Sulayman," that is, the envoys (p-1080). The clause ﴿He said: "Do you aid me with wealth?"﴾ is resumptive, answering an implied question, and the interrogation is one of disapproval: he said, disapproving of their supplying him with wealth, given the height of his authority and the abundance of his wealth.

Hamza recited with the assimilation of the *nūn* of the grammatical inflection (*nūn al-iʿrāb*) into the *nūn* of protection (*nūn al-wiqāya*). The rest recited with two *nūns* without assimilation. As for the *yāʾ*, Nafiʿ, Abu ʿAmr and Hamza pronounce it when connected and omit it at a pause; Ibn Kathir pronounces it in both situations; and the rest omit it in both situations. It is reported from Nafiʿ that he recited with a single *nūn*.

﴿What Allah has given me is better than what He has given you﴾, that is, what Allah has given me of prophethood, great sovereignty and abundant wealth is better than what He has given you of wealth, of which this gift is a part.

Abu ʿAmr, Nafiʿ and Hafs recited ﴿Allah has given me﴾ with an open *yāʾ*. Yaʿqub recited with the *yāʾ* pronounced at a pause and omitted in connection. The rest recited without a *yāʾ* in both connection and pause.

Then he turned away from the earlier disapproval and said: ﴿Rather, you are the ones who rejoice in your gift﴾, rebuking them for their rejoicing in this gift, a rejoicing of pride and vanity. As for me, I do not rejoice in it, and the world is not among my needs, because Allah, glorified is He, has given me of it what He has not given to anyone of the worlds, and along with that He has honoured me with prophethood.

The purpose of this turning away from Sulayman is to explain the reason that prompted them to send the gift, together with belittling them and disparaging them.

﴿Return to them, for we will surely bring them armies they cannot withstand﴾, that is, Sulayman said to the envoy: "Return to them," that is, to Bilqis and her people. He addressed the singular here after addressing the plural before, either because the one who will return is only the envoy, or because he singled out the leader of the envoys for the address here and addressed them with him earlier, for the sake of variety in speech (*iftinān*).

ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAbbas recited "return" in the plural. It was said the pronoun refers to the hoopoe. The *lām* in ﴿we will surely bring them﴾ is the answer to an omitted oath.

Al-Nahhas said: I heard Ibn Kaysan say: it is the *lām* of emphasis, the *lām* of command and the *lām* of genitive; this is the view of the expert grammarians, because they return a thing to its origin, and this is not attainable except by one who has been trained in Arabic. The meaning of ﴿they cannot withstand﴾ is that they have no power to face them. The clause is in the genitive position as a qualifier of *junūd* ("armies").

﴿And we will surely expel them from their land in which they are abased﴾ is coordinated with the answer to the oath, that is, we will expel them from their land in which they are abased, meaning while they are abased after having been honoured. The clause ﴿while they are humbled﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*). It was said it is an emphatic circumstance, because *ṣaghār* ("humbling") is *dhilla* ("abasement"). It was also said that *ṣaghār* here means being taken captive and being kept at a distance; and it was said *ṣaghār* is the humiliation that results in abasement.

When the envoy returned to Bilqis, she prepared herself to march to Sulayman, and Gabriel informed Sulayman of this.

Sulayman said: ﴿O assembly, which of you will bring me her throne﴾, that is, the throne of Bilqis, which was previously described as great. ﴿Before they come to me in submission﴾, that is, before she and her people come to me in submission.

It was said: Sulayman only intended to take her throne before they reached him and submitted, because if she and her people submitted, it would not be lawful to take their property without their consent.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: the apparent reading of the reports is that this statement from Sulayman came after the arrival of her gift, his rejecting it, and his sending the hoopoe with the letter; and this is the view of most of the commentators.

It was said: summoning the throne before her arrival was so that he could show her the power that comes from Allah, and make it a sign of his prophethood. It was also said he wanted to test her intellect, and for this reason he said ﴿Disguise her throne for her﴾ and so on. It was also said he wanted to test the truthfulness of the hoopoe in its description of the throne as great. The first view is the one held by most.

﴿A powerful one of the jinn said: "I will bring it to you before you rise from your place"﴾. The majority recited with a *kasra* on the *ʿayn*, a sukun on the *fāʾ*, a *kasra* on the *rāʾ*, a sukun on the *yāʾ* (underdotted), and with a *tāʾ*. Abu Rajaʾ, ʿIsa al-Thaqafi, Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ and Abu al-Simmal recited *ʿifrīha* with a *fatḥa* on the underdotted *yāʾ* followed by the feminine *tāʾ* which becomes a *hāʾ*; this recitation is reported from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq. Abu Hayyan recited with a *fatḥa* on the *ʿayn*.

*Al-ʿifrīt* is the rebellious, thick-set and mighty one.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 27, verses 27–40 (part 2 of 2):

Al-Nahhas said: It is said of a strong person who has cunning and shrewdness: ʿifr, ʿifriyah and ʿifrīt (a powerful, cunning jinn). Qatadah said: he is the one who is very cunning (al-dāhiyah). It was also said: he is the chief of the jinn.

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: A group read ﴿ʿifr﴾ with a kasrah on the ʿayn (ʿifr), its plural being ʿifār. Among the verses of the Arabs that match the reading of the majority is what al-Kisāʾī recited:

"Then a devil among them, an ʿifrīt, said: What is wrong with you that you do not stay, nor spend the night?"

Among the verses that match the second reading is the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

"As if he were a star following an ʿifriyah, / Shot down in the blackness of the night, streaking."

The meaning of the ʿifrīt's words is that he will bring the throne to Sulayman before he rises from his seat in which he sits to judge between the people. ﴿And indeed I am strong for it, trustworthy﴾: I am strong enough to carry it, trustworthy with what is in it.

It is said: the name of this ʿifrīt was Kūdan, which al-Nahhas mentioned from Wahb ibn Munabbih. Al-Suhayli said: Dhakwān. It was also said: his name is Daʿwān, and it was said: Ṣakhr.

As for His saying ﴿ātīka﴾ (I will bring you): it is a present-tense verb, and its origin is ﴿ aʾtīka﴾ with two hamzahs. The second was replaced by an alif. It was also said that it is an active participle (ism fāʿil).

﴿He who had knowledge of the Scripture said: I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you﴾. Most of the exegetes said: the name of this one who had knowledge of the Scripture is Āṣif ibn Barkhiyā. He was from the Children of Israel and was a minister of Sulayman. He knew the Greatest Name of Allah (ism Allah al-aʿẓam), by which, when He is called upon, He answers, and when He is asked by it, He gives.

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: A group said he was Sulayman himself, and the address in this case is to the ʿifrīt. As if Sulayman was slow to accept what the ʿifrīt had said, so he said to him, belittling him: ﴿I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you﴾. It was also said: he was Jibril, and it was said: he was al-Khiḍr. The first view is the more likely.

It has been said other than this, based on what has no basis.

By al-ṭarf (glance) is meant the moving and opening of the eyelids for looking, and its returning (irtidād) is their closing.

It was said: it refers to the meaning of al-maṭrūf, that is, the thing that one looks at. It was also said: it is the eyelid itself, and it is expressed by it to indicate speed of action, as you say to your companion: do that in a glance (lahẓah).

This was said by Mujahid. Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: he said to Sulayman: Look at the sky, and he did not blink until he brought it and placed it before him.

The meaning: until your glance returns to you after you extend it toward the sky. The first of these views is the most likely.

Then the third: ﴿So when he saw it set firmly before him﴾. It was said: there is an ellipsis in the verse, and the implied meaning is: Sulayman permitted him, so he called upon Allah and brought it. Then, when Sulayman saw it set firmly before him (p-1081), that is, he saw the throne present with him. ﴿He said: This is of the favor of my Lord, to test me whether I will be grateful or ungrateful﴾. The reference in his saying "this" is to the presence of the throne. "To test me" means: to examine me, whether I will thank Him for it and acknowledge that it is from His favor, without any power or strength from me; or whether I will be ungrateful by abandoning thanks and not fulfilling it.

Al-Akhfash said: the meaning is: that He may look whether I will be grateful or ungrateful. Others said: the meaning of "to test me" is "to make me worship Him," and this is a metaphor, since the original meaning of ibtilāʾ (testing) is examination. ﴿And whoever is grateful, he is grateful only for his own self﴾, because by gratitude he merits the perfection and continuation of the blessing. The meaning: the benefit of that does not return except to the one who is grateful. ﴿And whoever is ungrateful﴾ by abandoning thanks, ﴿then indeed my Lord is Free of need﴾ from his gratitude, ﴿Generous﴾ in not hastening punishment by removing His blessings from him and taking back what He had given him of them. The ʾam in ﴿am akfur﴾ (or am I ungrateful) is the connecting ʾam (al-ʾam al-muttaṣilah), which is used to link two alternatives.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying ﴿Take this letter of mine and deliver it to them, then withdraw from them﴾: he said: be near them ﴿and see what they will return﴾. So he set off with the letter until, when he reached the middle of her throne, he threw the letter to her, and it was read to her, and in it was: ﴿Indeed it is from Sulayman, and indeed it says: In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾.

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from him regarding ﴿a noble letter﴾ that he said: it was sealed. Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Maymun ibn Mihran that the Prophet (ﷺ) "used to write: In your name, O Allah, until the revelation came: ﴿Indeed it is from Sulayman, and indeed it says: In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾."

Abu Dawud transmitted in his Marasil from Abu Malik, marfūʿan (traced to the Prophet), the like of it.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying ﴿Advise me in my matter﴾, that he said: she gathered the chiefs of her kingdom and consulted them about her opinion. Their opinion and hers agreed to invade him. So she set out, until when she was near, she said: I will send to him a gift. If he accepts it, then he is a king, and I will fight him; and if he rejects it, I will follow him, for he is a prophet. When her envoys approached Sulayman, he knew their news, so he ordered the devils, and they overlaid a thousand palaces of gold and silver. When her envoys saw the palaces of gold, they said: What will he do with our gift when his palaces are of gold and silver? When they entered upon him with their gift, ﴿he said: Would you aid me with wealth?﴾ Then Sulayman said: ﴿Which of you will bring me her throne before they come to me in submission?﴾ Sulayman's scribe said: Raise your gaze. So he raised his gaze, and when his glance returned to him, behold, there was the throne. ﴿He said: Disguise her throne for her﴾. So they removed its gems, its supports, and whatever was on it of anything. Then it was said to her: ﴿Is your throne like this?﴾ She said: ﴿It is as though it were it﴾ [al-Naml: 42]. He ordered the devils, and they made for her a smooth palace of glass, and in it were made images of fish. So ﴿it was said to her: Enter the palace﴾ [al-Naml: 44]. She uncovered her shins, and behold, there was hair on them. At that point he ordered the preparation of depilatory (nūrah), and it was prepared. Then it was said to her: ﴿Indeed, it is a palace smoothed with glass.﴾ She said: ﴿My Lord, indeed I have wronged myself, and I have submitted with Sulayman to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾. [al-Naml: 44]

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him regarding His saying ﴿Indeed, kings, when they enter a town, they ruin it﴾, that he said: when they take it by force, they lay it waste.

Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him, and said: The Lord, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿And thus they do﴾.

Ibn Abi Shaybah in al-Musannaf, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him regarding His saying ﴿And indeed I am sending to them a gift﴾, that he said: she sent a brick of gold. When they came, behold, the walls of the city were of gold. That is His saying ﴿Would you aid me with wealth?﴾, and so on.

Thabit al-Bunani said: she sent to him sheets of gold in cases of brocade.

Mujahid said: female slaves whose clothing was the clothing of boys, and boys whose clothing was the clothing of girls.

Ikrimah said: she sent two hundred horses, on each horse a boy and a girl, and on each horse a color that was not on the other.

Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: the gift was jewels. It was also said other than this, which there is no benefit in lengthening by mentioning.

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted through the chain of ʿAli ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying ﴿before they come to me in submission﴾, that he said: obedient.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him, that he said: the name of the ʿifrīt was Ṣakhr.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also regarding ﴿before you rise from your place﴾, that he said: from your seat.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also regarding ﴿He who had knowledge of the Scripture said﴾, that he said: he is Āṣif ibn Barkhiyā, and he was a righteous man who knew the Greatest Name.

Abu ʿUbayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid, who said regarding the reading of Ibn Masʿud: "He who had knowledge of the Scripture said: I will look into the Book of my Lord, then I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you." He said: then that scholar spoke a word that entered the throne into a tunnel beneath the earth until it emerged before them.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying ﴿before your glance returns to you﴾, that he said: he said to Sulayman: Look at the sky. He said: so he did not blink until he brought it to him, and placed it before him.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn ʿAsakir transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: The throne of the woman of Sheba did not travel between the earth and the sky, but the earth was split open with it, so it moved beneath the earth until it appeared before Sulayman.

The commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 27, verses 27–40 (part 1 of 2):

The clause ﴿He said, "We shall see"﴾ is a resumptive clause (*mustaʾnafa*), answering an implied question. Its meaning is: Sulayman said to the hoopoe, "We shall see regarding what you have told us of this story: ﴿whether you have spoken the truth or you have been among the liars﴾." This interrogative clause is in the accusative position as the object of *sanandhuru* ("we shall see"), and *am* (أم) here is the *muttasila* (connecting) *am*. His saying ﴿or you have been among the liars﴾ is more emphatic than saying "or have you lied," because the meaning is: "among those who have the attribute of lying, for whom it has become a disposition (*khuluq*)" (p-1079).

*Al-naẓar* is contemplation and close examination. It contains guidance to seeking out information, uncovering realities, and not accepting the report of informants out of blind imitation (*taqlid*) or reliance on them, when one is able to verify it by some means.

Then Sulayman explained this "looking" that he had promised. He said: ﴿Take this letter of mine and throw it to them﴾, that is, to the people of Sheba.

Al-Zajjaj said: regarding *alqihi* ("throw it") there are five forms: the *yāʾ* is pronounced and omitted; the *kasra* is pronounced to indicate the *yāʾ*; the *hāʾ* is given a *ḍamma* with a *wāw* pronounced; the *wāw* is omitted with the *ḍamma* retained to indicate it; and the *hāʾ* is given a *sukūn*.

Abu ʿAmr, Hamza and Abu Bakr recited with this fifth form. Qalun recited with the *kasra* on the *hāʾ* only, without a *yāʾ*. Two variants are transmitted from Hisham: pronouncing the *yāʾ* and omitting it with the *kasra* on the *hāʾ*. The rest recited with the *yāʾ* pronounced.

The phrase ﴿this letter of mine﴾ may be understood with *hādhā* as an adjective of *kitāb* ("letter"), or as an apposition (*badal*) to it, or as an explanatory clarification (*bayān*) of it. He specifically assigned the hoopoe to deliver the letter because it was the one who reported the story, and because it had shown signs of understanding and knowledge that made it fit for the role of a messenger.

﴿Then withdraw from them﴾, that is, step aside from them. He commanded this because stepping aside after delivering the letter is among the finest etiquettes that the envoys of kings observe. What is meant is to withdraw to a place from which it can hear their conversation, so that it may inform Sulayman of what it heard. It was said that *tawallī* means returning to him, but the first view is preferable because of His saying: ﴿then see what they return with﴾, that is, reflect and consider what they say to one another and what they discuss among themselves.

She (i.e., Bilqis) said: ﴿O assembly, a noble letter has been delivered to me﴾. There is an ellipsis in the speech, and the implied sense is: the hoopoe went and threw it to them, and she heard them say: "O assembly," and so on. She described the letter as *karīm* ("noble") because it came from a great person in her estimation, so she magnified it out of honour for Sulayman. It was also said she described it so because it contained noble speech, and it was said she described it so because it reached her sealed with the seal of Sulayman; and the dignity of a letter is its sealing, as is reported in a hadith traced to the Prophet (ﷺ). Then she explained what this letter contained.

She said: ﴿It is from Sulayman, and it begins: "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate"﴾, that is, what it contained of speech and what it included of words opens with the invocation of the Name, and after the invocation: ﴿Do not exalt yourselves over me﴾, that is, do not act arrogantly as tyrannical kings do. The *an* here is the explanatory *an* (*al-mufassira*). It was said it is the verbal *an* (*maṣdariyya*), and the *lā* is prohibitive; it was also said it is negative. The clause's position is nominative, as an apposition to *kitāb* ("letter"), or as the predicate of an omitted subject, that is: "it is: do not exalt yourselves."

The majority recited ﴿It is from Sulayman, and it begins﴾ with the *kasra* on both, as a resumption (*istiʾnaf*). ʿIkrima and Ibn Abi ʿAblah recited with a *fatḥa* on both, according to the omission of the preposition. Ubayy recited "inna min Sulayman wa-inna bismillah" by omitting the two pronouns and giving the two *nūns* a *sukūn*, as being explanatory. ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿud recited "wa-innahu min Sulayman" with an added *wāw*, and this is also reported from Ubayy. Ashhab al-ʿUqayli and Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ recited ﴿do not exalt yourselves﴾ with the *ghayn* (*an lā taghlū*), from *ghuluww*, which is going beyond the limit in greatness. ﴿And come to me in submission﴾, that is, submitting to the religion, believing in what you have been brought.

She (Bilqis) said: ﴿O assembly, advise me in my affair﴾. *Al-malaʾ* means the notables of the people, and the meaning is: "O notables, counsel me and make clear to me the right course in this matter, and answer me with what sound judgment requires." She expressed the request for counsel with *iftāʾ* ("giving a legal opinion") because in it lies a resolution to what has become unclear to her in the matter. There is an ellipsis in the speech, and the implied sense is: when Bilqis read the letter she gathered the notables of her people and said to them: "O assembly, a letter has been delivered to me," "O assembly, advise me." She repeated *qālat* ("she said") for greater emphasis on what she was saying to them. Then she increased her courtesy and her winning over of their hearts, so that they would sincerely advise her and counsel her with what is right. She said: ﴿I have never decided on a matter until you witness it﴾, that is, I have never settled on any affair until you are present before me and counsel me.

They (the notables) answered her: ﴿We are possessed of strength﴾ in numbers and equipment, ﴿and possessed of great might﴾ in war and battle, having such courage and valour that we defend ourselves, our land and our kingdom. Then they entrusted the matter to her, knowing the soundness of her opinion and the strength of her intellect, and they said: ﴿The command is yours﴾, that is, it is left to your opinion and judgment. ﴿So see what you will command﴾, that is, reflect on what you will command us, for we are listeners to your command and obedient to it.

When she heard their entrusting the matter to her, ﴿she said: "Indeed, when kings enter a town, they corrupt it"﴾, that is, when they enter any of the towns, they ruin its buildings, change its meanings, destroy its wealth and scatter the shared bond of its people. ﴿And they make the most honourable of its people abased﴾, that is, they humiliate its nobles and lower their ranks, so that they become abased. They do this only so that their rule may be complete, their dominion firmly established, and awe may take root in their hearts.

Al-Zajjaj said: that is, if they enter it by force, through fighting and conquest. The purpose of her saying this was to warn her people against Sulayman's march toward them and his entry into their lands. Allah, glorified is He, confirmed what she said, and He said: ﴿And thus they do﴾, that is, they do the same deed.

Ibn al-Anbari said: the pause at His saying ﴿and make the most honourable of its people abased﴾ is a complete pause (*waqf tāmm*), then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said, confirming her words: ﴿And thus they do﴾. It was also said this clause is part of her own speech, so it is part of what she said. According to the first view, this clause is resumptive and has no place in the grammatical structure (*lā maḥalla lahā min al-iʿrāb*).

Then, when she had presented them with this preface and explained to them the harm in kings entering their land, she made clear to them the view she held and stated its rightness to them. She said: ﴿And I am sending them a gift﴾, that is, I will test this man by sending my envoys to him with a gift containing precious wealth. If he is a king, we will please him with it and be spared his affair; and if he is a prophet, it will not satisfy him, because the ultimate aim of his purpose and the final goal of his desire is calling to the religion, so nothing will save us from him except answering him, following him, adopting his religion and walking his path. For this reason she said: ﴿So I will see what the envoys will return with﴾. The *fā'* here is for coordination with *mursila* ("sending"), and *bima* is connected to *yarjiʿu* ("return"). The meaning is: "I shall observe what my envoys return with from the messengers bearing the gift, whether acceptance or rejection, and act according to what that requires." The commentators have been lengthy in mentioning this gift, and later in this discussion the closest of what has been said to correctness and soundness will be explained.

﴿When [the envoy] came to Sulayman﴾, that is, when her envoy bearing the gift came to Sulayman. The pronoun here refers to the category (*jins*), so it does not contradict their being a group, as her saying "what the envoys will return with" indicates. ʿAbdullah recited "when they came to Sulayman," that is, the envoys (p-1080). The clause ﴿He said: "Do you aid me with wealth?"﴾ is resumptive, answering an implied question, and the interrogation is one of disapproval: he said, disapproving of their supplying him with wealth, given the height of his authority and the abundance of his wealth.

Hamza recited with the assimilation of the *nūn* of the grammatical inflection (*nūn al-iʿrāb*) into the *nūn* of protection (*nūn al-wiqāya*). The rest recited with two *nūns* without assimilation. As for the *yāʾ*, Nafiʿ, Abu ʿAmr and Hamza pronounce it when connected and omit it at a pause; Ibn Kathir pronounces it in both situations; and the rest omit it in both situations. It is reported from Nafiʿ that he recited with a single *nūn*.

﴿What Allah has given me is better than what He has given you﴾, that is, what Allah has given me of prophethood, great sovereignty and abundant wealth is better than what He has given you of wealth, of which this gift is a part.

Abu ʿAmr, Nafiʿ and Hafs recited ﴿Allah has given me﴾ with an open *yāʾ*. Yaʿqub recited with the *yāʾ* pronounced at a pause and omitted in connection. The rest recited without a *yāʾ* in both connection and pause.

Then he turned away from the earlier disapproval and said: ﴿Rather, you are the ones who rejoice in your gift﴾, rebuking them for their rejoicing in this gift, a rejoicing of pride and vanity. As for me, I do not rejoice in it, and the world is not among my needs, because Allah, glorified is He, has given me of it what He has not given to anyone of the worlds, and along with that He has honoured me with prophethood.

The purpose of this turning away from Sulayman is to explain the reason that prompted them to send the gift, together with belittling them and disparaging them.

﴿Return to them, for we will surely bring them armies they cannot withstand﴾, that is, Sulayman said to the envoy: "Return to them," that is, to Bilqis and her people. He addressed the singular here after addressing the plural before, either because the one who will return is only the envoy, or because he singled out the leader of the envoys for the address here and addressed them with him earlier, for the sake of variety in speech (*iftinān*).

ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAbbas recited "return" in the plural. It was said the pronoun refers to the hoopoe. The *lām* in ﴿we will surely bring them﴾ is the answer to an omitted oath.

Al-Nahhas said: I heard Ibn Kaysan say: it is the *lām* of emphasis, the *lām* of command and the *lām* of genitive; this is the view of the expert grammarians, because they return a thing to its origin, and this is not attainable except by one who has been trained in Arabic. The meaning of ﴿they cannot withstand﴾ is that they have no power to face them. The clause is in the genitive position as a qualifier of *junūd* ("armies").

﴿And we will surely expel them from their land in which they are abased﴾ is coordinated with the answer to the oath, that is, we will expel them from their land in which they are abased, meaning while they are abased after having been honoured. The clause ﴿while they are humbled﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*). It was said it is an emphatic circumstance, because *ṣaghār* ("humbling") is *dhilla* ("abasement"). It was also said that *ṣaghār* here means being taken captive and being kept at a distance; and it was said *ṣaghār* is the humiliation that results in abasement.

When the envoy returned to Bilqis, she prepared herself to march to Sulayman, and Gabriel informed Sulayman of this.

Sulayman said: ﴿O assembly, which of you will bring me her throne﴾, that is, the throne of Bilqis, which was previously described as great. ﴿Before they come to me in submission﴾, that is, before she and her people come to me in submission.

It was said: Sulayman only intended to take her throne before they reached him and submitted, because if she and her people submitted, it would not be lawful to take their property without their consent.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: the apparent reading of the reports is that this statement from Sulayman came after the arrival of her gift, his rejecting it, and his sending the hoopoe with the letter; and this is the view of most of the commentators.

It was said: summoning the throne before her arrival was so that he could show her the power that comes from Allah, and make it a sign of his prophethood. It was also said he wanted to test her intellect, and for this reason he said ﴿Disguise her throne for her﴾ and so on. It was also said he wanted to test the truthfulness of the hoopoe in its description of the throne as great. The first view is the one held by most.

﴿A powerful one of the jinn said: "I will bring it to you before you rise from your place"﴾. The majority recited with a *kasra* on the *ʿayn*, a sukun on the *fāʾ*, a *kasra* on the *rāʾ*, a sukun on the *yāʾ* (underdotted), and with a *tāʾ*. Abu Rajaʾ, ʿIsa al-Thaqafi, Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ and Abu al-Simmal recited *ʿifrīha* with a *fatḥa* on the underdotted *yāʾ* followed by the feminine *tāʾ* which becomes a *hāʾ*; this recitation is reported from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq. Abu Hayyan recited with a *fatḥa* on the *ʿayn*.

*Al-ʿifrīt* is the rebellious, thick-set and mighty one.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 27, verses 27–40 (part 2 of 2):

Al-Nahhas said: It is said of a strong person who has cunning and shrewdness: ʿifr, ʿifriyah and ʿifrīt (a powerful, cunning jinn). Qatadah said: he is the one who is very cunning (al-dāhiyah). It was also said: he is the chief of the jinn.

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: A group read ﴿ʿifr﴾ with a kasrah on the ʿayn (ʿifr), its plural being ʿifār. Among the verses of the Arabs that match the reading of the majority is what al-Kisāʾī recited:

"Then a devil among them, an ʿifrīt, said: What is wrong with you that you do not stay, nor spend the night?"

Among the verses that match the second reading is the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

"As if he were a star following an ʿifriyah, / Shot down in the blackness of the night, streaking."

The meaning of the ʿifrīt's words is that he will bring the throne to Sulayman before he rises from his seat in which he sits to judge between the people. ﴿And indeed I am strong for it, trustworthy﴾: I am strong enough to carry it, trustworthy with what is in it.

It is said: the name of this ʿifrīt was Kūdan, which al-Nahhas mentioned from Wahb ibn Munabbih. Al-Suhayli said: Dhakwān. It was also said: his name is Daʿwān, and it was said: Ṣakhr.

As for His saying ﴿ātīka﴾ (I will bring you): it is a present-tense verb, and its origin is ﴿ aʾtīka﴾ with two hamzahs. The second was replaced by an alif. It was also said that it is an active participle (ism fāʿil).

﴿He who had knowledge of the Scripture said: I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you﴾. Most of the exegetes said: the name of this one who had knowledge of the Scripture is Āṣif ibn Barkhiyā. He was from the Children of Israel and was a minister of Sulayman. He knew the Greatest Name of Allah (ism Allah al-aʿẓam), by which, when He is called upon, He answers, and when He is asked by it, He gives.

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: A group said he was Sulayman himself, and the address in this case is to the ʿifrīt. As if Sulayman was slow to accept what the ʿifrīt had said, so he said to him, belittling him: ﴿I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you﴾. It was also said: he was Jibril, and it was said: he was al-Khiḍr. The first view is the more likely.

It has been said other than this, based on what has no basis.

By al-ṭarf (glance) is meant the moving and opening of the eyelids for looking, and its returning (irtidād) is their closing.

It was said: it refers to the meaning of al-maṭrūf, that is, the thing that one looks at. It was also said: it is the eyelid itself, and it is expressed by it to indicate speed of action, as you say to your companion: do that in a glance (lahẓah).

This was said by Mujahid. Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: he said to Sulayman: Look at the sky, and he did not blink until he brought it and placed it before him.

The meaning: until your glance returns to you after you extend it toward the sky. The first of these views is the most likely.

Then the third: ﴿So when he saw it set firmly before him﴾. It was said: there is an ellipsis in the verse, and the implied meaning is: Sulayman permitted him, so he called upon Allah and brought it. Then, when Sulayman saw it set firmly before him (p-1081), that is, he saw the throne present with him. ﴿He said: This is of the favor of my Lord, to test me whether I will be grateful or ungrateful﴾. The reference in his saying "this" is to the presence of the throne. "To test me" means: to examine me, whether I will thank Him for it and acknowledge that it is from His favor, without any power or strength from me; or whether I will be ungrateful by abandoning thanks and not fulfilling it.

Al-Akhfash said: the meaning is: that He may look whether I will be grateful or ungrateful. Others said: the meaning of "to test me" is "to make me worship Him," and this is a metaphor, since the original meaning of ibtilāʾ (testing) is examination. ﴿And whoever is grateful, he is grateful only for his own self﴾, because by gratitude he merits the perfection and continuation of the blessing. The meaning: the benefit of that does not return except to the one who is grateful. ﴿And whoever is ungrateful﴾ by abandoning thanks, ﴿then indeed my Lord is Free of need﴾ from his gratitude, ﴿Generous﴾ in not hastening punishment by removing His blessings from him and taking back what He had given him of them. The ʾam in ﴿am akfur﴾ (or am I ungrateful) is the connecting ʾam (al-ʾam al-muttaṣilah), which is used to link two alternatives.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying ﴿Take this letter of mine and deliver it to them, then withdraw from them﴾: he said: be near them ﴿and see what they will return﴾. So he set off with the letter until, when he reached the middle of her throne, he threw the letter to her, and it was read to her, and in it was: ﴿Indeed it is from Sulayman, and indeed it says: In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾.

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from him regarding ﴿a noble letter﴾ that he said: it was sealed. Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Maymun ibn Mihran that the Prophet (ﷺ) "used to write: In your name, O Allah, until the revelation came: ﴿Indeed it is from Sulayman, and indeed it says: In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾."

Abu Dawud transmitted in his Marasil from Abu Malik, marfūʿan (traced to the Prophet), the like of it.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying ﴿Advise me in my matter﴾, that he said: she gathered the chiefs of her kingdom and consulted them about her opinion. Their opinion and hers agreed to invade him. So she set out, until when she was near, she said: I will send to him a gift. If he accepts it, then he is a king, and I will fight him; and if he rejects it, I will follow him, for he is a prophet. When her envoys approached Sulayman, he knew their news, so he ordered the devils, and they overlaid a thousand palaces of gold and silver. When her envoys saw the palaces of gold, they said: What will he do with our gift when his palaces are of gold and silver? When they entered upon him with their gift, ﴿he said: Would you aid me with wealth?﴾ Then Sulayman said: ﴿Which of you will bring me her throne before they come to me in submission?﴾ Sulayman's scribe said: Raise your gaze. So he raised his gaze, and when his glance returned to him, behold, there was the throne. ﴿He said: Disguise her throne for her﴾. So they removed its gems, its supports, and whatever was on it of anything. Then it was said to her: ﴿Is your throne like this?﴾ She said: ﴿It is as though it were it﴾ [al-Naml: 42]. He ordered the devils, and they made for her a smooth palace of glass, and in it were made images of fish. So ﴿it was said to her: Enter the palace﴾ [al-Naml: 44]. She uncovered her shins, and behold, there was hair on them. At that point he ordered the preparation of depilatory (nūrah), and it was prepared. Then it was said to her: ﴿Indeed, it is a palace smoothed with glass.﴾ She said: ﴿My Lord, indeed I have wronged myself, and I have submitted with Sulayman to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾. [al-Naml: 44]

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him regarding His saying ﴿Indeed, kings, when they enter a town, they ruin it﴾, that he said: when they take it by force, they lay it waste.

Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him, and said: The Lord, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿And thus they do﴾.

Ibn Abi Shaybah in al-Musannaf, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him regarding His saying ﴿And indeed I am sending to them a gift﴾, that he said: she sent a brick of gold. When they came, behold, the walls of the city were of gold. That is His saying ﴿Would you aid me with wealth?﴾, and so on.

Thabit al-Bunani said: she sent to him sheets of gold in cases of brocade.

Mujahid said: female slaves whose clothing was the clothing of boys, and boys whose clothing was the clothing of girls.

Ikrimah said: she sent two hundred horses, on each horse a boy and a girl, and on each horse a color that was not on the other.

Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: the gift was jewels. It was also said other than this, which there is no benefit in lengthening by mentioning.

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted through the chain of ʿAli ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying ﴿before they come to me in submission﴾, that he said: obedient.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him, that he said: the name of the ʿifrīt was Ṣakhr.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also regarding ﴿before you rise from your place﴾, that he said: from your seat.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also regarding ﴿He who had knowledge of the Scripture said﴾, that he said: he is Āṣif ibn Barkhiyā, and he was a righteous man who knew the Greatest Name.

Abu ʿUbayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid, who said regarding the reading of Ibn Masʿud: "He who had knowledge of the Scripture said: I will look into the Book of my Lord, then I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you." He said: then that scholar spoke a word that entered the throne into a tunnel beneath the earth until it emerged before them.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying ﴿before your glance returns to you﴾, that he said: he said to Sulayman: Look at the sky. He said: so he did not blink until he brought it to him, and placed it before him.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn ʿAsakir transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: The throne of the woman of Sheba did not travel between the earth and the sky, but the earth was split open with it, so it moved beneath the earth until it appeared before Sulayman.

The commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 27, verses 27–40 (part 1 of 2):

The clause ﴿He said, "We shall see"﴾ is a resumptive clause (*mustaʾnafa*), answering an implied question. Its meaning is: Sulayman said to the hoopoe, "We shall see regarding what you have told us of this story: ﴿whether you have spoken the truth or you have been among the liars﴾." This interrogative clause is in the accusative position as the object of *sanandhuru* ("we shall see"), and *am* (أم) here is the *muttasila* (connecting) *am*. His saying ﴿or you have been among the liars﴾ is more emphatic than saying "or have you lied," because the meaning is: "among those who have the attribute of lying, for whom it has become a disposition (*khuluq*)" (p-1079).

*Al-naẓar* is contemplation and close examination. It contains guidance to seeking out information, uncovering realities, and not accepting the report of informants out of blind imitation (*taqlid*) or reliance on them, when one is able to verify it by some means.

Then Sulayman explained this "looking" that he had promised. He said: ﴿Take this letter of mine and throw it to them﴾, that is, to the people of Sheba.

Al-Zajjaj said: regarding *alqihi* ("throw it") there are five forms: the *yāʾ* is pronounced and omitted; the *kasra* is pronounced to indicate the *yāʾ*; the *hāʾ* is given a *ḍamma* with a *wāw* pronounced; the *wāw* is omitted with the *ḍamma* retained to indicate it; and the *hāʾ* is given a *sukūn*.

Abu ʿAmr, Hamza and Abu Bakr recited with this fifth form. Qalun recited with the *kasra* on the *hāʾ* only, without a *yāʾ*. Two variants are transmitted from Hisham: pronouncing the *yāʾ* and omitting it with the *kasra* on the *hāʾ*. The rest recited with the *yāʾ* pronounced.

The phrase ﴿this letter of mine﴾ may be understood with *hādhā* as an adjective of *kitāb* ("letter"), or as an apposition (*badal*) to it, or as an explanatory clarification (*bayān*) of it. He specifically assigned the hoopoe to deliver the letter because it was the one who reported the story, and because it had shown signs of understanding and knowledge that made it fit for the role of a messenger.

﴿Then withdraw from them﴾, that is, step aside from them. He commanded this because stepping aside after delivering the letter is among the finest etiquettes that the envoys of kings observe. What is meant is to withdraw to a place from which it can hear their conversation, so that it may inform Sulayman of what it heard. It was said that *tawallī* means returning to him, but the first view is preferable because of His saying: ﴿then see what they return with﴾, that is, reflect and consider what they say to one another and what they discuss among themselves.

She (i.e., Bilqis) said: ﴿O assembly, a noble letter has been delivered to me﴾. There is an ellipsis in the speech, and the implied sense is: the hoopoe went and threw it to them, and she heard them say: "O assembly," and so on. She described the letter as *karīm* ("noble") because it came from a great person in her estimation, so she magnified it out of honour for Sulayman. It was also said she described it so because it contained noble speech, and it was said she described it so because it reached her sealed with the seal of Sulayman; and the dignity of a letter is its sealing, as is reported in a hadith traced to the Prophet (ﷺ). Then she explained what this letter contained.

She said: ﴿It is from Sulayman, and it begins: "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate"﴾, that is, what it contained of speech and what it included of words opens with the invocation of the Name, and after the invocation: ﴿Do not exalt yourselves over me﴾, that is, do not act arrogantly as tyrannical kings do. The *an* here is the explanatory *an* (*al-mufassira*). It was said it is the verbal *an* (*maṣdariyya*), and the *lā* is prohibitive; it was also said it is negative. The clause's position is nominative, as an apposition to *kitāb* ("letter"), or as the predicate of an omitted subject, that is: "it is: do not exalt yourselves."

The majority recited ﴿It is from Sulayman, and it begins﴾ with the *kasra* on both, as a resumption (*istiʾnaf*). ʿIkrima and Ibn Abi ʿAblah recited with a *fatḥa* on both, according to the omission of the preposition. Ubayy recited "inna min Sulayman wa-inna bismillah" by omitting the two pronouns and giving the two *nūns* a *sukūn*, as being explanatory. ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿud recited "wa-innahu min Sulayman" with an added *wāw*, and this is also reported from Ubayy. Ashhab al-ʿUqayli and Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ recited ﴿do not exalt yourselves﴾ with the *ghayn* (*an lā taghlū*), from *ghuluww*, which is going beyond the limit in greatness. ﴿And come to me in submission﴾, that is, submitting to the religion, believing in what you have been brought.

She (Bilqis) said: ﴿O assembly, advise me in my affair﴾. *Al-malaʾ* means the notables of the people, and the meaning is: "O notables, counsel me and make clear to me the right course in this matter, and answer me with what sound judgment requires." She expressed the request for counsel with *iftāʾ* ("giving a legal opinion") because in it lies a resolution to what has become unclear to her in the matter. There is an ellipsis in the speech, and the implied sense is: when Bilqis read the letter she gathered the notables of her people and said to them: "O assembly, a letter has been delivered to me," "O assembly, advise me." She repeated *qālat* ("she said") for greater emphasis on what she was saying to them. Then she increased her courtesy and her winning over of their hearts, so that they would sincerely advise her and counsel her with what is right. She said: ﴿I have never decided on a matter until you witness it﴾, that is, I have never settled on any affair until you are present before me and counsel me.

They (the notables) answered her: ﴿We are possessed of strength﴾ in numbers and equipment, ﴿and possessed of great might﴾ in war and battle, having such courage and valour that we defend ourselves, our land and our kingdom. Then they entrusted the matter to her, knowing the soundness of her opinion and the strength of her intellect, and they said: ﴿The command is yours﴾, that is, it is left to your opinion and judgment. ﴿So see what you will command﴾, that is, reflect on what you will command us, for we are listeners to your command and obedient to it.

When she heard their entrusting the matter to her, ﴿she said: "Indeed, when kings enter a town, they corrupt it"﴾, that is, when they enter any of the towns, they ruin its buildings, change its meanings, destroy its wealth and scatter the shared bond of its people. ﴿And they make the most honourable of its people abased﴾, that is, they humiliate its nobles and lower their ranks, so that they become abased. They do this only so that their rule may be complete, their dominion firmly established, and awe may take root in their hearts.

Al-Zajjaj said: that is, if they enter it by force, through fighting and conquest. The purpose of her saying this was to warn her people against Sulayman's march toward them and his entry into their lands. Allah, glorified is He, confirmed what she said, and He said: ﴿And thus they do﴾, that is, they do the same deed.

Ibn al-Anbari said: the pause at His saying ﴿and make the most honourable of its people abased﴾ is a complete pause (*waqf tāmm*), then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said, confirming her words: ﴿And thus they do﴾. It was also said this clause is part of her own speech, so it is part of what she said. According to the first view, this clause is resumptive and has no place in the grammatical structure (*lā maḥalla lahā min al-iʿrāb*).

Then, when she had presented them with this preface and explained to them the harm in kings entering their land, she made clear to them the view she held and stated its rightness to them. She said: ﴿And I am sending them a gift﴾, that is, I will test this man by sending my envoys to him with a gift containing precious wealth. If he is a king, we will please him with it and be spared his affair; and if he is a prophet, it will not satisfy him, because the ultimate aim of his purpose and the final goal of his desire is calling to the religion, so nothing will save us from him except answering him, following him, adopting his religion and walking his path. For this reason she said: ﴿So I will see what the envoys will return with﴾. The *fā'* here is for coordination with *mursila* ("sending"), and *bima* is connected to *yarjiʿu* ("return"). The meaning is: "I shall observe what my envoys return with from the messengers bearing the gift, whether acceptance or rejection, and act according to what that requires." The commentators have been lengthy in mentioning this gift, and later in this discussion the closest of what has been said to correctness and soundness will be explained.

﴿When [the envoy] came to Sulayman﴾, that is, when her envoy bearing the gift came to Sulayman. The pronoun here refers to the category (*jins*), so it does not contradict their being a group, as her saying "what the envoys will return with" indicates. ʿAbdullah recited "when they came to Sulayman," that is, the envoys (p-1080). The clause ﴿He said: "Do you aid me with wealth?"﴾ is resumptive, answering an implied question, and the interrogation is one of disapproval: he said, disapproving of their supplying him with wealth, given the height of his authority and the abundance of his wealth.

Hamza recited with the assimilation of the *nūn* of the grammatical inflection (*nūn al-iʿrāb*) into the *nūn* of protection (*nūn al-wiqāya*). The rest recited with two *nūns* without assimilation. As for the *yāʾ*, Nafiʿ, Abu ʿAmr and Hamza pronounce it when connected and omit it at a pause; Ibn Kathir pronounces it in both situations; and the rest omit it in both situations. It is reported from Nafiʿ that he recited with a single *nūn*.

﴿What Allah has given me is better than what He has given you﴾, that is, what Allah has given me of prophethood, great sovereignty and abundant wealth is better than what He has given you of wealth, of which this gift is a part.

Abu ʿAmr, Nafiʿ and Hafs recited ﴿Allah has given me﴾ with an open *yāʾ*. Yaʿqub recited with the *yāʾ* pronounced at a pause and omitted in connection. The rest recited without a *yāʾ* in both connection and pause.

Then he turned away from the earlier disapproval and said: ﴿Rather, you are the ones who rejoice in your gift﴾, rebuking them for their rejoicing in this gift, a rejoicing of pride and vanity. As for me, I do not rejoice in it, and the world is not among my needs, because Allah, glorified is He, has given me of it what He has not given to anyone of the worlds, and along with that He has honoured me with prophethood.

The purpose of this turning away from Sulayman is to explain the reason that prompted them to send the gift, together with belittling them and disparaging them.

﴿Return to them, for we will surely bring them armies they cannot withstand﴾, that is, Sulayman said to the envoy: "Return to them," that is, to Bilqis and her people. He addressed the singular here after addressing the plural before, either because the one who will return is only the envoy, or because he singled out the leader of the envoys for the address here and addressed them with him earlier, for the sake of variety in speech (*iftinān*).

ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAbbas recited "return" in the plural. It was said the pronoun refers to the hoopoe. The *lām* in ﴿we will surely bring them﴾ is the answer to an omitted oath.

Al-Nahhas said: I heard Ibn Kaysan say: it is the *lām* of emphasis, the *lām* of command and the *lām* of genitive; this is the view of the expert grammarians, because they return a thing to its origin, and this is not attainable except by one who has been trained in Arabic. The meaning of ﴿they cannot withstand﴾ is that they have no power to face them. The clause is in the genitive position as a qualifier of *junūd* ("armies").

﴿And we will surely expel them from their land in which they are abased﴾ is coordinated with the answer to the oath, that is, we will expel them from their land in which they are abased, meaning while they are abased after having been honoured. The clause ﴿while they are humbled﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*). It was said it is an emphatic circumstance, because *ṣaghār* ("humbling") is *dhilla* ("abasement"). It was also said that *ṣaghār* here means being taken captive and being kept at a distance; and it was said *ṣaghār* is the humiliation that results in abasement.

When the envoy returned to Bilqis, she prepared herself to march to Sulayman, and Gabriel informed Sulayman of this.

Sulayman said: ﴿O assembly, which of you will bring me her throne﴾, that is, the throne of Bilqis, which was previously described as great. ﴿Before they come to me in submission﴾, that is, before she and her people come to me in submission.

It was said: Sulayman only intended to take her throne before they reached him and submitted, because if she and her people submitted, it would not be lawful to take their property without their consent.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: the apparent reading of the reports is that this statement from Sulayman came after the arrival of her gift, his rejecting it, and his sending the hoopoe with the letter; and this is the view of most of the commentators.

It was said: summoning the throne before her arrival was so that he could show her the power that comes from Allah, and make it a sign of his prophethood. It was also said he wanted to test her intellect, and for this reason he said ﴿Disguise her throne for her﴾ and so on. It was also said he wanted to test the truthfulness of the hoopoe in its description of the throne as great. The first view is the one held by most.

﴿A powerful one of the jinn said: "I will bring it to you before you rise from your place"﴾. The majority recited with a *kasra* on the *ʿayn*, a sukun on the *fāʾ*, a *kasra* on the *rāʾ*, a sukun on the *yāʾ* (underdotted), and with a *tāʾ*. Abu Rajaʾ, ʿIsa al-Thaqafi, Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ and Abu al-Simmal recited *ʿifrīha* with a *fatḥa* on the underdotted *yāʾ* followed by the feminine *tāʾ* which becomes a *hāʾ*; this recitation is reported from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq. Abu Hayyan recited with a *fatḥa* on the *ʿayn*.

*Al-ʿifrīt* is the rebellious, thick-set and mighty one.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 27, verses 27–40 (part 2 of 2):

Al-Nahhas said: It is said of a strong person who has cunning and shrewdness: ʿifr, ʿifriyah and ʿifrīt (a powerful, cunning jinn). Qatadah said: he is the one who is very cunning (al-dāhiyah). It was also said: he is the chief of the jinn.

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: A group read ﴿ʿifr﴾ with a kasrah on the ʿayn (ʿifr), its plural being ʿifār. Among the verses of the Arabs that match the reading of the majority is what al-Kisāʾī recited:

"Then a devil among them, an ʿifrīt, said: What is wrong with you that you do not stay, nor spend the night?"

Among the verses that match the second reading is the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

"As if he were a star following an ʿifriyah, / Shot down in the blackness of the night, streaking."

The meaning of the ʿifrīt's words is that he will bring the throne to Sulayman before he rises from his seat in which he sits to judge between the people. ﴿And indeed I am strong for it, trustworthy﴾: I am strong enough to carry it, trustworthy with what is in it.

It is said: the name of this ʿifrīt was Kūdan, which al-Nahhas mentioned from Wahb ibn Munabbih. Al-Suhayli said: Dhakwān. It was also said: his name is Daʿwān, and it was said: Ṣakhr.

As for His saying ﴿ātīka﴾ (I will bring you): it is a present-tense verb, and its origin is ﴿ aʾtīka﴾ with two hamzahs. The second was replaced by an alif. It was also said that it is an active participle (ism fāʿil).

﴿He who had knowledge of the Scripture said: I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you﴾. Most of the exegetes said: the name of this one who had knowledge of the Scripture is Āṣif ibn Barkhiyā. He was from the Children of Israel and was a minister of Sulayman. He knew the Greatest Name of Allah (ism Allah al-aʿẓam), by which, when He is called upon, He answers, and when He is asked by it, He gives.

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: A group said he was Sulayman himself, and the address in this case is to the ʿifrīt. As if Sulayman was slow to accept what the ʿifrīt had said, so he said to him, belittling him: ﴿I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you﴾. It was also said: he was Jibril, and it was said: he was al-Khiḍr. The first view is the more likely.

It has been said other than this, based on what has no basis.

By al-ṭarf (glance) is meant the moving and opening of the eyelids for looking, and its returning (irtidād) is their closing.

It was said: it refers to the meaning of al-maṭrūf, that is, the thing that one looks at. It was also said: it is the eyelid itself, and it is expressed by it to indicate speed of action, as you say to your companion: do that in a glance (lahẓah).

This was said by Mujahid. Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: he said to Sulayman: Look at the sky, and he did not blink until he brought it and placed it before him.

The meaning: until your glance returns to you after you extend it toward the sky. The first of these views is the most likely.

Then the third: ﴿So when he saw it set firmly before him﴾. It was said: there is an ellipsis in the verse, and the implied meaning is: Sulayman permitted him, so he called upon Allah and brought it. Then, when Sulayman saw it set firmly before him (p-1081), that is, he saw the throne present with him. ﴿He said: This is of the favor of my Lord, to test me whether I will be grateful or ungrateful﴾. The reference in his saying "this" is to the presence of the throne. "To test me" means: to examine me, whether I will thank Him for it and acknowledge that it is from His favor, without any power or strength from me; or whether I will be ungrateful by abandoning thanks and not fulfilling it.

Al-Akhfash said: the meaning is: that He may look whether I will be grateful or ungrateful. Others said: the meaning of "to test me" is "to make me worship Him," and this is a metaphor, since the original meaning of ibtilāʾ (testing) is examination. ﴿And whoever is grateful, he is grateful only for his own self﴾, because by gratitude he merits the perfection and continuation of the blessing. The meaning: the benefit of that does not return except to the one who is grateful. ﴿And whoever is ungrateful﴾ by abandoning thanks, ﴿then indeed my Lord is Free of need﴾ from his gratitude, ﴿Generous﴾ in not hastening punishment by removing His blessings from him and taking back what He had given him of them. The ʾam in ﴿am akfur﴾ (or am I ungrateful) is the connecting ʾam (al-ʾam al-muttaṣilah), which is used to link two alternatives.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying ﴿Take this letter of mine and deliver it to them, then withdraw from them﴾: he said: be near them ﴿and see what they will return﴾. So he set off with the letter until, when he reached the middle of her throne, he threw the letter to her, and it was read to her, and in it was: ﴿Indeed it is from Sulayman, and indeed it says: In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾.

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from him regarding ﴿a noble letter﴾ that he said: it was sealed. Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Maymun ibn Mihran that the Prophet (ﷺ) "used to write: In your name, O Allah, until the revelation came: ﴿Indeed it is from Sulayman, and indeed it says: In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾."

Abu Dawud transmitted in his Marasil from Abu Malik, marfūʿan (traced to the Prophet), the like of it.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying ﴿Advise me in my matter﴾, that he said: she gathered the chiefs of her kingdom and consulted them about her opinion. Their opinion and hers agreed to invade him. So she set out, until when she was near, she said: I will send to him a gift. If he accepts it, then he is a king, and I will fight him; and if he rejects it, I will follow him, for he is a prophet. When her envoys approached Sulayman, he knew their news, so he ordered the devils, and they overlaid a thousand palaces of gold and silver. When her envoys saw the palaces of gold, they said: What will he do with our gift when his palaces are of gold and silver? When they entered upon him with their gift, ﴿he said: Would you aid me with wealth?﴾ Then Sulayman said: ﴿Which of you will bring me her throne before they come to me in submission?﴾ Sulayman's scribe said: Raise your gaze. So he raised his gaze, and when his glance returned to him, behold, there was the throne. ﴿He said: Disguise her throne for her﴾. So they removed its gems, its supports, and whatever was on it of anything. Then it was said to her: ﴿Is your throne like this?﴾ She said: ﴿It is as though it were it﴾ [al-Naml: 42]. He ordered the devils, and they made for her a smooth palace of glass, and in it were made images of fish. So ﴿it was said to her: Enter the palace﴾ [al-Naml: 44]. She uncovered her shins, and behold, there was hair on them. At that point he ordered the preparation of depilatory (nūrah), and it was prepared. Then it was said to her: ﴿Indeed, it is a palace smoothed with glass.﴾ She said: ﴿My Lord, indeed I have wronged myself, and I have submitted with Sulayman to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾. [al-Naml: 44]

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him regarding His saying ﴿Indeed, kings, when they enter a town, they ruin it﴾, that he said: when they take it by force, they lay it waste.

Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him, and said: The Lord, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿And thus they do﴾.

Ibn Abi Shaybah in al-Musannaf, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him regarding His saying ﴿And indeed I am sending to them a gift﴾, that he said: she sent a brick of gold. When they came, behold, the walls of the city were of gold. That is His saying ﴿Would you aid me with wealth?﴾, and so on.

Thabit al-Bunani said: she sent to him sheets of gold in cases of brocade.

Mujahid said: female slaves whose clothing was the clothing of boys, and boys whose clothing was the clothing of girls.

Ikrimah said: she sent two hundred horses, on each horse a boy and a girl, and on each horse a color that was not on the other.

Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: the gift was jewels. It was also said other than this, which there is no benefit in lengthening by mentioning.

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted through the chain of ʿAli ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying ﴿before they come to me in submission﴾, that he said: obedient.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him, that he said: the name of the ʿifrīt was Ṣakhr.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also regarding ﴿before you rise from your place﴾, that he said: from your seat.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also regarding ﴿He who had knowledge of the Scripture said﴾, that he said: he is Āṣif ibn Barkhiyā, and he was a righteous man who knew the Greatest Name.

Abu ʿUbayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid, who said regarding the reading of Ibn Masʿud: "He who had knowledge of the Scripture said: I will look into the Book of my Lord, then I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you." He said: then that scholar spoke a word that entered the throne into a tunnel beneath the earth until it emerged before them.
