The commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 27, verses 54–66 (part 1 of 2):

The word *Lūṭan* (Lot) is in the accusative, governed by a implied verb coordinated with *arsalnā* (We sent), meaning: "And We sent Lot." *Idh* (when) in *idh qāla* is an adverb of time for the implied verb. It may also be read as governed by an implied "remember" (*udhkur*). The meaning is: "And We sent Lot at the time he said to his people: ﴿Do you commit the abomination﴾, that is, the act most extreme in ugliness and shamefulness. They were the people of Sodom (*Sadūm*). The clause ﴿while you see﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), and it carries the emphasis of the rebuke. The meaning is: "while you know that it is an abomination." That is more grievous for your sins. The verb *tubṣirūna* ("you see") may be taken as sight of the heart, meaning knowledge, or as sight in its ordinary sense, since they did not hide when committing the abomination, out of arrogance and defiance. The explanation of this story has already been given in full in Surat al-A'rāf.

﴿Indeed, do you come to men with desire﴾: this repeats the rebuke and makes explicit that this abomination is sodomy (*al-lūṭa*). *Shahwatan* (out of desire) is in the accusative either as a reason (*'illa*), meaning "for desire," or as an attribute of an omitted verbal noun, meaning "a coming in desire," or as a circumstantial accusative (*bi-ma'na al-ḥāl*), meaning "lusting after them." ﴿Rather than women﴾ means passing over the women who are the proper place for that. ﴿Rather, you are a people who are ignorant﴾ of the prohibition or of the punishment for this disobedience. Al-Khalīl and Sībawayh preferred lightening the hamza in *a-innakum*.

﴿So the answer of his people was only that they said: "Expel the family of Lot from your town. Indeed, they are people who keep themselves pure."﴾ The majority read *jawāba* in the accusative as the predicate (*khabar*) of *kāna*, with its subject being *illā an qālū*, meaning "only their saying." Ibn Abī Ishāq read *jawābun* in the nominative, as the subject (*ism*) of *kāna*, with its predicate being what follows. Then they gave as the reason for what they commanded one another, namely the expulsion, their words: "Indeed, they are people who keep themselves pure," meaning that they abstain from the backsides of men. They said this in mockery of them.

﴿So We saved him and his family﴾ from the punishment, ﴿except his wife. We had decreed that she would be among those who remained behind﴾, meaning We had decreed that she would be among those left to the punishment. *Qaddarnā* means "We decreed." The majority read *qaddarnā* with the doubled letter (*tashdīd*), and 'Āṣim read it without doubling (*takhfīf*). The meaning is one, though the heavier form signifies more meaning through more letters.

﴿And We rained upon them a rain﴾: the repetition indicates the intensity of the rain and that it was unfamiliar. ﴿And evil was the rain of those who were warned﴾. The object of the dispraise is omitted, meaning: "evil was the rain of those warned, their rain." By "those warned" are meant those who were warned and did not accept. All of this has been explained in al-A'rāf and ash-Shu'arā'.

﴿Say: "Praise be to Allah, and peace upon His servants whom He has chosen."﴾ Al-Farrā' said: The people of meanings (*ahl al-ma'ānī*) said: It was said to Lot: "Say, Praise be to Allah for their destruction." Others disagreed and said: This is an address to our Prophet (ﷺ). That is, it was said: "Praise be to Allah for the destruction of the disbelievers of the former nations, and peace upon His servants." ﴿Whom He has chosen﴾. Al-Naḥḥās said: This is more correct, because the Qur'an was sent down to the Prophet (ﷺ), and everything in it is addressed to him, unless its meaning cannot be valid except for someone else. It was said: The servants meant by "whom He has chosen" are the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). But it is better to take it in its generality, so that the prophets and their followers are included.

﴿Is Allah better, or what they associate with Him?﴾ That is: Is Allah, whose acts and attributes you have mentioned, which indicate the greatness of His power, better, or what they associate with Him of idols? This "betterness" is not in its original meaning. Rather, it is like the saying of the poet:
*"Do you satirize him, when you are not his equal? Then your evil and his good is ransom."*
So what is in the verse is of the kind of mockery (*tahakkum*) directed at them, since there is no good in them at all.

Sībawayh related that the Arabs say: "Is happiness more beloved to you, or misery?" though there is no good in misery at all.

It was also said: The meaning is: "Is the reward of Allah better, or the punishment of what you associate with Him?" It was also said: He said this to them in accordance with their belief, since they believed that there was good in worshipping idols. It was also said: the intent of this interrogation is information (*khabar*).

The majority read *tushrikūna* with the second-person (*al-fawqiyya*, addressing "you"), which is the choice of Abū 'Ubayd and Abū Ḥātim. Abū 'Amr, 'Āṣim and Ya'qūb read *yushrikūna* with the third person (*al-taḥtiyya*). The *am* in *amma yushrikūna* is the connected (*muttaṣila*) *am*. The *am* in His saying ﴿Or who created the heavens and the earth﴾ is the disconnected (*munqaṭi'a*) *am*. Abū Ḥātim said: The implied sense is: "Are your gods better, or He who created the heavens and the earth and was capable of creating them?" It was also said: The meaning is: "Is the worship of what you worship of your idols better, or the worship of Him who created the heavens and the earth?" On this reading, the *am* is connected, and in it is the sense of rebuke and mockery, as in the first clause. Al-A'mash read *amman* with the *mīm* lightened.

﴿And He sent down for you water from the sky﴾, meaning a kind of water, namely rain. ﴿Then We caused to grow thereby gardens﴾: *ḥadā'iq* is the plural of *ḥadīqa*. Al-Farrā' said: The *ḥadīqa* is an orchard enclosed by a wall. If it has no wall, it is an orchard but not a *ḥadīqa*. Qatādah and 'Ikrimah said: the *ḥadā'iq* are palm trees.

﴿Of beauty and splendor﴾, meaning of loveliness and radiance. *Bahja* is the beauty that delights whoever sees it. He did not say *dhawāta bahjatin* (in the feminine plural) because what is meant is a group of gardens.

﴿It was not for you to cause their trees to grow﴾, meaning: it was not right for you to do that. The sense of this negation is prohibition. The meaning is: who did this? That is, it was not possible for humans, and this is not within their capacity, because of their inability to bring a thing from non-existence into existence.

Then He, glory be to Him, said, rebuking and reproaching them: ﴿Is there a god with Allah?﴾ That is: Is there a worshipped one along with Allah, who has done these acts, so that He should be associated with Him and made a partner in worship? It was also read *ilāhan* (in the accusative) with the implied "Do you call upon a god?"

Then He turned away from their reproach and rebuke with what preceded, and moved to explain the evil of their condition, with a shift from address to the third person, and said: ﴿Rather, they are a people who deviate﴾, meaning: they set up equals to Allah, or they deviate from the truth into falsehood. Then He began to argue from the conditions of the earth and what is upon it, and said: ﴿Or who made the earth a stable place﴾. *Qarār* means the stable, firm place, meaning He spread it out and leveled it so that one can settle upon it.

It was said: this clause and what follows it of the three clauses are an apposition (*badal*) of His saying ﴿Or who created the heavens and the earth﴾, but there is no need for that. Rather, it and what follows it are a shift and transition from the rebuke with what came before to rebuke with something else.

﴿And made rivers through it﴾: *khilāl* means the middle. Its explanation has already been given in His saying: ﴿And We caused a river to gush forth between them﴾ [al-Kahf: 33]. ﴿And made for it firm mountains﴾, meaning mountains fixed to hold it and prevent it from moving. ﴿And placed between the two seas a barrier﴾: *ḥājiz* means the preventer, meaning He placed between the two seas a barrier of His power. The two seas are the sweet and the salty, so that one does not mix with the other, and neither changes the other. Its explanation has already passed in Surat al-Furqān.

﴿Is there a god with Allah?﴾ That is: when it is established that none is able to do that except Allah, then is there a god in existence who makes His making and creates His creation? So how do they associate with Him what neither harms nor benefits? ﴿Rather, most of them do not know﴾ the oneness of their Lord and the authority of His power.

﴿Or who responds to the distressed one when he calls upon Him﴾: this is an argument from Him, glory be to Him, from the need of humans for Him in general. *Al-muḍṭarr* is the passive participle of *iḍṭirār* (compulsion), meaning the afflicted, distressed one, who has no strength or power. It was said: it is the sinner. It was said: it is the one afflicted by harm of poverty or sickness, who is compelled to plead to Allah.

The *al-* in *al-muḍṭarr* is generic (*li-l-jins*), not comprehensive (*li-l-istighrāq*). The supplication of some of the distressed may not be answered, due to an obstacle caused by the servant himself that stands between him and the answer to his prayer. Otherwise, Allah, glory be to Him, has guaranteed the answer to the supplication of the distressed one when he calls upon Him, and He has informed us of this about Himself. The reason the supplication of the distressed is answered is that the distress that comes upon him produces sincerity and cutting off attention from all but Allah. Allah, glory be to Him, has informed us that He answers the supplication of those who are sincere to Him in religion, even if they were disbelievers. He said: ﴿Until, when you are in the ship and they sail with them by a good wind and they rejoice therein, a violent wind comes upon them and the waves come at them from everywhere, and they think they are encompassed, they call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion: "If You save us from this, we will surely be among the grateful"﴾ [Yūnus: 22]. And He said: ﴿Then when He delivered them to the land, immediately they associate﴾ [al-'Ankabūt: 65]. So He answered them in their necessity and sincerity, while knowing that they would return to their polytheism.

﴿And removes the evil﴾, that is, what harms the servant, without specification. It was said it is harm, and it was said it is oppression. ﴿And makes you successors of the earth﴾: meaning each generation among you succeeds the generation before it after their passing away. The meaning: He destroys a generation and brings others into being. It was said: He makes your offspring successors among you. It was said: He makes the Muslims successors to the disbelievers, who inherit their land and dwellings.

﴿Is there a god with Allah?﴾, who bestows upon you these great blessings? ﴿Little do you remember﴾, meaning: you remember only a little.

The majority read with the second person (*al-fawqiyya*). Abū 'Amr, Hishām and Ya'qūb read it with the third person (*al-taḥtiyya*), as information, in response to His saying ﴿Rather, most of them do not know﴾. Abū Ḥātim chose this reading.

﴿Or who guides you in the darknesses of the land and the sea﴾, meaning: who guides you in the dark nights when you travel on land or sea. It was said: what is meant is the wastelands (*mafāwiz*) of the land that have no landmarks, and the deep waters (*lujaj*) of the seas, and He compared them to darkness because there is nothing by which they can be guided in them.

﴿And who sends the winds as glad tidings before His mercy﴾. The mercy here means rain, meaning: He sends the winds before the rain, and before its descent. ﴿Is there a god with Allah?﴾, who does that and brings it into existence? ﴿Exalted is Allah above what they associate with Him﴾, meaning He is far beyond and sanctified above the existence of what they make His partner.

﴿Or who originates creation and then repeats it?﴾ They used to acknowledge that Allah, glory be to Him, is the Creator, so He obliged them to acknowledge resurrection (*al-i'āda*), meaning: if He is capable of initiating creation, He is capable of repeating it. (p-١٠٨٦) ﴿And who provides for you from the heaven and the earth﴾ by rain and vegetation, meaning: is He better, or what you make His partner, which has no power over any of that? ﴿Is there a god with Allah?﴾ so that you make him a partner? ﴿Say: "Bring your proof, if you are truthful."﴾ That is: produce your proof that Allah has a partner, or produce your proof that there is another creator who creates like His creation. In this there is a rebuke for them and mockery of them.

﴿Say: None in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah﴾: that is, none of the created beings in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen which Allah has kept exclusively for His knowledge. The exception in His saying *illā Allāh* is disconnected (*munqaṭi'*), meaning: but Allah knows that. The raising of what follows *illā* together with the exception being disconnected is according to the Tamimi dialect, as in their saying:
*"Except the wild cattle, and except the she-camels."*
It was said: the subject (*fā'il*) of *ya'lamu* is what follows *illā*, and *man fī al-samāwāt* is its object, and *al-ghayb* is an apposition (*badal*) of *man*, meaning: none knows the unseen of those in the heavens and the earth except Allah. It was said: it is a connected exception (*istithnā' muttaṣil*) from *man*. Al-Zajjāj said: *illā Allāh* is an apposition of *man*.

Al-Farrā' said: What follows *illā* is raised because what follows it is the predicate (*khabar*), like their saying: "No one went except your father," and this is like the saying of al-Zajjāj. Al-Zajjāj said: Whoever puts it in the accusative does so as an exception.

﴿And they do not perceive when they will be resurrected﴾: that is, they do not know when they will be raised from the graves. *Ayyāna* is compounded from *ayy* and *inna*, and its explanation has already been given. The pronoun refers to the disbelievers.

Al-Sulamī read *iyyāna* with a kasra on the hamza, which is the dialect of the Banū Sulaym. It is in the accusative governed by *yub'athūna*, and it suspends (*mu'allaqa*) *yash'urūna*, so that it and what follows it are in the accusative position by removal of the preposition, meaning: they do not perceive the time of their resurrection. The meaning of *ayyāna* is the meaning of *matā* (when).

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 27, verses 54–66 (part 2 of 2)**

﴿Nay, their knowledge has been completed (ibtadarak) concerning the Hereafter.﴾ The majority of readers recite *idtarak* (ادّارَكَ). Its original form is *tadarak* (تَدارَكَ), in which the *ta'* is assimilated into the *dal* (*idgham*, assimilation of consonants), and a connective hamza (*hamzat al-wasl*, the hamza used to allow beginning with a sukun) is added so that the word can be pronounced at the start of an utterance.

Abu Ja'far, Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Humayd read *bal adraka* (بَلْ أدْرَكَ), from *al-idrak* (إدراك, "reaching" or "attaining").

'Ata' ibn Yasar, Sulayman ibn Yasar and al-A'mash read *bala ddaraka* (بَلَ ادَّرَكَ), with a fatha on the *lam* of *bal* and a shadda on the *dal*.

Ibn Muhaysin read *bal adraka* (بَلْ أدْرَكَ) as an interrogative (*al-istifham*, question).

Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Raja', Shayba, al-A'mash and al-A'raj read *bala adarraka* (بَلى أدّارَكَ), with the *ya'* affirmed in *bala*, a hamza of cutting (*hamzat al-qat'*), and a shadda on the *dal*.

Ubayy read *bal tadaraka* (بَلْ تَدارَكَ).

The meaning of the verse is: "Nay, their knowledge became complete concerning the Hereafter, because they saw everything they had been promised and witnessed it directly."

It has also been said that its meaning is: "Their knowledge followed one after another concerning the Hereafter." The second reading means: "All of their knowledge concerning the Hereafter, together with direct witnessing, [came to them]; and that is at the time when knowledge will not benefit them, because they used to deny in the world."

Al-Zajjaj said: it has the sense of denial (*al-inkar*), and this is supported by His words after it: ﴿Nay, they are blind to it﴾, meaning: their knowledge did not reach the knowledge of the Hereafter. It has also been said that the meaning is: "Nay, their knowledge went astray and vanished concerning the Hereafter, so they have no knowledge." The meaning of the third reading is like the meaning of the first, since *if'tala* (افْتَعَلَ) and *tafa'ala* (تَفاعَلَ) may both come with the same meaning. The fourth reading has the sense of denial.

Al-Farra' said: "This is a good interpretation, as if it were directed at the deniers in the manner of mockery toward them." There are other readings of this verse, but it is not appropriate to occupy oneself with mentioning and explaining them.

﴿Nay, they are in doubt concerning it﴾, meaning: nay, they are now in the world, in doubt about the Hereafter. Then He turned away from that to what is more severe than it, saying: ﴿Nay, they are blind to it﴾, so they do not perceive any of its signs, because of the corruption of the insights (*basa'ir*) by which perception occurs. *'Amun* (عَمُونَ) is the plural of *'amin* (عَمٍ), meaning one who is blind of heart. The intended meaning is to show their ignorance of it, in such a way that they are not guided to anything that leads to knowledge of it.

Whoever says that the meaning of the first verse, namely ﴿Nay, their knowledge became complete concerning the Hereafter﴾, is that their knowledge was perfected and completed along with direct witnessing, must necessarily interpret His words ﴿Nay, they are in doubt﴾ and what follows as referring to their state in the world. Whoever says that the meaning of the first verse is mockery of them and rebuke of them does not need to restrict His words ﴿Nay, they are in doubt﴾ and what follows to their state in the world. By this the meaning of these verses becomes clear and manifestly evident.

Ibn Abi Shayba, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bazzar, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His words ﴿And peace be upon His servants whom He has chosen﴾, that he said: "They are the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ), whom Allah chose for His Prophet." The same was narrated from Sufyan al-Thawri.

The preferable view is what we have previously mentioned, namely generality, so that the companions of our Prophet (ﷺ) enter into this primarily.

Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i and al-Tabarani transmitted from a man of Balhajm, who said: "I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, to what do you call?' He said: 'I call to Allah alone, who, if harm touches you and you call upon Him, removes it from you.'" This is a portion of a long hadith.

Ahmad has narrated it through another route, in which he named the companion, saying: "'Affan narrated to us: Hammad ibn Salama narrated to us: Yunus narrated to us: 'Ubayd ibn 'Ubayda al-Hujaymi narrated to us, from his father, from Abu Tamima al-Hujaymi, from Jabir ibn Sulaym al-Hujaymi."

This hadith has other routes in the collections of Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others transmitted from the hadith of 'A'isha, who said: "Whoever says any one of three things has greatly slandered Allah." And Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿Say: No one in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah.﴾

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning ﴿Nay, their knowledge became complete concerning the Hereafter﴾, that he said: "When knowledge no longer benefits."

Abu 'Ubayd in his *Fada'il* (Virtues of the Qur'an), Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him that he recited *bal iddaraka 'ilmuhum fi al-akhirah* (بَلِ ادَّرَكَ عِلْمُهم في الآخِرَةِ), and said: "Their knowledge was not overtaken."

Abu 'Ubayd said: he means that he recited it with the interrogative.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him, that he said concerning *bal iddaraka 'ilmuhum fi al-akhirah*: "Their knowledge vanished."

The commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 27, verses 54–66 (part 1 of 2):

The word *Lūṭan* (Lot) is in the accusative, governed by a implied verb coordinated with *arsalnā* (We sent), meaning: "And We sent Lot." *Idh* (when) in *idh qāla* is an adverb of time for the implied verb. It may also be read as governed by an implied "remember" (*udhkur*). The meaning is: "And We sent Lot at the time he said to his people: ﴿Do you commit the abomination﴾, that is, the act most extreme in ugliness and shamefulness. They were the people of Sodom (*Sadūm*). The clause ﴿while you see﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), and it carries the emphasis of the rebuke. The meaning is: "while you know that it is an abomination." That is more grievous for your sins. The verb *tubṣirūna* ("you see") may be taken as sight of the heart, meaning knowledge, or as sight in its ordinary sense, since they did not hide when committing the abomination, out of arrogance and defiance. The explanation of this story has already been given in full in Surat al-A'rāf.

﴿Indeed, do you come to men with desire﴾: this repeats the rebuke and makes explicit that this abomination is sodomy (*al-lūṭa*). *Shahwatan* (out of desire) is in the accusative either as a reason (*'illa*), meaning "for desire," or as an attribute of an omitted verbal noun, meaning "a coming in desire," or as a circumstantial accusative (*bi-ma'na al-ḥāl*), meaning "lusting after them." ﴿Rather than women﴾ means passing over the women who are the proper place for that. ﴿Rather, you are a people who are ignorant﴾ of the prohibition or of the punishment for this disobedience. Al-Khalīl and Sībawayh preferred lightening the hamza in *a-innakum*.

﴿So the answer of his people was only that they said: "Expel the family of Lot from your town. Indeed, they are people who keep themselves pure."﴾ The majority read *jawāba* in the accusative as the predicate (*khabar*) of *kāna*, with its subject being *illā an qālū*, meaning "only their saying." Ibn Abī Ishāq read *jawābun* in the nominative, as the subject (*ism*) of *kāna*, with its predicate being what follows. Then they gave as the reason for what they commanded one another, namely the expulsion, their words: "Indeed, they are people who keep themselves pure," meaning that they abstain from the backsides of men. They said this in mockery of them.

﴿So We saved him and his family﴾ from the punishment, ﴿except his wife. We had decreed that she would be among those who remained behind﴾, meaning We had decreed that she would be among those left to the punishment. *Qaddarnā* means "We decreed." The majority read *qaddarnā* with the doubled letter (*tashdīd*), and 'Āṣim read it without doubling (*takhfīf*). The meaning is one, though the heavier form signifies more meaning through more letters.

﴿And We rained upon them a rain﴾: the repetition indicates the intensity of the rain and that it was unfamiliar. ﴿And evil was the rain of those who were warned﴾. The object of the dispraise is omitted, meaning: "evil was the rain of those warned, their rain." By "those warned" are meant those who were warned and did not accept. All of this has been explained in al-A'rāf and ash-Shu'arā'.

﴿Say: "Praise be to Allah, and peace upon His servants whom He has chosen."﴾ Al-Farrā' said: The people of meanings (*ahl al-ma'ānī*) said: It was said to Lot: "Say, Praise be to Allah for their destruction." Others disagreed and said: This is an address to our Prophet (ﷺ). That is, it was said: "Praise be to Allah for the destruction of the disbelievers of the former nations, and peace upon His servants." ﴿Whom He has chosen﴾. Al-Naḥḥās said: This is more correct, because the Qur'an was sent down to the Prophet (ﷺ), and everything in it is addressed to him, unless its meaning cannot be valid except for someone else. It was said: The servants meant by "whom He has chosen" are the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). But it is better to take it in its generality, so that the prophets and their followers are included.

﴿Is Allah better, or what they associate with Him?﴾ That is: Is Allah, whose acts and attributes you have mentioned, which indicate the greatness of His power, better, or what they associate with Him of idols? This "betterness" is not in its original meaning. Rather, it is like the saying of the poet:
*"Do you satirize him, when you are not his equal? Then your evil and his good is ransom."*
So what is in the verse is of the kind of mockery (*tahakkum*) directed at them, since there is no good in them at all.

Sībawayh related that the Arabs say: "Is happiness more beloved to you, or misery?" though there is no good in misery at all.

It was also said: The meaning is: "Is the reward of Allah better, or the punishment of what you associate with Him?" It was also said: He said this to them in accordance with their belief, since they believed that there was good in worshipping idols. It was also said: the intent of this interrogation is information (*khabar*).

The majority read *tushrikūna* with the second-person (*al-fawqiyya*, addressing "you"), which is the choice of Abū 'Ubayd and Abū Ḥātim. Abū 'Amr, 'Āṣim and Ya'qūb read *yushrikūna* with the third person (*al-taḥtiyya*). The *am* in *amma yushrikūna* is the connected (*muttaṣila*) *am*. The *am* in His saying ﴿Or who created the heavens and the earth﴾ is the disconnected (*munqaṭi'a*) *am*. Abū Ḥātim said: The implied sense is: "Are your gods better, or He who created the heavens and the earth and was capable of creating them?" It was also said: The meaning is: "Is the worship of what you worship of your idols better, or the worship of Him who created the heavens and the earth?" On this reading, the *am* is connected, and in it is the sense of rebuke and mockery, as in the first clause. Al-A'mash read *amman* with the *mīm* lightened.

﴿And He sent down for you water from the sky﴾, meaning a kind of water, namely rain. ﴿Then We caused to grow thereby gardens﴾: *ḥadā'iq* is the plural of *ḥadīqa*. Al-Farrā' said: The *ḥadīqa* is an orchard enclosed by a wall. If it has no wall, it is an orchard but not a *ḥadīqa*. Qatādah and 'Ikrimah said: the *ḥadā'iq* are palm trees.

﴿Of beauty and splendor﴾, meaning of loveliness and radiance. *Bahja* is the beauty that delights whoever sees it. He did not say *dhawāta bahjatin* (in the feminine plural) because what is meant is a group of gardens.

﴿It was not for you to cause their trees to grow﴾, meaning: it was not right for you to do that. The sense of this negation is prohibition. The meaning is: who did this? That is, it was not possible for humans, and this is not within their capacity, because of their inability to bring a thing from non-existence into existence.

Then He, glory be to Him, said, rebuking and reproaching them: ﴿Is there a god with Allah?﴾ That is: Is there a worshipped one along with Allah, who has done these acts, so that He should be associated with Him and made a partner in worship? It was also read *ilāhan* (in the accusative) with the implied "Do you call upon a god?"

Then He turned away from their reproach and rebuke with what preceded, and moved to explain the evil of their condition, with a shift from address to the third person, and said: ﴿Rather, they are a people who deviate﴾, meaning: they set up equals to Allah, or they deviate from the truth into falsehood. Rather, it and what follows it are a shift and transition from the rebuke with what came before to rebuke with something else.

﴿And made rivers through it﴾: *khilāl* means the middle. Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Raja', Shayba, al-A'mash and al-A'raj read *bala adarraka* (بَلى أدّارَكَ), with the *ya'* affirmed in *bala*, a hamza of cutting (*hamzat al-qat'*), and a shadda on the *dal*.

Ubayy read *bal tadaraka* (بَلْ تَدارَكَ).

The meaning of the verse is: "Nay, their knowledge became complete concerning the Hereafter, because they saw everything they had been promised and witnessed it directly."

It has also been said that its meaning is: "Their knowledge followed one after another concerning the Hereafter." The second reading means: "All of their knowledge concerning the Hereafter, together with direct witnessing, [came to them]; and that is at the time when knowledge will not benefit them, because they used to deny in the world."

Al-Zajjaj said: it has the sense of denial (*al-inkar*), and this is supported by His words after it: ﴿Nay, they are blind to it﴾, meaning: their knowledge did not reach the knowledge of the Hereafter. It has also been said that the meaning is: "Nay, their knowledge went astray and vanished concerning the Hereafter, so they have no knowledge." The meaning of the third reading is like the meaning of the first, since *if'tala* (افْتَعَلَ) and *tafa'ala* (تَفاعَلَ) may both come with the same meaning. The fourth reading has the sense of denial.

Al-Farra' said: "This is a good interpretation, as if it were directed at the deniers in the manner of mockery toward them." There are other readings of this verse, but it is not appropriate to occupy oneself with mentioning and explaining them.

﴿Nay, they are in doubt concerning it﴾, meaning: nay, they are now in the world, in doubt about the Hereafter. Then He turned away from that to what is more severe than it, saying: ﴿Nay, they are blind to it﴾, so they do not perceive any of its signs, because of the corruption of the insights (*basa'ir*) by which perception occurs. *'Amun* (عَمُونَ) is the plural of *'amin* (عَمٍ), meaning one who is blind of heart. The intended meaning is to show their ignorance of it, in such a way that they are not guided to anything that leads to knowledge of it.

Whoever says that the meaning of the first verse, namely ﴿Nay, their knowledge became complete concerning the Hereafter﴾, is that their knowledge was perfected and completed along with direct witnessing, must necessarily interpret His words ﴿Nay, they are in doubt﴾ and what follows as referring to their state in the world. Whoever says that the meaning of the first verse is mockery of them and rebuke of them does not need to restrict His words ﴿Nay, they are in doubt﴾ and what follows to their state in the world. By this the meaning of these verses becomes clear and manifestly evident.

Ibn Abi Shayba, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bazzar, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His words ﴿And peace be upon His servants whom He has chosen﴾, that he said: "They are the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ), whom Allah chose for His Prophet." The same was narrated from Sufyan al-Thawri.

The preferable view is what we have previously mentioned, namely generality, so that the companions of our Prophet (ﷺ) enter into this primarily.

Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i and al-Tabarani transmitted from a man of Balhajm, who said: "I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, to what do you call?' He said: 'I call to Allah alone, who, if harm touches you and you call upon Him, removes it from you.'" This is a portion of a long hadith.

Ahmad has narrated it through another route, in which he named the companion, saying: "'Affan narrated to us: Hammad ibn Salama narrated to us: Yunus narrated to us: 'Ubayd ibn 'Ubayda al-Hujaymi narrated to us, from his father, from Abu Tamima al-Hujaymi, from Jabir ibn Sulaym al-Hujaymi."

This hadith has other routes in the collections of Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others transmitted from the hadith of 'A'isha, who said: "Whoever says any one of three things has greatly slandered Allah." And Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿Say: No one in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah.﴾

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning ﴿Nay, their knowledge became complete concerning the Hereafter﴾, that he said: "When knowledge no longer benefits."

Abu 'Ubayd in his *Fada'il* (Virtues of the Qur'an), Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him that he recited *bal iddaraka 'ilmuhum fi al-akhirah* (بَلِ ادَّرَكَ عِلْمُهم في الآخِرَةِ), and said: "Their knowledge was not overtaken."

Abu 'Ubayd said: he means that he recited it with the interrogative.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him, that he said concerning *bal iddaraka 'ilmuhum fi al-akhirah*: "Their knowledge vanished."

The commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 27, verses 54–66 (part 1 of 2):

The word *Lūṭan* (Lot) is in the accusative, governed by a implied verb coordinated with *arsalnā* (We sent), meaning: "And We sent Lot." *Idh* (when) in *idh qāla* is an adverb of time for the implied verb. It may also be read as governed by an implied "remember" (*udhkur*). The meaning is: "And We sent Lot at the time he said to his people: ﴿Do you commit the abomination﴾, that is, the act most extreme in ugliness and shamefulness. They were the people of Sodom (*Sadūm*). The clause ﴿while you see﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), and it carries the emphasis of the rebuke. The meaning is: "while you know that it is an abomination." That is more grievous for your sins. The verb *tubṣirūna* ("you see") may be taken as sight of the heart, meaning knowledge, or as sight in its ordinary sense, since they did not hide when committing the abomination, out of arrogance and defiance. The explanation of this story has already been given in full in Surat al-A'rāf.

﴿Indeed, do you come to men with desire﴾: this repeats the rebuke and makes explicit that this abomination is sodomy (*al-lūṭa*). *Shahwatan* (out of desire) is in the accusative either as a reason (*'illa*), meaning "for desire," or as an attribute of an omitted verbal noun, meaning "a coming in desire," or as a circumstantial accusative (*bi-ma'na al-ḥāl*), meaning "lusting after them." ﴿Rather than women﴾ means passing over the women who are the proper place for that. ﴿Rather, you are a people who are ignorant﴾ of the prohibition or of the punishment for this disobedience. Al-Khalīl and Sībawayh preferred lightening the hamza in *a-innakum*.

﴿So the answer of his people was only that they said: "Expel the family of Lot from your town. Indeed, they are people who keep themselves pure."﴾ The majority read *jawāba* in the accusative as the predicate (*khabar*) of *kāna*, with its subject being *illā an qālū*, meaning "only their saying." Ibn Abī Ishāq read *jawābun* in the nominative, as the subject (*ism*) of *kāna*, with its predicate being what follows. Then they gave as the reason for what they commanded one another, namely the expulsion, their words: "Indeed, they are people who keep themselves pure," meaning that they abstain from the backsides of men. They said this in mockery of them.

﴿So We saved him and his family﴾ from the punishment, ﴿except his wife. We had decreed that she would be among those who remained behind﴾, meaning We had decreed that she would be among those left to the punishment. *Qaddarnā* means "We decreed." The majority read *qaddarnā* with the doubled letter (*tashdīd*), and 'Āṣim read it without doubling (*takhfīf*). The meaning is one, though the heavier form signifies more meaning through more letters.

﴿And We rained upon them a rain﴾: the repetition indicates the intensity of the rain and that it was unfamiliar. ﴿And evil was the rain of those who were warned﴾. The object of the dispraise is omitted, meaning: "evil was the rain of those warned, their rain." By "those warned" are meant those who were warned and did not accept. All of this has been explained in al-A'rāf and ash-Shu'arā'.

﴿Say: "Praise be to Allah, and peace upon His servants whom He has chosen."﴾ Al-Farrā' said: The people of meanings (*ahl al-ma'ānī*) said: It was said to Lot: "Say, Praise be to Allah for their destruction." Others disagreed and said: This is an address to our Prophet (ﷺ). That is, it was said: "Praise be to Allah for the destruction of the disbelievers of the former nations, and peace upon His servants." ﴿Whom He has chosen﴾. Al-Naḥḥās said: This is more correct, because the Qur'an was sent down to the Prophet (ﷺ), and everything in it is addressed to him, unless its meaning cannot be valid except for someone else. It was said: The servants meant by "whom He has chosen" are the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). But it is better to take it in its generality, so that the prophets and their followers are included.

﴿Is Allah better, or what they associate with Him?﴾ That is: Is Allah, whose acts and attributes you have mentioned, which indicate the greatness of His power, better, or what they associate with Him of idols? This "betterness" is not in its original meaning. Rather, it is like the saying of the poet:
*"Do you satirize him, when you are not his equal? Then your evil and his good is ransom."*
So what is in the verse is of the kind of mockery (*tahakkum*) directed at them, since there is no good in them at all.

Sībawayh related that the Arabs say: "Is happiness more beloved to you, or misery?" though there is no good in misery at all.

It was also said: The meaning is: "Is the reward of Allah better, or the punishment of what you associate with Him?" It was also said: He said this to them in accordance with their belief, since they believed that there was good in worshipping idols. It was also said: the intent of this interrogation is information (*khabar*).

The majority read *tushrikūna* with the second-person (*al-fawqiyya*, addressing "you"), which is the choice of Abū 'Ubayd and Abū Ḥātim. Abū 'Amr, 'Āṣim and Ya'qūb read *yushrikūna* with the third person (*al-taḥtiyya*). The *am* in *amma yushrikūna* is the connected (*muttaṣila*) *am*. The *am* in His saying ﴿Or who created the heavens and the earth﴾ is the disconnected (*munqaṭi'a*) *am*. Abū Ḥātim said: The implied sense is: "Are your gods better, or He who created the heavens and the earth and was capable of creating them?" It was also said: The meaning is: "Is the worship of what you worship of your idols better, or the worship of Him who created the heavens and the earth?" On this reading, the *am* is connected, and in it is the sense of rebuke and mockery, as in the first clause. Al-A'mash read *amman* with the *mīm* lightened.

﴿And He sent down for you water from the sky﴾, meaning a kind of water, namely rain. ﴿Then We caused to grow thereby gardens﴾: *ḥadā'iq* is the plural of *ḥadīqa*. Al-Farrā' said: The *ḥadīqa* is an orchard enclosed by a wall. If it has no wall, it is an orchard but not a *ḥadīqa*. Qatādah and 'Ikrimah said: the *ḥadā'iq* are palm trees.

﴿Of beauty and splendor﴾, meaning of loveliness and radiance. *Bahja* is the beauty that delights whoever sees it. He did not say *dhawāta bahjatin* (in the feminine plural) because what is meant is a group of gardens.

﴿It was not for you to cause their trees to grow﴾, meaning: it was not right for you to do that. The sense of this negation is prohibition. The meaning is: who did this? That is, it was not possible for humans, and this is not within their capacity, because of their inability to bring a thing from non-existence into existence.

Then He, glory be to Him, said, rebuking and reproaching them: ﴿Is there a god with Allah?﴾ That is: Is there a worshipped one along with Allah, who has done these acts, so that He should be associated with Him and made a partner in worship? It was also read *ilāhan* (in the accusative) with the implied "Do you call upon a god?"

Then He turned away from their reproach and rebuke with what preceded, and moved to explain the evil of their condition, with a shift from address to the third person, and said: ﴿Rather, they are a people who deviate﴾, meaning: they set up equals to Allah, or they deviate from the truth into falsehood. Then He began to argue from the conditions of the earth and what is upon it, and said: ﴿Or who made the earth a stable place﴾. *Qarār* means the stable, firm place, meaning He spread it out and leveled it so that one can settle upon it.

It was said: this clause and what follows it of the three clauses are an apposition (*badal*) of His saying ﴿Or who created the heavens and the earth﴾, but there is no need for that. Rather, it and what follows it are a shift and transition from the rebuke with what came before to rebuke with something else.

﴿And made rivers through it﴾: *khilāl* means the middle. Its explanation has already been given in His saying: ﴿And We caused a river to gush forth between them﴾ [al-Kahf: 33]. ﴿And made for it firm mountains﴾, meaning mountains fixed to hold it and prevent it from moving. ﴿And placed between the two seas a barrier﴾: *ḥājiz* means the preventer, meaning He placed between the two seas a barrier of His power. The two seas are the sweet and the salty, so that one does not mix with the other, and neither changes the other. Its explanation has already passed in Surat al-Furqān.

﴿Is there a god with Allah?﴾ That is: when it is established that none is able to do that except Allah, then is there a god in existence who makes His making and creates His creation? So how do they associate with Him what neither harms nor benefits? ﴿Rather, most of them do not know﴾ the oneness of their Lord and the authority of His power.

﴿Or who responds to the distressed one when he calls upon Him﴾: this is an argument from Him, glory be to Him, from the need of humans for Him in general. *Al-muḍṭarr* is the passive participle of *iḍṭirār* (compulsion), meaning the afflicted, distressed one, who has no strength or power. It was said: it is the sinner. It was said: it is the one afflicted by harm of poverty or sickness, who is compelled to plead to Allah.

The *al-* in *al-muḍṭarr* is generic (*li-l-jins*), not comprehensive (*li-l-istighrāq*). The supplication of some of the distressed may not be answered, due to an obstacle caused by the servant himself that stands between him and the answer to his prayer. Otherwise, Allah, glory be to Him, has guaranteed the answer to the supplication of the distressed one when he calls upon Him, and He has informed us of this about Himself. The reason the supplication of the distressed is answered is that the distress that comes upon him produces sincerity and cutting off attention from all but Allah. Allah, glory be to Him, has informed us that He answers the supplication of those who are sincere to Him in religion, even if they were disbelievers. He said: ﴿Until, when you are in the ship and they sail with them by a good wind and they rejoice therein, a violent wind comes upon them and the waves come at them from everywhere, and they think they are encompassed, they call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion: "If You save us from this, we will surely be among the grateful"﴾ [Yūnus: 22]. And He said: ﴿Then when He delivered them to the land, immediately they associate﴾ [al-'Ankabūt: 65]. So He answered them in their necessity and sincerity, while knowing that they would return to their polytheism.

﴿And removes the evil﴾, that is, what harms the servant, without specification. It was said it is harm, and it was said it is oppression. ﴿And makes you successors of the earth﴾: meaning each generation among you succeeds the generation before it after their passing away. The meaning: He destroys a generation and brings others into being. It was said: He makes your offspring successors among you. It was said: He makes the Muslims successors to the disbelievers, who inherit their land and dwellings.

﴿Is there a god with Allah?﴾, who bestows upon you these great blessings? ﴿Little do you remember﴾, meaning: you remember only a little.

The majority read with the second person (*al-fawqiyya*). Abū 'Amr, Hishām and Ya'qūb read it with the third person (*al-taḥtiyya*), as information, in response to His saying ﴿Rather, most of them do not know﴾. Abū Ḥātim chose this reading.

﴿Or who guides you in the darknesses of the land and the sea﴾, meaning: who guides you in the dark nights when you travel on land or sea. It was said: what is meant is the wastelands (*mafāwiz*) of the land that have no landmarks, and the deep waters (*lujaj*) of the seas, and He compared them to darkness because there is nothing by which they can be guided in them.

﴿And who sends the winds as glad tidings before His mercy﴾. The mercy here means rain, meaning: He sends the winds before the rain, and before its descent. ﴿Is there a god with Allah?﴾, who does that and brings it into existence? ﴿Exalted is Allah above what they associate with Him﴾, meaning He is far beyond and sanctified above the existence of what they make His partner.

﴿Or who originates creation and then repeats it?﴾ They used to acknowledge that Allah, glory be to Him, is the Creator, so He obliged them to acknowledge resurrection (*al-i'āda*), meaning: if He is capable of initiating creation, He is capable of repeating it. (p-١٠٨٦) ﴿And who provides for you from the heaven and the earth﴾ by rain and vegetation, meaning: is He better, or what you make His partner, which has no power over any of that? ﴿Is there a god with Allah?﴾ so that you make him a partner? ﴿Say: "Bring your proof, if you are truthful."﴾ That is: produce your proof that Allah has a partner, or produce your proof that there is another creator who creates like His creation. In this there is a rebuke for them and mockery of them.

﴿Say: None in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah﴾: that is, none of the created beings in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen which Allah has kept exclusively for His knowledge. The exception in His saying *illā Allāh* is disconnected (*munqaṭi'*), meaning: but Allah knows that. The raising of what follows *illā* together with the exception being disconnected is according to the Tamimi dialect, as in their saying:
*"Except the wild cattle, and except the she-camels."*
It was said: the subject (*fā'il*) of *ya'lamu* is what follows *illā*, and *man fī al-samāwāt* is its object, and *al-ghayb* is an apposition (*badal*) of *man*, meaning: none knows the unseen of those in the heavens and the earth except Allah. It was said: it is a connected exception (*istithnā' muttaṣil*) from *man*. Al-Zajjāj said: *illā Allāh* is an apposition of *man*.

Al-Farrā' said: What follows *illā* is raised because what follows it is the predicate (*khabar*), like their saying: "No one went except your father," and this is like the saying of al-Zajjāj. Al-Zajjāj said: Whoever puts it in the accusative does so as an exception.

﴿And they do not perceive when they will be resurrected﴾: that is, they do not know when they will be raised from the graves. *Ayyāna* is compounded from *ayy* and *inna*, and its explanation has already been given. The pronoun refers to the disbelievers.

Al-Sulamī read *iyyāna* with a kasra on the hamza, which is the dialect of the Banū Sulaym. It is in the accusative governed by *yub'athūna*, and it suspends (*mu'allaqa*) *yash'urūna*, so that it and what follows it are in the accusative position by removal of the preposition, meaning: they do not perceive the time of their resurrection. The meaning of *ayyāna* is the meaning of *matā* (when).

Indeed, they are people who keep themselves pure."﴾ The majority read *jawāba* in the accusative as the predicate (*khabar*) of *kāna*, with its subject being *illā an qālū*, meaning "only their saying." Ibn Abī Ishāq read *jawābun* in the nominative, as the subject (*ism*) of *kāna*, with its predicate being what follows. Then they gave as the reason for what they commanded one another, namely the expulsion, their words: "Indeed, they are people who keep themselves pure," meaning that they abstain from the backsides of men. They said this in mockery of them.

﴿So We saved him and his family﴾ from the punishment, ﴿except his wife. We had decreed that she would be among those who remained behind﴾, meaning We had decreed that she would be among those left to the punishment. *Qaddarnā* means "We decreed." The majority read *qaddarnā* with the doubled letter (*tashdīd*), and 'Āṣim read it without doubling (*takhfīf*). The meaning is one, though the heavier form signifies more meaning through more letters.

﴿And We rained upon them a rain﴾: the repetition indicates the intensity of the rain and that it was unfamiliar. ﴿And evil was the rain of those who were warned﴾. The object of the dispraise is omitted, meaning: "evil was the rain of those warned, their rain." By "those warned" are meant those who were warned and did not accept. All of this has been explained in al-A'rāf and ash-Shu'arā'.

﴿Say: "Praise be to Allah, and peace upon His servants whom He has chosen."﴾ Al-Farrā' said: The people of meanings (*ahl al-ma'ānī*) said: It was said to Lot: "Say, Praise be to Allah for their destruction." Others disagreed and said: This is an address to our Prophet (ﷺ). That is, it was said: "Praise be to Allah for the destruction of the disbelievers of the former nations, and peace upon His servants." ﴿Whom He has chosen﴾. Al-Naḥḥās said: This is more correct, because the Qur'an was sent down to the Prophet (ﷺ), and everything in it is addressed to him, unless its meaning cannot be valid except for someone else. It was said: The servants meant by "whom He has chosen" are the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). But it is better to take it in its generality, so that the prophets and their followers are included.

﴿Is Allah better, or what they associate with Him?﴾ That is: Is Allah, whose acts and attributes you have mentioned, which indicate the greatness of His power, better, or what they associate with Him of idols? This "betterness" is not in its original meaning. Rather, it is like the saying of the poet:
*"Do you satirize him, when you are not his equal? Then your evil and his good is ransom."*
So what is in the verse is of the kind of mockery (*tahakkum*) directed at them, since there is no good in them at all.

Sībawayh related that the Arabs say: "Is happiness more beloved to you, or misery?" though there is no good in misery at all.

It was also said: The meaning is: "Is the reward of Allah better, or the punishment of what you associate with Him?" It was also said: He said this to them in accordance with their belief, since they believed that there was good in worshipping idols. It was also said: the intent of this interrogation is information (*khabar*).

The majority read *tushrikūna* with the second-person (*al-fawqiyya*, addressing "you"), which is the choice of Abū 'Ubayd and Abū Ḥātim. Abū 'Amr, 'Āṣim and Ya'qūb read *yushrikūna* with the third person (*al-taḥtiyya*). The *am* in *amma yushrikūna* is the connected (*muttaṣila*) *am*. The *am* in His saying ﴿Or who created the heavens and the earth﴾ is the disconnected (*munqaṭi'a*) *am*. Abū Ḥātim said: The implied sense is: "Are your gods better, or He who created the heavens and the earth and was capable of creating them?" It was also said: The meaning is: "Is the worship of what you worship of your idols better, or the worship of Him who created the heavens and the earth?" On this reading, the *am* is connected, and in it is the sense of rebuke and mockery, as in the first clause. Al-A'mash read *amman* with the *mīm* lightened.

﴿And He sent down for you water from the sky﴾, meaning a kind of water, namely rain. ﴿Then We caused to grow thereby gardens﴾: *ḥadā'iq* is the plural of *ḥadīqa*. Al-Farrā' said: The *ḥadīqa* is an orchard enclosed by a wall. If it has no wall, it is an orchard but not a *ḥadīqa*. Qatādah and 'Ikrimah said: the *ḥadā'iq* are palm trees.

﴿Of beauty and splendor﴾, meaning of loveliness and radiance. *Bahja* is the beauty that delights whoever sees it. He did not say *dhawāta bahjatin* (in the feminine plural) because what is meant is a group of gardens.

﴿It was not for you to cause their trees to grow﴾, meaning: it was not right for you to do that. The sense of this negation is prohibition. The meaning is: who did this? That is, it was not possible for humans, and this is not within their capacity, because of their inability to bring a thing from non-existence into existence.

Then He, glory be to Him, said, rebuking and reproaching them: ﴿Is there a god with Allah?﴾ That is: Is there a worshipped one along with Allah, who has done these acts, so that He should be associated with Him and made a partner in worship? It was also read *ilāhan* (in the accusative) with the implied "Do you call upon a god?"

Then He turned away from their reproach and rebuke with what preceded, and moved to explain the evil of their condition, with a shift from address to the third person, and said: ﴿Rather, they are a people who deviate﴾, meaning: they set up equals to Allah, or they deviate from the truth into falsehood. Then He began to argue from the conditions of the earth and what is upon it, and said: ﴿Or who made the earth a stable place﴾. *Qarār* means the stable, firm place, meaning He spread it out and leveled it so that one can settle upon it.

It was said: this clause and what follows it of the three clauses are an apposition (*badal*) of His saying ﴿Or who created the heavens and the earth﴾, but there is no need for that. Rather, it and what follows it are a shift and transition from the rebuke with what came before to rebuke with something else.

﴿And made rivers through it﴾: *khilāl* means the middle. Its explanation has already been given in His saying: ﴿And We caused a river to gush forth between them﴾ [al-Kahf: 33]. ﴿And made for it firm mountains﴾, meaning mountains fixed to hold it and prevent it from moving. ﴿And placed between the two seas a barrier﴾: *ḥājiz* means the preventer, meaning He placed between the two seas a barrier of His power. The two seas are the sweet and the salty, so that one does not mix with the other, and neither changes the other. Its explanation has already passed in Surat al-Furqān.

﴿Is there a god with Allah?﴾ That is: when it is established that none is able to do that except Allah, then is there a god in existence who makes His making and creates His creation? So how do they associate with Him what neither harms nor benefits? ﴿Rather, most of them do not know﴾ the oneness of their Lord and the authority of His power.

﴿Or who responds to the distressed one when he calls upon Him﴾: this is an argument from Him, glory be to Him, from the need of humans for Him in general. *Al-muḍṭarr* is the passive participle of *iḍṭirār* (compulsion), meaning the afflicted, distressed one, who has no strength or power. It was said: it is the sinner. It was said: it is the one afflicted by harm of poverty or sickness, who is compelled to plead to Allah.

The *al-* in *al-muḍṭarr* is generic (*li-l-jins*), not comprehensive (*li-l-istighrāq*). The supplication of some of the distressed may not be answered, due to an obstacle caused by the servant himself that stands between him and the answer to his prayer. Otherwise, Allah, glory be to Him, has guaranteed the answer to the supplication of the distressed one when he calls upon Him, and He has informed us of this about Himself. The reason the supplication of the distressed is answered is that the distress that comes upon him produces sincerity and cutting off attention from all but Allah. Allah, glory be to Him, has informed us that He answers the supplication of those who are sincere to Him in religion, even if they were disbelievers. He said: ﴿Until, when you are in the ship and they sail with them by a good wind and they rejoice therein, a violent wind comes upon them and the waves come at them from everywhere, and they think they are encompassed, they call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion: "If You save us from this, we will surely be among the grateful"﴾ [Yūnus: 22]. And He said: ﴿Then when He delivered them to the land, immediately they associate﴾ [al-'Ankabūt: 65]. So He answered them in their necessity and sincerity, while knowing that they would return to their polytheism.

﴿And removes the evil﴾, that is, what harms the servant, without specification. It was said it is harm, and it was said it is oppression. ﴿And makes you successors of the earth﴾: meaning each generation among you succeeds the generation before it after their passing away. The meaning: He destroys a generation and brings others into being. It was said: He makes your offspring successors among you. It was said: He makes the Muslims successors to the disbelievers, who inherit their land and dwellings.

﴿Is there a god with Allah?﴾, who bestows upon you these great blessings? ﴿Little do you remember﴾, meaning: you remember only a little.

The majority read with the second person (*al-fawqiyya*). Abū 'Amr, Hishām and Ya'qūb read it with the third person (*al-taḥtiyya*), as information, in response to His saying ﴿Rather, most of them do not know﴾. Abū Ḥātim chose this reading.

﴿Or who guides you in the darknesses of the land and the sea﴾, meaning: who guides you in the dark nights when you travel on land or sea. It was said: what is meant is the wastelands (*mafāwiz*) of the land that have no landmarks, and the deep waters (*lujaj*) of the seas, and He compared them to darkness because there is nothing by which they can be guided in them.

﴿And who sends the winds as glad tidings before His mercy﴾. The mercy here means rain, meaning: He sends the winds before the rain, and before its descent. ﴿Is there a god with Allah?﴾, who does that and brings it into existence? ﴿Exalted is Allah above what they associate with Him﴾, meaning He is far beyond and sanctified above the existence of what they make His partner.

﴿Or who originates creation and then repeats it?﴾ They used to acknowledge that Allah, glory be to Him, is the Creator, so He obliged them to acknowledge resurrection (*al-i'āda*), meaning: if He is capable of initiating creation, He is capable of repeating it. (p-١٠٨٦) ﴿And who provides for you from the heaven and the earth﴾ by rain and vegetation, meaning: is He better, or what you make His partner, which has no power over any of that? ﴿Is there a god with Allah?﴾ so that you make him a partner? ﴿Say: "Bring your proof, if you are truthful."﴾ That is: produce your proof that Allah has a partner, or produce your proof that there is another creator who creates like His creation. In this there is a rebuke for them and mockery of them.

﴿Say: None in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah﴾: that is, none of the created beings in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen which Allah has kept exclusively for His knowledge. The exception in His saying *illā Allāh* is disconnected (*munqaṭi'*), meaning: but Allah knows that. The raising of what follows *illā* together with the exception being disconnected is according to the Tamimi dialect, as in their saying:
*"Except the wild cattle, and except the she-camels."*
It was said: the subject (*fā'il*) of *ya'lamu* is what follows *illā*, and *man fī al-samāwāt* is its object, and *al-ghayb* is an apposition (*badal*) of *man*, meaning: none knows the unseen of those in the heavens and the earth except Allah. It was said: it is a connected exception (*istithnā' muttaṣil*) from *man*. Al-Zajjāj said: *illā Allāh* is an apposition of *man*.

Al-Farrā' said: What follows *illā* is raised because what follows it is the predicate (*khabar*), like their saying: "No one went except your father," and this is like the saying of al-Zajjāj. Al-Zajjāj said: Whoever puts it in the accusative does so as an exception.

﴿And they do not perceive when they will be resurrected﴾: that is, they do not know when they will be raised from the graves. *Ayyāna* is compounded from *ayy* and *inna*, and its explanation has already been given. The pronoun refers to the disbelievers.

Al-Sulamī read *iyyāna* with a kasra on the hamza, which is the dialect of the Banū Sulaym. It is in the accusative governed by *yub'athūna*, and it suspends (*mu'allaqa*) *yash'urūna*, so that it and what follows it are in the accusative position by removal of the preposition, meaning: they do not perceive the time of their resurrection. The meaning of *ayyāna* is the meaning of *matā* (when).

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 27, verses 54–66 (part 2 of 2)**

﴿Nay, their knowledge has been completed (ibtadarak) concerning the Hereafter.﴾ The majority of readers recite *idtarak* (ادّارَكَ). Its original form is *tadarak* (تَدارَكَ), in which the *ta'* is assimilated into the *dal* (*idgham*, assimilation of consonants), and a connective hamza (*hamzat al-wasl*, the hamza used to allow beginning with a sukun) is added so that the word can be pronounced at the start of an utterance.

Abu Ja'far, Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Humayd read *bal adraka* (بَلْ أدْرَكَ), from *al-idrak* (إدراك, "reaching" or "attaining").

'Ata' ibn Yasar, Sulayman ibn Yasar and al-A'mash read *bala ddaraka* (بَلَ ادَّرَكَ), with a fatha on the *lam* of *bal* and a shadda on the *dal*.

Ibn Muhaysin read *bal adraka* (بَلْ أدْرَكَ) as an interrogative (*al-istifham*, question).

Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Raja', Shayba, al-A'mash and al-A'raj read *bala adarraka* (بَلى أدّارَكَ), with the *ya'* affirmed in *bala*, a hamza of cutting (*hamzat al-qat'*), and a shadda on the *dal*.

Ubayy read *bal tadaraka* (بَلْ تَدارَكَ).

The meaning of the verse is: "Nay, their knowledge became complete concerning the Hereafter, because they saw everything they had been promised and witnessed it directly."

It has also been said that its meaning is: "Their knowledge followed one after another concerning the Hereafter." The second reading means: "All of their knowledge concerning the Hereafter, together with direct witnessing, [came to them]; and that is at the time when knowledge will not benefit them, because they used to deny in the world."

Al-Zajjaj said: it has the sense of denial (*al-inkar*), and this is supported by His words after it: ﴿Nay, they are blind to it﴾, meaning: their knowledge did not reach the knowledge of the Hereafter. It has also been said that the meaning is: "Nay, their knowledge went astray and vanished concerning the Hereafter, so they have no knowledge." The meaning of the third reading is like the meaning of the first, since *if'tala* (افْتَعَلَ) and *tafa'ala* (تَفاعَلَ) may both come with the same meaning. The fourth reading has the sense of denial.

Al-Farra' said: "This is a good interpretation, as if it were directed at the deniers in the manner of mockery toward them." There are other readings of this verse, but it is not appropriate to occupy oneself with mentioning and explaining them.

﴿Nay, they are in doubt concerning it﴾, meaning: nay, they are now in the world, in doubt about the Hereafter. Then He turned away from that to what is more severe than it, saying: ﴿Nay, they are blind to it﴾, so they do not perceive any of its signs, because of the corruption of the insights (*basa'ir*) by which perception occurs. *'Amun* (عَمُونَ) is the plural of *'amin* (عَمٍ), meaning one who is blind of heart. The intended meaning is to show their ignorance of it, in such a way that they are not guided to anything that leads to knowledge of it.

Whoever says that the meaning of the first verse, namely ﴿Nay, their knowledge became complete concerning the Hereafter﴾, is that their knowledge was perfected and completed along with direct witnessing, must necessarily interpret His words ﴿Nay, they are in doubt﴾ and what follows as referring to their state in the world. Whoever says that the meaning of the first verse is mockery of them and rebuke of them does not need to restrict His words ﴿Nay, they are in doubt﴾ and what follows to their state in the world. By this the meaning of these verses becomes clear and manifestly evident.

Ibn Abi Shayba, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bazzar, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His words ﴿And peace be upon His servants whom He has chosen﴾, that he said: "They are the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ), whom Allah chose for His Prophet." The same was narrated from Sufyan al-Thawri.

The preferable view is what we have previously mentioned, namely generality, so that the companions of our Prophet (ﷺ) enter into this primarily.

Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i and al-Tabarani transmitted from a man of Balhajm, who said: "I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, to what do you call?' He said: 'I call to Allah alone, who, if harm touches you and you call upon Him, removes it from you.'" This is a portion of a long hadith.

Ahmad has narrated it through another route, in which he named the companion, saying: "'Affan narrated to us: Hammad ibn Salama narrated to us: Yunus narrated to us: 'Ubayd ibn 'Ubayda al-Hujaymi narrated to us, from his father, from Abu Tamima al-Hujaymi, from Jabir ibn Sulaym al-Hujaymi."

This hadith has other routes in the collections of Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others transmitted from the hadith of 'A'isha, who said: "Whoever says any one of three things has greatly slandered Allah." And Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿Say: No one in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah.﴾

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning ﴿Nay, their knowledge became complete concerning the Hereafter﴾, that he said: "When knowledge no longer benefits."

Abu 'Ubayd in his *Fada'il* (Virtues of the Qur'an), Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him that he recited *bal iddaraka 'ilmuhum fi al-akhirah* (بَلِ ادَّرَكَ عِلْمُهم في الآخِرَةِ), and said: "Their knowledge was not overtaken."

Abu 'Ubayd said: he means that he recited it with the interrogative.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him, that he said concerning *bal iddaraka 'ilmuhum fi al-akhirah*: "Their knowledge vanished."
