It is also in Sahih Muslim from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, raised (to the Prophet ﷺ). Likewise the hadith of Ibn Umar, raised (to the Prophet ﷺ): "The first of the signs to emerge will be the rising of the sun from the west, and the emergence of the creature before the people in the forenoon." It is also in Sahih Muslim.

[p-1087] When He, glory be to Him, mentioned that the polytheists are in doubt about the Resurrection and that they are blind to reflecting on its proofs, He wished to explain the ultimate basis of their objection, which is merely the improbability of raising the dead after they have become dust. So He said: ﴿And those who disbelieve say, "When we are dust, and our fathers too, shall we really be brought forth?"﴾ The governing element (al-'amil) of *idha* (ﷺ "when") is omitted, and it is indicated by *mukhrajun* ("brought forth"). Its implied sense is: "Shall we be resurrected or brought out when we have become dust?" The reason *mukhrajun* does not govern it is that the interrogative hamza and the *inna* and the lam of commencement (*lam al-ibtida'*) come between them.

Abu 'Amr recited with two interrogatives, but he lightened the hamza. 'Asim and Hamza recited with two interrogatives, but both of them made the two hamzas fully pronounced (*tahqiq*). Nafi' recited with one hamza. Ibn 'Amir, Warsh and Ya'qub recited *a-idha* with two hamzas and *wa-inna-na* with two nuns, as a statement (*khabar*). Abu 'Ubayd preferred the recitation of Nafi', and he rejected those who combined two interrogatives. The meaning of the verse is that they denied and deemed improbable that they would come out of their graves alive after having become dust.

Then they reinforced this improbability with something that amounts to denial of the Resurrection, so they said: ﴿Indeed we have been promised this, we and our fathers before, [but] this is nothing but the fables of the ancients﴾ — "this" meaning the Resurrection; ﴿we and our fathers before﴾, that is, before Muhammad's promise to us. The clause is a new sentence (*mustanifa*) and is used to affirm the denial, introduced with an oath for greater emphasis. ﴿Nothing but the fables of the ancients﴾: their tales and their fabricated falsehoods. The meaning of *asatir* (fables) has already been verified in the commentary on Surat al-Mu'minun.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, threatened them for not accepting what the prophets brought concerning the announcement of the Resurrection. So He commanded them to reflect on the states of the earlier nations who denied the prophets, and on what they were punished with and how their end turned out. He said: ﴿Say, "Travel through the earth and then observe how was the end of the guilty"﴾ — [the guilty] for denying what the prophets brought concerning the announcement of the Resurrection. The meaning of "observe" is witnessing their traces with the eye, for in direct witnessing there is greater lesson.

It has also been said: the meaning is, "Then look with your hearts and your insights at how was the end of those who denied their messengers." The first is preferable because of the command to travel through the earth.

﴿And do not grieve over them﴾ — for what has befallen them of persistence in disbelief. ﴿And do not be in distress﴾. *Al-Dayq* means constraint (*haraj*). It is said: "The thing became narrow (*dāqa*) — *dayqan* with a fatha, and *diqan* with a kasra." Both have been recited, and they are two dialects.

Ibn al-Sikkit said: It is said, "In the chest of so-and-so is *dayq* and *diq*," which is that by which the chests are constrained.

The interpretation of this verse has already been given at the end of Surat al-Nahl.

﴿And they say, "When is this promise?" — that is, the punishment with which you threaten us — ﴿if you are truthful﴾ in that.

﴿Say, "Perhaps there has followed you﴾ — *radifa lakum*. It is said: "I rode behind the man" (*radiftu al-rajul*) and "I made him ride behind me" (*ardaftuhu*) when I mounted behind him; and *radifahu* when he followed him and came after him. The meaning: Say, O Muhammad, to these disbelievers: "Perhaps this punishment with which you are threatened has followed you and overtaken you," so the *lam* is additional for emphasis; or it means "has drawn near to you and approached you," in which case the *lam* is not additional.

Ibn Shajara said: The meaning of *radifa lakum* is "followed you." He said: From it comes *ridf* of a woman, because it follows her from behind. From it is the saying of Abu Dhu'ayb:

"Blackness returned as whiteness in its forelocks; no welcome to the whiteness of grey hair, since it came behind."

Al-Jawhari said: *Ardafahu* is a dialectal variant of *radifahu*, like *tabi'ahu* and *atba'ahu*, with the same meaning.

Khuzayma ibn Malik ibn Nahd said:

"When Orion followed the Pleiades, I suspected the family of Fatima of suspicious things."

Al-Farra' said: *Radifa lakum* means "drew near to you," and for this reason it is said *lakum* ("to you").

Al-A'raj recited *radafa lakum* with a fatha on the dal, and it is a dialect; the kasra is more well-known.

Ibn 'Abbas recited *azifa lakum* ("has drawn near to you"). The word ﴿some of what you seek to hasten﴾ is raised (*irtifa'*) as the subject of *radifa*. The intended meaning is: some of what you seek to hasten of the punishment. That is, perhaps some of it has come near and approached and drawn close. It has been said: this is their punishment by killing on the day of Badr. It has been said: it is the punishment of the grave.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned His favor in delaying the punishment, so He said: ﴿And indeed your Lord is full of bounty toward mankind﴾ in delaying punishment. The best view is that the verse is to be taken in its general sense, and the delay of punishment is among His bounties and blessings, glory be to Him. ﴿But most of them do not give thanks﴾ for His favor and blessing, and they do not recognize the right of His kindness.

Then He explained that He is aware of what is in their breasts, so He said: ﴿And indeed your Lord knows what their breasts conceal﴾ — that is, what they hide.

Al-Jumhur recited *tukinnu* with a damma on the *ta'* from *akanna*. Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn al-Sumayfa' and Humayd recited with a fatha on the *ta'* and a damma on the *kaf*; it is said "*kannantuhu*" meaning "I concealed it," and "I hid its trace."

﴿And what they reveal﴾ — what they make manifest of their sayings and their deeds.

﴿And there is not a thing hidden in the heaven and the earth but that it is in a clear Record﴾. The exegetes said: there is not a hidden thing or a matter that is concealed from creation in the heaven and the earth but that it is in a clear Record, which is that it is clarified in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). The word *ghā'ibah* is an adjective, and the *ta'* is for intensification.

Al-Hasan said: The *ghā'ibah* here is the Resurrection.

Muqatil said: The knowledge of what they seek to hasten of the punishment is made clear with Allah, even though it is hidden from creation.

Ibn Shajara said: The *ghā'ibah* here is all that Allah has hidden from His creation, and its being hidden from them is made clear in *Umm al-Kitab* (the Mother of the Book). So how could anything of that be hidden from Him? And among that is what they seek to hasten of the punishment, for it is fixed to a time and delayed to a term whose knowledge is with Allah. So how could they seek to hasten it before its appointed term?

﴿Indeed, this Qur'an relates to the Children of Israel most of that about which they differ﴾. That is because the People of the Book split into sects and formed parties, some of them attacking others and some disowning others. So the Qur'an came clarifying what they differed about of the truth. Had they acted upon it, they would have found in it what would remove their differences and repel their division.

﴿And indeed it is a guidance and a mercy for the believers﴾ — that is, the Qur'an is indeed a guidance and mercy for whoever believes in Allah and follows His Messenger. (p-1088) He specified the believers because they are the ones who benefit from it, and among them are those of the Children of Israel who believed.

﴿Indeed, your Lord will judge between them by His ruling﴾ — that is, He will judge between the disputing among the Children of Israel by what He rules in truth, so He rewards the righteous and punishes the wrongdoer. It has also been said: He will judge between them in this world, so He will make manifest what they distorted.

Al-Jumhur recited *bi-hukmihi* with a damma on the *ha'* and a sukun on the *kaf*. Jinah recited it with a kasra on it and a fatha on the *kaf*, as the plural of *hikmah* (wisdom).

﴿And He is the All-Mighty, the All-Knowing﴾ — *al-'Aziz* is the One who cannot be overcome, and *al-'Alim* is the One who knows what He judges by; or it means the one of abundant knowledge.

Then He, glory be to Him, commanded him to rely upon Him and to be unconcerned, so He said: ﴿So rely upon Allah﴾. The *fa'* is for the ordering of the command upon what was mentioned before. The meaning: entrust your affair to Him and depend on Him, for He is your helper.

Then He gave two reasons for that. The first is His saying: ﴿Indeed you are upon the clear truth﴾ — that is, the manifest; it has also been said: the one that makes manifest.

The second reason is His saying: ﴿Indeed you cannot make the dead hear﴾, for when he knows that their state is like the state of the dead in the absence of benefit from hearing, or like the state of the deaf who do not hear, do not understand and do not get guided, that becomes a strong reason for not giving them any regard. He likened the disbelievers to the dead who have no sensation and no intellect, and to the deaf who do not hear admonitions and do not respond to the call to Allah.

Then He mentioned a further clause to complete and reinforce the comparison, so He said: ﴿When they turn away, retreating﴾ — that is, when they turn away from the truth with complete aversion, for the deaf man does not hear a call when he is facing it, so how much more so when he is turned away from it, retreating and withdrawn.

The apparent sense of the negation of making the dead hear is general, so nothing is excepted from it except what has come with evidence. As it is established in the Sahih that he (ﷺ) addressed the slain in the well of Badr, and it was said to him: "O Messenger of Allah, you are speaking to bodies that have no spirits in them." Likewise is what has come that the dead man hears the sound of the sandals of those who escort him when they turn away.

Ibn Muhaysin, Humayd, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Abi Ishaq recited *la yasma'u* with a *ya'* with a fatha, and a fatha on the *mim*, and its subject is *al-summu* (the deaf). The rest recited *tusmi'u* with a damma on the *ta'* (second person) and a kasra on the *mim*, from *asma'a* (to make hear).

Qatada said: The deaf man, when he turns away retreating, and you call him, does not hear; likewise the disbeliever does not hear what he is called to of faith.

Then He set blindness as an example for them, so He said: ﴿And you cannot guide the blind away from their error﴾ — that is, you are not one who guides whom Allah has blinded from the truth with guidance that brings him to the goal sought from it, which is faith, and that is not within your capacity. A similar statement is His saying: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love﴾ [al-Qasas: 56]. Al-Jumhur recited *bi-hadi al-'umy* with *hadi* in construct with *al-'umy*.

Yahya ibn al-Harith and Abu Hayyan recited *bi-hadin al-'umya* with *hadin* nunated and *al-'umya* in the accusative.

Hamza recited *tahdi* as a present-tense verb, and in the reading of 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) it is *wa-ma an tahdiya al-'umya*.

﴿You cannot make hear except those who believe in Our verses﴾ — that is, you cannot make hear except those who believe, not those who disbelieve. By "those who believe in the verses" is meant those who affirm the Qur'an. The clause ﴿so they are Muslims﴾ is a reason for the faith, that is: so they are submissive and sincere.

Then He threatened the servants by mentioning a part of the signs of the Hour and its terrors, so He said: ﴿And when the word befalls them﴾.

The meaning of the falling of the word upon them has been disputed. Qatada said: the anger became obligatory upon them. Mujahid said: the word became binding upon them that they will not believe. It has been said: the punishment became binding upon them. It has been said: the wrath became obligatory. The meanings are close.

It has been said: the intended "word" is what the Qur'an stated concerning the coming of the Hour and the various kinds of terror in it, which they used to seek to hasten. It has been said: the word falls by the death of the scholars and the departure of knowledge. It has been said: [it falls] when they do not enjoin the good and forbid the evil.

The conclusion is that the intended meaning of *waqa'a* ("fell") is "became obligatory," and the intended meaning of "the word" is its content; or the verbal noun is used in place of the passive participle, i.e., *al-maqul* ("the said"). The answer to the condition is: ﴿We will bring forth for them a creature from the earth to speak to them﴾.

The views differ about this creature. It has been said: it is the young camel of the she-camel of Salih, which comes out when the Hour draws near and is among the signs of the Hour.

It has been said: it is a creature with hair and long legs, called *al-Jassasa*.

It has been said: it is a creature in the form of the children of Adam, which is in the clouds, while its feet are on the earth.

It has been said: its head is the head of a bull, its eye is the eye of a pig, its ear is the ear of an elephant, its horn is the horn of a stag, its neck is the neck of an ostrich, its chest is the chest of a lion, its color is the color of a leopard, its flank is the flank of a cat, its tail is the tail of a ram, and its legs are the legs of a camel, with twelve cubits between every joint and joint.

It has been said: it is the serpent that rose above the wall of the Ka'bah, which the eagle snatched away when Quraysh wished to rebuild the Ka'bah. The meaning is that it is the one that comes out at the end of time. It has been said: it is a creature with no tail and with a beard. It has been said: it is a speaking human being who debates the people of innovation and argues with the disbelievers. It has been said other things that there is no benefit in lengthening by mentioning. Al-Qurtubi, in his tafsir, preferred the first view.

They differed about the place from which it will come out. It has been said: from Mount Safa in Makkah. It has been said: it comes out from Mount Abu Qubays.

It has been said: it has three emergences: one emergence in some of the deserts, until people fight over it and much blood is shed, then it hides; and it emerges in the towns; then it emerges from the greatest, most honored and most noble of the mosques. It has been said: it emerges from between the Corner and the Station (al-Maqam). It has been said: it emerges in Tihamah. It has been said: from the mosque of Kufa, from the place where the oven boiled over. It has been said: from the land of al-Ta'if. It has been said: from a rock in the valley of Ajyad. It has been said: from a crack in the Ka'bah.

They differed about the meaning of His saying "it will speak to them." It has been said: it will speak to them about the falsehood of religions other than the religion of Islam. It has been said: it will speak to them with what displeases them. It has been said: it will speak to them with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿that mankind were not certain of Our verses﴾ — that is, of its emergence, because its emergence is among the signs.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 27, verses 67–82 (part 2 of 2):

The majority of reciters read ﴿تُكَلِّمُهم﴾ (tukallimuhum) from *al-taklim* (speaking). This is supported by Ubayy's reading ﴿تُنَبِّئُهم﴾ (tunabbi'uhum, "informs them"). Ibn Abbas, Abu Zur'a, Abu Raja' and al-Hasan read ﴿تَكْلَمُهم﴾ (takla­muhum), with a fatha on the taa' and a sukun on the kaaf, from *al-kalm*, which means wounding.

Ikrimah said: that is, it will brand them with a mark. It was also said: it will wound them. It was also said that the reading of the majority is derived from *al-kalm* with a fatha on the kaaf and a sukun on the lam, meaning wounding, and that the doubled letter indicates intensification. This was stated by Abu Hatim.

The majority read ﴿إنَّ النّاسَ كانُوا بِآياتِنا لا يُوقِنُونَ﴾ (inna al-nasa kanu bi-ayatina la yuqinun, "Indeed the people were not certain of Our signs") with a kasra on *inna*, as a new sentence (*isti'naf*). The Kufans and Ibn Abi Ishaq read it with a fatha on *anna*. Al-Akhfash said: the meaning according to the fatha reading is ﴿بِأنَّ النّاسَ﴾ (bi-anna al-nasa, "that the people..."). Ibn Mas'ud also read it as ﴿بِأنَّ النّاسَ﴾ with the preposition *bi*.

Abu Ubayd said: its position is in the accusative, as the object of the verb falling upon it. That is, [the beast] informs them that the people... On this reading, what the people spoke is the statement ﴿أنَّ النّاسَ كانُوا بِآياتِنا لا يُوقِنُونَ﴾, as we indicated earlier.

As for the reading with a kasra, the clause is a new sentence, as we indicated earlier, and it is not part of the speech of the beast.

A group of exegetes stated this explicitly, and al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' affirmed it.

Al-Akhfash said: the kasra on *inna* is based on an implied verb of saying, meaning: it says to them, "Indeed the people...," and so the meaning of the first reading returns to the meaning of the second reading. The word "people" in the verse is meant in its general sense, so it includes every responsible person. It was also said that the intended meaning is the disbelievers specifically, and it was said that it is the disbelievers of Makkah. The first view is the better one.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas, concerning his words ﴿عَسى أنْ يَكُونَ رَدِفَ لَكُمْ﴾ ("It may be that some of it has come close behind you"), that he said: it has drawn near to you.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him concerning ﴿وإنَّ رَبَّكَ لَيَعْلَمُ ما تُكِنُّ صُدُورُهم وما يُعْلِنُونَ﴾ ("Indeed your Lord knows what their breasts conceal and what they disclose"), that he said: He knows what they did by night and by day.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him concerning ﴿وما مِن غائِبَةٍ﴾ ("And there is not any hidden thing") and the verse, that he said: there is no thing in the heavens and the earth, secret or open, but He knows it.

Ibn al-Mubarak in al-Zuhd, Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Na'im ibn Hammad, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn Umar, concerning His words ﴿وإذا وقَعَ القَوْلُ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾ ("And when the word comes to pass against them") and the verse, that he said: when they do not enjoin what is right (*ma'ruf*) and do not forbid what is wrong (*munkar*).

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted it from him as a marfu' report (traced to the Prophet ﷺ).

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir transmitted from Abu al-Aliyah that he explained ﴿وقَعَ القَوْلُ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾ as what was revealed to Nuh: that none of your people will believe except those who have already believed.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas, concerning His words ﴿دابَّةً مِنَ الأرْضِ تُكَلِّمُهُمْ﴾ ("a creature from the earth will speak to them"), that he said: it will talk to them (*tuhaddithuhum*).

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him that he said: its speech is that it informs them that the people were not certain of Our signs.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Abu Dawud Nufay' al-A'ma, who said: I asked Ibn Abbas about His words *tukallimuhum* (it speaks to them): is it from speaking with the tongue, or from *al-kalm*, which is wounding? He said: all of that, by God, it does: it speaks to the believer and it wounds the disbeliever, that is, it wounds him.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn Umar concerning the verse that he said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "That is not speech nor words, but it is a mark that brands whoever God has commanded it to brand. Its emergence will be from al-Safa on the night of Mina, and in the morning they will be between its head and its tail, and no one who is pushed back will be pushed back and no wounder will wound. Then, when it has finished what God commanded it to do, whoever perishes perishes and whoever is saved is saved, and the first step it takes will be at Antioch."

Abd ibn Humayd transmitted from Ibn Abbas, who said: the creature has hair and feathers, combined with every colour, and it has four legs, and it emerges with a heel of the pilgrims.

Ahmad and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Abu Umamah, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "The creature will emerge and brand them on their noses. Then they will live among you until a man buys a creature, and it is said to him: From whom did you buy it? He says: From the man who was branded."

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn Abbas that the creature has three emergences, and he mentioned something similar to what we have already cited.

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Hudhayfah ibn Usayd, raised (to the Prophet ﷺ), who said: "The creature will emerge from among the most sacred mosques."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Na'im ibn Hammad, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas, who said: it will emerge from one of the valleys of Tihamah.

Al-Tayalisi, Ahmad, Na'im ibn Hammad, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan, Ibn Majah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th transmitted from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "The creature of the earth will emerge, and with it will be the staff of Musa and the seal of Sulayman. It will illuminate the face of the believer with the seal, and it will brand the nose of the disbeliever with the staff, until people gather at the table, and the believer is recognized from the disbeliever."

Al-Tayalisi, Na'im ibn Hammad, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who declared it sahih, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th transmitted from Hudhayfah ibn Asid al-Ghifari, who said: "The Messenger of God ﷺ mentioned the creature and said: It has three emergences in the course of time," and he mentioned something similar to what we have already cited, in a long hadith.

Concerning its description, the place of its emergence, what it does, and when it emerges, there are many hadiths, some of which are sahih, some hasan, and some da'if.

As for its emerging and its being one of the signs of the Hour, the hadiths reported on this are sahih.

Among them is what is established in the Sahih, such as the hadith of Hudhayfah, raised (to the Prophet ﷺ): "The Hour will not come until you see ten signs," and he mentioned the creature among them. It is in Sahih Muslim and in the four Sunan. Likewise the hadith: "Hasten to good deeds before the sun rises from the west, and the Dajjal, and the creature." It is also in Sahih Muslim from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, raised (to the Prophet ﷺ). Likewise the hadith of Ibn Umar, raised (to the Prophet ﷺ): "The first of the signs to emerge will be the rising of the sun from the west, and the emergence of the creature before the people in the forenoon." It is also in Sahih Muslim.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 27, verse 83–93 (part 1 of 2):

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned a brief outline of the terrors of the Day of Resurrection, and said: ﴿And on the day We gather from every nation a crowd﴾. The governing element of the adverbial phrase (al-zarf) is a verb that has been omitted, and it is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-hashr means gathering.

It has been said: what is meant by this gathering is the gathering of punishment (hashr al-ʿadhab), after the general gathering that encompasses all of creation. Min (from) here denotes the starting point (li-ibtida' al-ghayah). Al-fawj is a group, like al-zumrah (a company). Min in ﴿of those who deny Our signs﴾ is explanatory (bayaniyyah). ﴿Then they are driven on﴾ means their first is held back until their last joins them. Its verification has already been discussed fully in this surah. It has also been said that its meaning is: they are pushed back. From this is the saying of al-Shammakh:

*"How many a host, a mighty army, have we held back"*

The meaning of the verse is: Mention, O Muhammad, a day when We will gather from every nation of the nations a group who denied Our signs; then, at that gathering, their first will be turned back upon their last, or they will be pushed; that is, make this known to them, or explain it to them, as a warning and a frightening.

﴿Until, when they arrive﴾ at the place of reckoning, God says to them, as rebuke and reproach: ﴿Did you deny My signs﴾ which I sent down upon My messengers and commanded them to convey to you, ﴿while you did not encompass them in knowledge﴾? Rather, you denied them at the very outset, being ignorant of them, not looking into them, nor reasoning about their soundness or falsehood, out of rebellion, obstinacy, and audacity against God and His messengers. In this there is further reproach and rebuke, because whoever denies something without having encompassed it in knowledge has, in his denial, lied, and has proclaimed his own ignorance, unfairness, bad understanding, and deficiency of comprehension. Of this kind is whoever takes it upon himself to disparage one of the religious sciences (al-ʿulum al-shariʿyyah), or a science that is a prerequisite of them and a means by which one reaches them, and which yields greater insight into understanding them and grasping their meanings, such as all the sciences of the Arabic language, which are twelve sciences, and the science of usul al-fiqh (principles of jurisprudence), by which one arrives at deriving the legal rulings from their detailed evidences, along with its inclusion of the general rules of the language. Likewise every science that is of further benefit in understanding the Book of God and the Sunnah of His Messenger. Such a person has proclaimed with the loudest voice that he is ignorant, a disputer in falsehood, a slanderer of the religious sciences, deserving that some calamity of the calamities of punishment should befall him, which will restrain him from his ignorance and error and from his slander of what he does not know, nor has knowledge of, nor encompasses its reality, until he becomes a lesson to others and an admonition by which the likes of him are warned, namely the weak-minded, the frail in religion, the rabble of those who falsely and deceitfully clothe themselves in knowledge.

In His saying ﴿Or what were you doing﴾, the particle am (or) is the disjunctive one (al-munqatiʿah). The meaning is: or what was it that you were doing that occupied you from looking into them and reflecting on their meanings? This interrogation is by way of rebuke for them.

﴿And the word will come into effect against them﴾: its explanation has already been given shortly before. The ba' in ﴿for what they did wrong﴾ is causal: that is, the word becomes binding upon them because of the wrongdoing, the greatest kind of which is associating partners with God. ﴿So they will not speak﴾ when the word takes effect against them; that is, they have no excuse to speak with, or they will not be able to speak because of the great terror they see.

Most of the exegetes said: a seal will be placed upon their mouths, so they will not speak. Then, after He had frightened them with the terrors of the Resurrection, He, glory be to Him, mentioned what may serve as evidence for monotheism, for the gathering, and for prophethood, as an intensification of guidance and a completion of the argument.

He said: ﴿Have they not seen that We made the night for them to rest therein, and the day giving sight?﴾ That is: We made the night for repose, settling, and sleep, because of the darkness in it, for they do not strive therein for livelihood; and the day giving sight, so that they may see therein what they strive for of livelihood, which they cannot do without. The attribution of sight to the day, when sight belongs to people, is an intensification of its brightness, as if it sees what is in it.

It has been said: there is an ellipsis in the speech; the implied sense is: and We made the night dark so that they may rest. He omitted "dark" because "giving sight" points to it. Its verification has already been discussed in al-Isra' and in Yunus. ﴿Indeed in that are signs﴾: that is, indicators and proofs ﴿for a people who believe﴾ in God, glory be to Him.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned another sign of the Resurrection, saying: ﴿And the day the Trumpet is blown﴾. It is conjoined to ﴿And the day We gather﴾ and is in the accusative governed by the same governing element mentioned earlier.

Al-Farra' said: the meaning is: that is the day the Trumpet is blown; but the first is preferable.

Al-Sur is a horn into which Israfil blows, and the complete discussion of it has already been given in al-An'am.

The blasts of the Trumpet are three: the first is the blast of terror (nafkhat al-fazaʿ), the second is the blast of swooning (nafkhat al-saʿq), and the third is the blast of resurrection (nafkhat al-baʿth).

It has been said that they are two blasts, and that the blast of terror is either part of the blast of swooning or of the blast of resurrection. Al-Qushayri, al-Qurtubi, and others chose this view.

Al-Mawardi said: the blast mentioned here is the blast of rising from the graves. ﴿So whoever is in the heavens and whoever is in the earth will be terrified﴾: that is, they fear and are startled because of the intensity of what they hear. It has been said that the meaning of "terrified" here is hurrying and responding to a call, from the saying "fazia'tu ilayka fi kadha" (I hastened to you in such and such a matter) when I quickly responded to your summons. The first is preferable for the meaning of the verse.

He expressed it in the past tense although it is conjoined to a present (imperfect) verb, to indicate the certainty of its occurrence, as the scholars of rhetoric (ʿulama' al-bayan) have mentioned.

Al-Farra' said: it is to be understood according to meaning, because the meaning is: when it is blown, except whom God wills, that is, except whom God wills not to be terrified at that blast.

Scholars differed about who is meant by the exception. It has been said: they are the martyrs and the prophets. It has been said: the angels. It has been said: Jibril, Mika'il, Israfil, and the Angel of Death. It has been said: the dark-eyed houris. It has been said: all the believers, on the evidence of His saying afterward: ﴿Whoever brings a good deed will have better than it, and they will be secure from the terror of that day﴾. It is possible that the exception includes all of those mentioned, and there is no obstacle to that.

﴿And all will come to Him, humbled﴾. The majority read ʾatūhu (ءاتوه), in the form of the active participle, with a pronoun referring back to God, glory be to Him.

Al-A'mash, Yahya ibn Wathhab, Hamzah, and Hafs from ʿAsim read ʾatawhu as a past verb (fiʿl madi), and so did Ibn Mas'ud.

Qatadah read ʾatāhu.

Al-Zajjaj said: whoever reads it as a past verb has made it singular in agreement with the word kull (all), and whoever reads it as an active participle has made it plural in agreement with its meaning. This is a manifest error, for neither reading contains singularity; singularity is found only in Qatadah's reading. The meaning of dakhirin is humbled and abased, and it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl). The majority read dakhirin, while al-A'raj read dakhirin without an alif. Its explanation has already passed in surah al-Nahl.

﴿And you see the mountains, you think them solid﴾ is conjoined to "is blown".

The address is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), or to everyone who is fit to see. ﴿You think them solid﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier, either of the subject of "you see" or of its object, because the seeing is visual. It has been said that it is a substitute (badal) for the first clause, but this is weak. This is the third sign of the Hour. The meaning of ﴿you think them solid﴾ is: standing still. The clause ﴿while they pass as the clouds pass﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier, meaning: while they move with a swift motion like the motion of clouds driven by the winds.

Al-Qutaybi said: that is because the mountains will be gathered and set in motion, while in the sight of the eye they seem to be standing still while they move.

Al-Qushayri said: this is on the Day of Resurrection, and similar to it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the mountains will be set in motion and become a mirage﴾ (al-Naba' 78:20).

The people of Kufa read tahsabuha with a fatha on the sin; the rest read it with a kasra.

﴿The handiwork of God, who perfected everything﴾. The accusative of "handiwork" (ṣun'a) is as a verbal noun (maṣdar), according to al-Khalil, Sibawayh, and others; that is, God did that as a handiwork. It has been said that it is a verbal noun emphasizing His saying ﴿And the day the Trumpet is blown﴾. It has been said that it is in the accusative as an incitement, that is: look at the handiwork of God. The meaning of ﴿who perfected everything﴾ is: who made it firm and sound. It is said: a man is tiqn, meaning skilled in things.

﴿Indeed He is Aware of what you do﴾ is a justification for what precedes it: that He, glory be to Him, did what He did and perfected everything. Khabir (Aware) means one who knows the outward and the inward.

The majority read with the second-person ta' (tafʿalūn, "you do"), while Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and Hisham read it with the third-person ya' (yafʿalūn, "they do"), as a report.

﴿Whoever comes with a good deed, for him is better than it﴾. The alif-lam is generic: that is, whoever comes with a good deed of this kind, for him, from the recompense and reward with God, is better than it; that is, more excellent and greater than it. It has been said: "better" means a good that accrues from its source. The first is preferable.

It has been said: what is meant by "good deed" here is: there is no god but God. It has been said: sincerity. It has been said: performing the obligations. The generalization is preferable, and there is no basis for specifying it, even though some of the early generations (salaf) held that view.

It has been said: this clause explains His saying ﴿Indeed He is Aware of what you do﴾. It has also been said: it explains His saying ﴿And all will come to Him, humbled﴾.

ʿAsim, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read ﴿and they from terror﴾ with tanwin and with a fatha on the mim of yawmaʾidh (that day). Nafi' read it with the fatha on the mim without tanwin.

The rest read the word "terror" in the construct with yawmaʾidh.

Abu ʿUbayd said: this is more pleasing to me, because it is more general of the two interpretations, for its meaning is: security from the terror of that entire day; whereas with tanwin, it becomes security from some terror and not others.

It has been said: it is a verbal noun that covers much, so the preference cannot be completed on the basis of what was mentioned, and the two readings have one meaning.

It has been said: what is meant by "terror" here is the greatest terror mentioned in His saying: ﴿The greatest terror will not grieve them﴾ (al-Anbiya' 21:103). The rationale for Nafi''s reading is that he put yawm in the accusative as a time adverb, since its case inflection (iʿrab) is not fully declinable (ghayr mutamakkin). Since the attribution of "terror" to a non-declinable time expression, it became indeclinable. A full discussion of this has already passed in surah Hud.

﴿And whoever comes with an evil deed, their faces will be overturned into the Fire﴾.

A group of the Companions and those after them, to the point that it was said it is agreed upon among the interpreters, said: what is meant by "evil deed" here is associating partners with God. The reason for specification is His saying: ﴿their faces will be overturned into the Fire﴾, since this recompense is not given except for the like of the evil of associating partners. The meaning of ﴿their faces will be overturned into the Fire﴾ is that they will be thrown into it on their faces, cast into it and hurled upon it. It is said: kababtu al-rajul (I overturned the man) when you throw him onto his face, so he falls prone (fa-nkabba wa-akabba). The clause ﴿Are you recompensed except for what you used to do?﴾ is in an implied speech: that is, it will be said; and the speaker is the guardians of Hell, meaning: you are recompensed only with the recompense of your deeds.

﴿I have only been commanded to worship the Lord of this city, who has made it sacred﴾. When He, glory be to Him, finished explaining the states of the beginning and the return, He commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to say this statement to them. That is: Say, O Muhammad, I have only been commanded to single out God for worship, with no partner to Him. By "the city" is meant Makkah. He singled it out from among all other lands because the Sacred House of God is in it, and because it is the most beloved of lands to His Messenger. The relative clause is an attribute of "the Lord." This is how the majority read it. Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Mas'ud read ﴿which He has made sacred﴾ with the relative clause as an attribute of "the city." The meaning of "made sacred" is: made it a sanctuary (haram) and a safe place, where no blood is shed, no one is wronged, its game is not hunted, and its grass is not cut. ﴿And to Him belongs everything﴾ among things, in creation, ownership, and disposal; that is, everything belongs to God. ﴿And I have been commanded to be among the Muslims﴾, that is: those who submit to God's command and surrender to Him in obedience, carrying out His order and avoiding His prohibition. By His saying "that I be" is meant: that I remain steadfast in what I am upon.

﴿And to recite the Qur'an﴾: that is, that I persist in its recitation and be constant in it.

It has been said: the intended meaning of "reciting the Qur'an" here is nothing other than reciting the call to faith, but the first view is preferable. ﴿Whoever is guided, he is only guided for his own soul﴾, because the benefit of that returns to him. That is, whoever is guided in general, or whoever is guided by what I recite to him and acts upon what it contains of faith. The first view is preferable. ﴿Whoever is guided, he is only guided for his own soul﴾, because the benefit of that returns to him. That is, whoever is guided in general, or whoever is guided by what I recite to him and acts upon what it contains of faith in God and the practice of His laws.

Al-Jumhur (the majority of reciters) read "wa-an atluwa" with the waw affixed after the lam, as being from tilawah (recitation), which is reading, or from tilw, which is following.

ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud) read "wa-ani-tlu" with the waw omitted, as an imperative addressed to him (ﷺ). Al-Farrāʾ (al-Farra') gave this reading that interpretation.

Al-Nahhas (al-Nahhas) said: "We do not know of anyone who read this reading, and it contradicts all the copies of the Qur'an." ﴿And whoever goes astray, say: I am only one of the warners﴾. That is: whoever goes astray through disbelief and turns away from guidance, say to him: I am only one of the warners, and I have fulfilled that by conveying it to you, and there is nothing incumbent upon me other than that.

It has been said: the answer is omitted, meaning: then the burden of his straying falls upon him, and "I am only one of the warners" has been placed in its position because it is like the cause for it.

﴿And say: Praise belongs to God﴾ for His blessings which He has bestowed upon me, of prophethood, knowledge and other than that. His saying: ﴿He will show you His signs, and you will recognize them﴾ is among what the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to say. That is: God will show you His signs in your own selves and in others, and you will recognize them, that is, you will recognize His signs and the proofs of His power and His oneness. This recognition does not benefit the disbelievers, because they recognized them at a time when faith is no longer accepted from them, and that is at the moment of the presence of death.

Then He concluded the surah with His saying: ﴿And your Lord is not unaware of what you do﴾. This is a statement from Him, glorified is He, not included within the speech which He commanded the Prophet (ﷺ) to say, and in it is intense warning and a great threat.

Ahl al-Madina, al-Sham and Hafs from ʿAsim read "taʿmalūna" with the second person (taʾ), as an address. The rest read it with the third person (yāʾ).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying ﴿dākhirīn﴾, that he said: "ṣāghirīn" (humbled).

These same related from him, regarding His saying ﴿And you see the mountains, you think them solid﴾, that he said: "qāʾimah" (standing). ﴿The handiwork of God, who perfected everything﴾, he said: "aḥkama" (made firm).

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also related from him, regarding His saying ﴿The handiwork of God, who perfected everything﴾, he said: "He made everything He created good and firm."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh related from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "﴿Whoever comes with a good deed, for him is better than it﴾, he said: it is 'There is no god but God'. ﴿And whoever comes with an evil deed, their faces will be thrown into the Fire﴾, he said: it is shirk (associating partners with God)." And if this is authentically from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), then turning to it in interpreting the speech of God, glorified is He, is necessary, and it is understood to mean: whoever says "There is no god but God" in its truth and what is due to it, then every act of obedience enters under that. And what al-Hakim in al-Kuna (al-Kuna) related from Safwan ibn ʿAssal supports this, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, faith and shirk will come kneeling before God, glorified is He. God will say to faith: Go, you and your people, to Paradise. And He will say to shirk: Go, you and your people, to the Fire."

﴿Whoever comes with a good deed, for him is better than it﴾, meaning His saying: "There is no god but God". ﴿And whoever comes with an evil deed﴾, meaning shirk, ﴿their faces will be thrown into the Fire﴾."

Ibn Mardawayh related from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah and Anas, and the like of it, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Daylami related from Kaʿb ibn ʿUjrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever comes with a good deed, meaning the testimony that there is no god but God, ﴿for him is better than it﴾, meaning by the good, Paradise. ﴿And whoever comes with an evil deed﴾, meaning shirk, ﴿their faces will be thrown into the Fire﴾." And he said: "This one saves, and this one destroys."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wal-Sifat, and al-Kharaʾiti in Makarim al-Akhlaq, related from Ibn Masʿud: ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed﴾, he said: "There is no god but God." ﴿And whoever comes with an evil deed﴾, he said: "with shirk."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related the like of this from Ibn ʿAbbas.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related regarding ﴿for him is better than it﴾, that he said: "For him there is good from it," meaning from its direction.

Ibn Abi Hatim also related from him, ﴿for him is better than it﴾, he said: "reward." He also related from him, that he said: "The town is Makkah."

Most of the exegetes said: a seal will be placed upon their mouths, so they will not speak. Then, after He had frightened them with the terrors of the Resurrection, He, glory be to Him, mentioned what may serve as evidence for monotheism, for the gathering, and for prophethood, as an intensification of guidance and a completion of the argument.

He said: ﴿Have they not seen that We made the night for them to rest therein, and the day giving sight?﴾ That is: We made the night for repose, settling, and sleep, because of the darkness in it, for they do not strive therein for livelihood; and the day giving sight, so that they may see therein what they strive for of livelihood, which they cannot do without. The attribution of sight to the day, when sight belongs to people, is an intensification of its brightness, as if it sees what is in it.

It has been said: there is an ellipsis in the speech; the implied sense is: and We made the night dark so that they may rest. He omitted "dark" because "giving sight" points to it. Its verification has already been discussed in al-Isra' and in Yunus. ﴿Indeed in that are signs﴾: that is, indicators and proofs ﴿for a people who believe﴾ in God, glory be to Him.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned another sign of the Resurrection, saying: ﴿And the day the Trumpet is blown﴾. It is conjoined to ﴿And the day We gather﴾ and is in the accusative governed by the same governing element mentioned earlier.

Al-Farra' said: the meaning is: that is the day the Trumpet is blown; but the first is preferable.

Al-Sur is a horn into which Israfil blows, and the complete discussion of it has already been given in al-An'am.

The blasts of the Trumpet are three: the first is the blast of terror (nafkhat al-fazaʿ), the second is the blast of swooning (nafkhat al-saʿq), and the third is the blast of resurrection (nafkhat al-baʿth).

It has been said that they are two blasts, and that the blast of terror is either part of the blast of swooning or of the blast of resurrection. Al-Qushayri, al-Qurtubi, and others chose this view.

Al-Mawardi said: the blast mentioned here is the blast of rising from the graves. ﴿So whoever is in the heavens and whoever is in the earth will be terrified﴾: that is, they fear and are startled because of the intensity of what they hear. It has been said that the meaning of "terrified" here is hurrying and responding to a call, from the saying "fazia'tu ilayka fi kadha" (I hastened to you in such and such a matter) when I quickly responded to your summons. The first is preferable for the meaning of the verse.

He expressed it in the past tense although it is conjoined to a present (imperfect) verb, to indicate the certainty of its occurrence, as the scholars of rhetoric (ʿulama' al-bayan) have mentioned.

Al-Farra' said: it is to be understood according to meaning, because the meaning is: when it is blown, except whom God wills, that is, except whom God wills not to be terrified at that blast.

Scholars differed about who is meant by the exception. It has been said: they are the martyrs and the prophets. It has been said: the angels. It has been said: Jibril, Mika'il, Israfil, and the Angel of Death. It has been said: the dark-eyed houris. It has been said: all the believers, on the evidence of His saying afterward: ﴿Whoever brings a good deed will have better than it, and they will be secure from the terror of that day﴾. It is possible that the exception includes all of those mentioned, and there is no obstacle to that.

﴿And all will come to Him, humbled﴾. The majority read ʾatūhu (ءاتوه), in the form of the active participle, with a pronoun referring back to God, glory be to Him.

Al-A'mash, Yahya ibn Wathhab, Hamzah, and Hafs from ʿAsim read ʾatawhu as a past verb (fiʿl madi), and so did Ibn Mas'ud.

Qatadah read ʾatāhu.

Al-Zajjaj said: whoever reads it as a past verb has made it singular in agreement with the word kull (all), and whoever reads it as an active participle has made it plural in agreement with its meaning. This is a manifest error, for neither reading contains singularity; singularity is found only in Qatadah's reading. The meaning of dakhirin is humbled and abased, and it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl). The majority read dakhirin, while al-A'raj read dakhirin without an alif. Its explanation has already passed in surah al-Nahl.

﴿And you see the mountains, you think them solid﴾ is conjoined to "is blown".

The address is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), or to everyone who is fit to see. ﴿You think them solid﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier, either of the subject of "you see" or of its object, because the seeing is visual. It has been said that it is a substitute (badal) for the first clause, but this is weak. This is the third sign of the Hour. The meaning of ﴿you think them solid﴾ is: standing still. The clause ﴿while they pass as the clouds pass﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier, meaning: while they move with a swift motion like the motion of clouds driven by the winds.

Al-Qutaybi said: that is because the mountains will be gathered and set in motion, while in the sight of the eye they seem to be standing still while they move.

Al-Qushayri said: this is on the Day of Resurrection, and similar to it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the mountains will be set in motion and become a mirage﴾ (al-Naba' 78:20).

The people of Kufa read tahsabuha with a fatha on the sin; the rest read it with a kasra.

﴿The handiwork of God, who perfected everything﴾. The accusative of "handiwork" (ṣun'a) is as a verbal noun (maṣdar), according to al-Khalil, Sibawayh, and others; that is, God did that as a handiwork. It has been said that it is a verbal noun emphasizing His saying ﴿And the day the Trumpet is blown﴾. It has been said that it is in the accusative as an incitement, that is: look at the handiwork of God. The meaning of ﴿who perfected everything﴾ is: who made it firm and sound. It is said: a man is tiqn, meaning skilled in things.

﴿Indeed He is Aware of what you do﴾ is a justification for what precedes it: that He, glory be to Him, did what He did and perfected everything. Khabir (Aware) means one who knows the outward and the inward.

The majority read with the second-person ta' (tafʿalūn, "you do"), while Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and Hisham read it with the third-person ya' (yafʿalūn, "they do"), as a report.

﴿Whoever comes with a good deed, for him is better than it﴾. The alif-lam is generic: that is, whoever comes with a good deed of this kind, for him, from the recompense and reward with God, is better than it; that is, more excellent and greater than it. It has been said: "better" means a good that accrues from its source. The first is preferable.

It has been said: what is meant by "good deed" here is: there is no god but God. It has been said: sincerity. It has been said: performing the obligations. The generalization is preferable, and there is no basis for specifying it, even though some of the early generations (salaf) held that view.

It has been said: this clause explains His saying ﴿Indeed He is Aware of what you do﴾. It has also been said: it explains His saying ﴿And all will come to Him, humbled﴾.

ʿAsim, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read ﴿and they from terror﴾ with tanwin and with a fatha on the mim of yawmaʾidh (that day). Nafi' read it with the fatha on the mim without tanwin.

The rest read the word "terror" in the construct with yawmaʾidh.

Abu ʿUbayd said: this is more pleasing to me, because it is more general of the two interpretations, for its meaning is: security from the terror of that entire day; whereas with tanwin, it becomes security from some terror and not others.

It has been said: it is a verbal noun that covers much, so the preference cannot be completed on the basis of what was mentioned, and the two readings have one meaning.

It has been said: what is meant by "terror" here is the greatest terror mentioned in His saying: ﴿The greatest terror will not grieve them﴾ (al-Anbiya' 21:103). The rationale for Nafi''s reading is that he put yawm in the accusative as a time adverb, since its case inflection (iʿrab) is not fully declinable (ghayr mutamakkin). Since the attribution of "terror" to a non-declinable time expression, it became indeclinable. A full discussion of this has already passed in surah Hud.

﴿And whoever comes with an evil deed, their faces will be overturned into the Fire﴾.

A group of the Companions and those after them, to the point that it was said it is agreed upon among the interpreters, said: what is meant by "evil deed" here is associating partners with God. The reason for specification is His saying: ﴿their faces will be overturned into the Fire﴾, since this recompense is not given except for the like of the evil of associating partners. The meaning of ﴿their faces will be overturned into the Fire﴾ is that they will be thrown into it on their faces, cast into it and hurled upon it. It is said: kababtu al-rajul (I overturned the man) when you throw him onto his face, so he falls prone (fa-nkabba wa-akabba). The clause ﴿Are you recompensed except for what you used to do?﴾ is in an implied speech: that is, it will be said; and the speaker is the guardians of Hell, meaning: you are recompensed only with the recompense of your deeds.

﴿I have only been commanded to worship the Lord of this city, who has made it sacred﴾. When He, glory be to Him, finished explaining the states of the beginning and the return, He commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to say this statement to them. That is: Say, O Muhammad, I have only been commanded to single out God for worship, with no partner to Him. By "the city" is meant Makkah. He singled it out from among all other lands because the Sacred House of God is in it, and because it is the most beloved of lands to His Messenger. The relative clause is an attribute of "the Lord." This is how the majority read it. Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Mas'ud read ﴿which He has made sacred﴾ with the relative clause as an attribute of "the city." The meaning of "made sacred" is: made it a sanctuary (haram) and a safe place, where no blood is shed, no one is wronged, its game is not hunted, and its grass is not cut. ﴿And to Him belongs everything﴾ among things, in creation, ownership, and disposal; that is, everything belongs to God. ﴿And I have been commanded to be among the Muslims﴾, that is: those who submit to God's command and surrender to Him in obedience, carrying out His order and avoiding His prohibition. By His saying "that I be" is meant: that I remain steadfast in what I am upon.

﴿And to recite the Qur'an﴾: that is, that I persist in its recitation and be constant in it.

It has been said: the intended meaning of "reciting the Qur'an" here is nothing other than reciting the call to faith, but the first view is preferable. ﴿Whoever is guided, he is only guided for his own soul﴾, because the benefit of that returns to him. That is, whoever is guided in general, or whoever is guided by what I recite to him and acts upon what it contains of faith. The first view is preferable. ﴿Whoever is guided, he is only guided for his own soul﴾, because the benefit of that returns to him. That is, whoever is guided in general, or whoever is guided by what I recite to him and acts upon what it contains of faith in God and the practice of His laws.

Al-Jumhur (the majority of reciters) read "wa-an atluwa" with the waw affixed after the lam, as being from tilawah (recitation), which is reading, or from tilw, which is following.

ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud) read "wa-ani-tlu" with the waw omitted, as an imperative addressed to him (ﷺ). Al-Farrāʾ (al-Farra') gave this reading that interpretation.

Al-Nahhas (al-Nahhas) said: "We do not know of anyone who read this reading, and it contradicts all the copies of the Qur'an." ﴿And whoever goes astray, say: I am only one of the warners﴾. That is: whoever goes astray through disbelief and turns away from guidance, say to him: I am only one of the warners, and I have fulfilled that by conveying it to you, and there is nothing incumbent upon me other than that.

It has been said: the answer is omitted, meaning: then the burden of his straying falls upon him, and "I am only one of the warners" has been placed in its position because it is like the cause for it.

﴿And say: Praise belongs to God﴾ for His blessings which He has bestowed upon me, of prophethood, knowledge and other than that. His saying: ﴿He will show you His signs, and you will recognize them﴾ is among what the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to say. That is: God will show you His signs in your own selves and in others, and you will recognize them, that is, you will recognize His signs and the proofs of His power and His oneness. This recognition does not benefit the disbelievers, because they recognized them at a time when faith is no longer accepted from them, and that is at the moment of the presence of death.

Then He concluded the surah with His saying: ﴿And your Lord is not unaware of what you do﴾. This is a statement from Him, glorified is He, not included within the speech which He commanded the Prophet (ﷺ) to say, and in it is intense warning and a great threat.

Ahl al-Madina, al-Sham and Hafs from ʿAsim read "taʿmalūna" with the second person (taʾ), as an address. The rest read it with the third person (yāʾ).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying ﴿dākhirīn﴾, that he said: "ṣāghirīn" (humbled).

These same related from him, regarding His saying ﴿And you see the mountains, you think them solid﴾, that he said: "qāʾimah" (standing). ﴿The handiwork of God, who perfected everything﴾, he said: "aḥkama" (made firm).

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also related from him, regarding His saying ﴿The handiwork of God, who perfected everything﴾, he said: "He made everything He created good and firm."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh related from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "﴿Whoever comes with a good deed, for him is better than it﴾, he said: it is 'There is no god but God'. ﴿And whoever comes with an evil deed, their faces will be thrown into the Fire﴾, he said: it is shirk (associating partners with God)." And if this is authentically from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), then turning to it in interpreting the speech of God, glorified is He, is necessary, and it is understood to mean: whoever says "There is no god but God" in its truth and what is due to it, then every act of obedience enters under that. And what al-Hakim in al-Kuna (al-Kuna) related from Safwan ibn ʿAssal supports this, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, faith and shirk will come kneeling before God, glorified is He. God will say to faith: Go, you and your people, to Paradise. And He will say to shirk: Go, you and your people, to the Fire."

﴿Whoever comes with a good deed, for him is better than it﴾, meaning His saying: "There is no god but God". ﴿And whoever comes with an evil deed﴾, meaning shirk, ﴿their faces will be thrown into the Fire﴾."

Ibn Mardawayh related from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah and Anas, and the like of it, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Daylami related from Kaʿb ibn ʿUjrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever comes with a good deed, meaning the testimony that there is no god but God, ﴿for him is better than it﴾, meaning by the good, Paradise. ﴿And whoever comes with an evil deed﴾, meaning shirk, ﴿their faces will be thrown into the Fire﴾." And he said: "This one saves, and this one destroys."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wal-Sifat, and al-Kharaʾiti in Makarim al-Akhlaq, related from Ibn Masʿud: ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed﴾, he said: "There is no god but God." ﴿And whoever comes with an evil deed﴾, he said: "with shirk."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related the like of this from Ibn ʿAbbas.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related regarding ﴿for him is better than it﴾, that he said: "For him there is good from it," meaning from its direction.

Ibn Abi Hatim also related from him, ﴿for him is better than it﴾, he said: "reward." He also related from him, that he said: "The town is Makkah."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 27, verse 83–93 (part 1 of 2):

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned a brief outline of the terrors of the Day of Resurrection, and said: ﴿And on the day We gather from every nation a crowd﴾. The governing element of the adverbial phrase (al-zarf) is a verb that has been omitted, and it is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-hashr means gathering.

It has been said: what is meant by this gathering is the gathering of punishment (hashr al-ʿadhab), after the general gathering that encompasses all of creation. Min (from) here denotes the starting point (li-ibtida' al-ghayah). Al-fawj is a group, like al-zumrah (a company). Min in ﴿of those who deny Our signs﴾ is explanatory (bayaniyyah). ﴿Then they are driven on﴾ means their first is held back until their last joins them. Its verification has already been discussed fully in this surah. It has also been said that its meaning is: they are pushed back. From this is the saying of al-Shammakh:

*"How many a host, a mighty army, have we held back"*

The meaning of the verse is: Mention, O Muhammad, a day when We will gather from every nation of the nations a group who denied Our signs; then, at that gathering, their first will be turned back upon their last, or they will be pushed; that is, make this known to them, or explain it to them, as a warning and a frightening.

﴿Until, when they arrive﴾ at the place of reckoning, God says to them, as rebuke and reproach: ﴿Did you deny My signs﴾ which I sent down upon My messengers and commanded them to convey to you, ﴿while you did not encompass them in knowledge﴾? Rather, you denied them at the very outset, being ignorant of them, not looking into them, nor reasoning about their soundness or falsehood, out of rebellion, obstinacy, and audacity against God and His messengers. In this there is further reproach and rebuke, because whoever denies something without having encompassed it in knowledge has, in his denial, lied, and has proclaimed his own ignorance, unfairness, bad understanding, and deficiency of comprehension. Of this kind is whoever takes it upon himself to disparage one of the religious sciences (al-ʿulum al-shariʿyyah), or a science that is a prerequisite of them and a means by which one reaches them, and which yields greater insight into understanding them and grasping their meanings, such as all the sciences of the Arabic language, which are twelve sciences, and the science of usul al-fiqh (principles of jurisprudence), by which one arrives at deriving the legal rulings from their detailed evidences, along with its inclusion of the general rules of the language. Likewise every science that is of further benefit in understanding the Book of God and the Sunnah of His Messenger. Such a person has proclaimed with the loudest voice that he is ignorant, a disputer in falsehood, a slanderer of the religious sciences, deserving that some calamity of the calamities of punishment should befall him, which will restrain him from his ignorance and error and from his slander of what he does not know, nor has knowledge of, nor encompasses its reality, until he becomes a lesson to others and an admonition by which the likes of him are warned, namely the weak-minded, the frail in religion, the rabble of those who falsely and deceitfully clothe themselves in knowledge.

In His saying ﴿Or what were you doing﴾, the particle am (or) is the disjunctive one (al-munqatiʿah). The meaning is: or what was it that you were doing that occupied you from looking into them and reflecting on their meanings? This interrogation is by way of rebuke for them.

﴿And the word will come into effect against them﴾: its explanation has already been given shortly before.
